note: The worksheet→activity coverage plan. One entry per new instrument; numbers continue after the 204 rebuild rows. Read by scripts/new-activity.js and scripts/audit-activity-coverage.js.

activities.title: The Hopscotch Court
activities.teaches: Name the number before, after and between, and count backward from 10 to 1.
activities.invention: THE HOPPER THAT HAS TO TURN AROUND. A hopscotch court of ten numbered squares (1–10; 11–20 on a second court above it in the to-20 setting) with one library animal standing on a square, facing forward (toward bigger numbers). A sign card above the court shows the task by icon only: an arrow forward = the number after, an arrow back = the number before, two flags on two squares = the number between them (the hopper then stands on the lower flag). The child taps the square where the hopper must land. Facing is physical: tapping a square BEHIND a forward-facing hopper makes it bump in place (a small shake, its facing arrow flashes) — the child must first tap the hopper to TURN it round, so 'before' is a turn plus one hop. A tap two squares away makes it hop there and leave a dotted trail of two arcs, so 'one before / one after' is seen as ONE hop, not two. Right: it lands, the square gets a chalk mark, bubble 'Yes — 6 comes before 7!'. Miss 1: the trail and the facing arrow stay lit; miss 2: the start square and the target square pulse. Countdown setting: every square is blank except the start (10, 12, 15 or 20); the hopper already faces back; the child hops square by square, choosing each landing number from a numeral strip under the court (the strip is reshuffled every hop), and the chosen numeral is stamped on the square — so the backward sequence is SAID by the child, never read. A wrong numeral bounces off; miss 2 reads the stamped run so far. The run ends on 1 and a library rocket (space/rocket) lifts off from square 1 — never 0.
activities.misconception: Confusing before with after (giving n+1 for "before"), giving n−2 / n+2, and being unable to count backward without restarting from 1.
activities.pictures: the hopper, one per round set, CSS-mirrored for the turn: farm-animals/rabbit, pets/frog, forest-creatures/squirrel, farm-animals/duck, animals/cat; space/rocket for the countdown finish; court, sign card, flags and trail drawn as apparatus
activities.settings: Range: up to 10 / up to 20 · Task: before–after–between mixed / countdown only
activities.rounds: Mixed: 9 rounds, ≥ 3 before, ≥ 3 after, ≥ 2 between; the hopper's start spread across the court (on an end square in ≤ 2 rounds; 'before 1' and 'after 10/20' never asked); between-flags are always two apart. Countdown: 8 runs (to 10: starts 10, 9, 8, 7 with ≥ 5 hops each; to 20: 20, 15, 12, 11 …). The answer is a square on a fixed court — its position IS the number, which is the skill, not a tell; the countdown numeral strip is reshuffled every hop so the right numeral has no fixed place. Order-only reshuffle per pass.
activities.distinct_from: Peek Path (#2) and Constellation Thread (#3) only go forward and hide the run-up; the Number Elevator (#19) is magnitude. This is the first instrument where DIRECTION is the content.
activities.risk: At 360 a row of ten squares is < 34 px: on phones each court wraps into two left-to-right rows of five (reading order, as on a hundreds chart) with squares ≥ 44 px, and the hop from 5 to 6 draws its arc down to the next row. The mirrored hopper must face the way it hops (check per noun).

activities.title: The Tally Fence
activities.teaches: Show a count with tally marks grouped in fives, and read a tally as fives and ones.
activities.invention: THE FENCE THAT LATCHES AT FIVE. Make mode: a field of identical library animals (one noun per round) waits beside an empty fence line. Tapping an animal walks it through the gate into the pen and drives one upright post into the fence. After four uprights the gate stands open and the next post arrives lying FLAT above the gap: the child must drag it diagonally across the four uprights to latch the bay (it snaps from top-left to bottom-right). If the child taps another animal instead, the gap is still open: that animal trots through and straight back out to the field, and no post is added — a fifth upright cannot be made. A latched bay tints slightly as one 'five'; the next post starts a new bay. When the field is empty the child types how many on the keypad. Read mode: a finished fence (no animals) is shown and the child types the number it shows. Miss 1: the latched bays pulse one after another with '5, 10, 15' rising above them; miss 2: every post gets a small numeral under it. Right: the gate swings shut and that many identical animals settle in the pen.
activities.misconception: Drawing five (or six) upright strokes before crossing, and counting every stroke one by one instead of reading a closed bundle as five.
activities.pictures: farm-animals/sheep, cow, pig, goat, horse, duck (identical instances, one noun per round); fence, posts and latch drawn as apparatus
activities.settings: Mode: make the tally / read the tally · Numbers up to 10 / up to 20
activities.rounds: Make: 9 rounds n = 3–10 (to 10) or 6–20 (to 20), including 4 (one before the latch), 5, 10 and 15 exactly; read: 9 fences with distinct n (never 0); keypad answers in both modes so there is no answer position; order-only reshuffle per pass.
activities.distinct_from: Counting Table / Treat Box count with the picture set itself; no instrument represents a count with a SYMBOL bundle. Not the Ten-Shelf (tens of egg cups): the five-latch is a different grouping and a written-mark representation.
activities.risk: None structural; post-and-latch geometry is inline SVG apparatus.

activities.title: The Bus Queue
activities.teaches: Find the 1st to 10th thing in a line, counting from the front — whichever end the front is.
activities.invention: THE DOOR THAT COUNTS FROM ITSELF. A queue of up to ten different library animals waits at a bus stop; the library bus stands at the front, its door at the left in some rounds and at the right in others. An ordinal ticket (3rd — numeral plus the locale's ordinal mark) waits on the kerb; the child drags it onto ONE animal (a ticket can only rest on a single animal). The door opens and the queue boards one at a time from the door end, each animal getting a lit place badge 1st, 2nd, 3rd … as it steps in; boarding stops at the ticket holder, who gets the big badge. If the child counted from the far end, boarding visibly starts at the door, not where they began, and stops on a different animal — the ticket holder is left on the kerb, shaking its ticket. If the child took 'the 3rd' as 'three of them', the badges still show only one '3rd'. Name-the-place mode: one animal holds a star; the child taps its place on a fixed row of ordinal keys 1st–10th. Race face (absorbed Bakery Queue): the same queue stands behind a drawn finish ribbon, which plays the door's role — the runner nearest the ribbon is 1st. Miss 1: the door end pulses and a dotted arrow runs from it along the queue; miss 2: the badges appear on every animal up to the answer. Right: the bus pulls away with the ticket holder in the window.
activities.misconception: Counting from the wrong end, and treating "3rd" as "three of them" (taking the first three).
activities.pictures: vehicles/bus at the front (CSS-mirrored so its door faces the queue); one animal of each kind per queue so every place is nameable: animals, farm-animals, zoo-animals, forest-creatures (e.g. cat, dog, pig, cow, duck, sheep, fox, zebra, panda, rabbit); finish ribbon, ticket and keys drawn as apparatus
activities.settings: Mode: find the place / name the place · Front: always left / either end · Line: bus stop / finish ribbon (race face)
activities.rounds: 9 rounds per mode, ordinals 1st–10th each used, the target ordinal never the same as its distance from the far end except when the queue is odd-length and target is the middle (allowed once); door side balanced 50/50 in either-end mode; the picked animal's screen position spread so left/right half ≤ 60 %.
activities.distinct_from: No existing activity teaches ordinals; distinct from Roll Book / Treat Box (cardinal count-out) because the answer is ONE item at a position, and the door end flips.
activities.risk: Ordinal marks are locale grammar and live only on the ticket and the keys: en 1st/2nd/3rd, de/da/no/fi 1./2./3., fr 1er/2e/3e, es 1.º, pt/it 1º, nl 1e/2e, sv 1:a/2:a/3:e — the native panel authors the glyph set and the task line (fi: the ordinal's case in the sentence).
absorbed: grade 1 "The Bakery Queue" (ordinal-queue): Ordinal numbers name a place in a line counted from the front: 1st, 2nd, 3rd ... — A QUEUE AT A DOOR: library animals stand in a line facing a shop door (the flag). The child taps the animal in the asked place (or drags the ordinal tag onto it); when the tag is placed, the animals in front step forward one by one, each wearing its place tag, and the door opens for the 1st. A "turn around" setting puts the door on the other side so the count starts from the other end. The race face: runners at different distances from a finish line; the nearest is 1st.

activities.title: The Class Photo Risers
activities.teaches: Put 3 to 5 objects in order from smallest to biggest (or shortest to tallest) by comparing them directly.
activities.invention: THE HEADLINE THAT MUST CLIMB. A photographer's riser stand: 3–5 empty spots on one level floor line and a faint dashed 'headline' rising from the first spot to the last. A tray holds ONE library picture at 3–5 sizes (sizes measured from the ink box, ≥ 18 % apart). The child drags each picture onto a spot; dropped, it stands on the floor line, so tops are compared from one baseline. When every spot is full the child taps the camera: each neighbour pair that breaks the climb flashes and the two lean toward each other ('swap us'); tapping the pair swaps them. Miss 2: faint height ticks appear behind the row. Right: the camera flashes and the photo slides into a small album strip above the stand. 'Biggest first' rounds turn the headline downhill.
activities.misconception: Ordering only the two extremes and dropping the middle ones anywhere; judging by width instead of height.
activities.pictures: one noun per round, uniformly scaled: height rounds use tall nouns — zoo-animals/giraffe, vegetables/carrot, christmas/candle, kitchen-tools/bottle, classroom/pencil, flowers/sunflower, space/rocket, beach/lighthouse, tools/ladder; size rounds use fruits/apple, toys/ball, farm-animals/pig, bakery/cupcake
activities.settings: Pictures: 3 / 4 / 5 · Order: smallest (shortest) first / biggest (tallest) first
activities.rounds: 9 rounds per count; sizes ≥ 18 % apart; the tray order is never already sorted or reverse-sorted, and the biggest picture appears in every tray position across a pass; height and size rounds alternate; order-only reshuffle.
activities.distinct_from: Not the Nesting Pots (#22: orders NUMERALS, sizes hidden); not the Faraway Shelf (grade 1: indirect length against a cord). Here the size is the visible attribute and the order is built and checked neighbour by neighbour.
activities.risk: Library pictures have different whitespace: heights must be measured from the INK box (the maze program already does this).

activities.title: The Market Scale
activities.teaches: Compare two objects by weight and tell which is heavier and which is lighter — and that a bigger thing is not always heavier.
activities.invention: THE PAN THAT GOES DOWN. A two-pan balance stands level and empty. Two library things wait on the counter, drawn at their REAL relative sizes (the pillow much bigger than the hammer), so size is visible and is the lure. The task line asks 'Which is heavier?' (or lighter) and the left pan carries a down-arrow (or up-arrow) icon. The child drags the one they choose onto the arrow pan; the other slides onto the right pan and the beam tips slowly to the truth, its angle growing with the real weight ratio. Right: the arrow pan sinks (or rises) as predicted and the bubble says 'Yes — the hammer is heavier than the pillow!'. Wrong: the beam tips against the arrow, plain to see; the child then swaps the two (drag either one across) so the round always ends with the truth on the scale — miss 2 makes the lower pan glow before the swap. Free play: any two things from a shelf can be weighed.
activities.misconception: Bigger means heavier.
activities.pictures: big-but-light: around-the-house/pillow, cushion; toys/balloon, ball, kite; easter/feather; clothing/hat. Small-but-heavy: tools/hammer, around-the-house/iron, key, beach/rock, kitchen-tools/pot, at-the-supermarket/can. Ordinary: fruits/apple, watermelon; vegetables/pumpkin, potato. A curated weight table (grams, hand-checked) for every noun used.
activities.settings: Ask: heavier / lighter / both · Big-but-light rounds: some / many
activities.rounds: 9 rounds, ≥ 3 big-but-light pairs and ≥ 2 small-but-heavy ones; weight ratio ≥ 3:1 so the answer is unambiguous from real life; the heavier thing is the LEFT counter picture in 40–60 % of rounds and the bigger-on-screen one in ≤ 50 %, so neither side nor size is a shortcut; heavier and lighter questions alternate in 'both'.
activities.distinct_from: Bramble (capacity) and Comparing Length cover the other K.MD.A.2 attributes; nothing weighs.
activities.risk: Needs a hand-checked weight table for ~60 library nouns (one reviewer pass); feather / balloon may be missing from the library — choose from what exists.

activities.title: The Sleeps Calendar
activities.teaches: Know the days of the week in order, what comes before and after today, and that the week repeats.
activities.invention: THE NIGHT BETWEEN EVERY DAY. Seven day cards (twelve month cards in the year setting) lie in a closed loop with a small moon — one sleep — on the rail between each pair of neighbours, so the last day of the week is joined to the first by one moon exactly like every other pair. Some cards are blank; the matching cards wait in a tray in shuffled order. The child drags a card onto a blank. Right: it clicks in and the moons on both sides of it light. Wrong: it bounces back and the moons from the nearest filled card to the blank light and pulse, so the child counts the sleeps from a known day; miss 2: the right card in the tray lifts a little. Yesterday–today–tomorrow mode: the full loop is shown with a library sun (weather/sunny) resting on today; the task line asks for tomorrow or yesterday (with a forward/back arrow icon) and the child drags the sun along the rail — it steps moon by moon, and stopping two moons away leaves both moons lit. Year setting: the same loop holds the twelve months; 'the month before/after' moves the sun one step. Right: the loop gives one slow turn so the wrap-around is felt.
activities.misconception: Treating the week as a line that ends; mixing the order of the middle days.
activities.pictures: weather/sunny as the today marker; cards, rail and moons drawn as apparatus; day and month names are the content
activities.settings: Ring: the week / the year (months) · Task: fill the blanks (2 or 4) / yesterday–today–tomorrow (one step back or forward)
activities.rounds: 9 per ring × task. Week start per locale (Monday; en follows en-US Sunday — the worksheet locale rule). Blanks spread so the wrap-around (last→first) is crossed in ≥ 3 rounds; today stands on every weekday across a pass and on the first or last day in ≥ 2 rounds so tomorrow/yesterday crosses the wrap; one right card per blank; tray order shuffled.
activities.distinct_from: No calendar activity exists.
activities.risk: Day/month spelling and capitalisation per locale (lowercase in fr/es/it/pt/nl/sv/da/no/fi); full names on cards, never abbreviations — card width set from the longest locale name (fi 'keskiviikko', de 'Donnerstag'). Seasons are NOT in this instrument (→ #238 season-wheel).
absorbed: grade 1 "The Year Ring" (year-ring): Days of the week and months of the year go round in order; yesterday is one step back, tomorrow one step forward; months belong to seasons. — A RING THAT TURNS: a ring of 7 day-beads (or 12 month-beads) with a "today" window. The child turns the ring with a drag; it clicks one bead at a time. Yesterday/tomorrow: the child turns to today and moves one click back or forward. Months in order: loose month beads must be threaded onto the ring after the one before; a bead in the wrong place will not close the ring. Seasons: arcs of the ring are painted with the season colours and the child drops months on the arc (hemisphere set per locale).

activities.title: The Toy Box Room
activities.teaches: Use position words — on, under, beside, in front of, behind, inside, outside, left and right — to place and find objects.
activities.invention: THE TOY THAT SETTLES WHERE THE WORD SAYS. One big open crate on four short legs stands in the middle of a room floor drawn in gentle perspective with three lanes: a back lane (behind), the crate's lane, and a front lane (in front of); a faint seam down the floor marks left and right. A library toy waits in a corner; the task line names one position word with a small icon (crate + dot). The child drags the toy anywhere and lets go: it settles into the nearest zone — on the lid → ON, into the open top → INSIDE (half hidden by the rim), between the legs → UNDER, the floor at the crate's side → BESIDE, the back lane → BEHIND (partly hidden by the crate), the front lane → IN FRONT OF; in the inside/outside rounds the crate is replaced by a drawn fence pen and the far floor is OUTSIDE. The toy only ever rests in one zone. Wrong: it stays where it settled and a ghost of it appears in the asked zone with a dotted arrow from the crate; miss 2: the asked zone glows. Find mode: three different toys already sit in three zones and the child taps the one the word names. Left/right rounds: the room is seen from the child's side, with two library hands (body-parts/hand, one CSS-mirrored) lying on the floor edges, so left and right are the child's own. Right: the toy gives a small hop and the crate creaks.
activities.misconception: Confusing on/in, under/behind, and left/right (mirror reversal).
activities.pictures: toys/ball, car, doll, blocks, robot, dinosaur, train; pets/cat, dog as movers (one per round); body-parts/hand (mirrored for the other hand); crate, fence pen and room lanes drawn as apparatus
activities.settings: Words: on–under–beside–inside–outside / left–right–front–behind · Mode: place it / find it
activities.rounds: 9 rounds per word set, every word used at least once and none three times running; in find mode the three toys' screen positions rotate so the answer is left/middle/right a third of the time each; one right answer because the crate (or pen) is the single reference.
activities.distinct_from: The Parking Tower (above / below / between on floors) remains for vertical order; this covers the in-room words it lacks.
activities.risk: Words live only in the task line, never on the apparatus. Native check that each zone matches the locale's word: de auf/unter/neben/in/vor/hinter, fr sur/sous/à côté de/dans/devant/derrière, fi postpositions (päällä, alla, vieressä, sisällä, edessä, takana, ulkopuolella). 'Behind' must stay legible: the toy is drawn partly hidden, never fully.

activities.title: The Geoboard Band
activities.teaches: Build named 2D shapes (triangle, square, rectangle, hexagon) by joining corners with straight sides.
activities.invention: THE BAND THAT SNAPS FROM PEG TO PEG. A pegboard (4×4 or 5×5 pegs) and one rubber band. The child taps a first peg, then each next peg: the band stretches to it as a straight side; tapping the first peg again closes the shape. Corners light only where the band really turns (three pegs in a line make one straight side, not a corner), and each straight side glows. The board then shows what was made: a corner dot and a side tick for every part, and the band stays put — if the task asked for a triangle and the child made four corners, the four lit corners are plain. A band that would cross itself snags (a small knot mark) and will not close. Right: the band twangs, the inside fills with colour and the shape slides onto a little shelf above the board, so the round's earlier shapes stay visible. Miss 1: the bubble counts what was made ('4 corners — a triangle has 3'); miss 2: the asked shape's corner count appears as dots beside the task line. 'A different way' rounds refuse a shape congruent to one already on the shelf (any turn or flip), so a triangle that does not point up, or a turned square, is needed. A square is accepted for 'rectangle' (it is one); for 'square', unequal sides show their peg-counts.
activities.misconception: Thinking a shape is defined by its look (a "triangle" must point up) rather than by its sides and corners; leaving shapes open.
activities.pictures: none (pegboard and band drawn as apparatus)
activities.settings: Shapes: triangle–square–rectangle / plus pentagon–hexagon · Board: 4×4 / 5×5
activities.rounds: 9 rounds; the asked shape never repeats twice in a row; any correct construction is accepted (many right constructions, one right property), ≥ 2 'a different way' rounds per pass; free play beside the task names the corners and sides of anything made.
activities.distinct_from: Count the Sides / Pip's Museum name existing shapes; Mim's Glow Workshop composes from pieces; nothing builds a shape from sides.
activities.risk: Pentagon and hexagon only on 5×5. 'A different way' needs a lattice-polygon congruence test (rotations/reflections of the vertex list). Peg tap targets ≥ 44 px at 360 → the 5×5 board is ≥ 260 px.

activities.title: The Alphabet Lockers
activities.teaches: Know the order of the alphabet (before, after, between), fill gaps, and put words in ABC order by the first letter and, when first letters match, by the second.
activities.invention: THE LOCKER THAT ONLY SHUTS BETWEEN ITS NEIGHBOURS. A corridor of lockers runs the locale alphabet as ONE snake (rows of 7–10 at 704, of 5–6 at 360; a bend arrow joins row ends so adjacency is never broken). Closed doors show their letter; 3 or 6 doors stand open and empty. Letter tiles wait in a tray. Drag a tile into an open locker: if it is the letter between the two closed neighbours, the door swings shut with a click and the latch lights. Miss 1: the tile bounces back and the two neighbouring doors light. Miss 2: the doors from the nearest closed letter open one by one along the corridor, ending on the empty locker (the order walks itself to the gap). Success: when every door is shut, a light runs the whole corridor A→Z (Å/Ä/Ö, Æ/Ø/Å, Ñ included). WORD MODE (G1-245/262–264): 4–6 picture-word cards; each card dropped on the corridor slides to the locker of its FIRST letter and hangs there; when two cards share a locker, that locker opens into a small second corridor and the two slide again to their SECOND letters. A card is accepted only at its own locker (a card dropped by last letter or by length slides off). Finally the cards drop into the answer row in corridor order — the order is read off the corridor, never guessed. DOT-HOP mode (K-309, G1-426): the closed doors are tapped in order to light the corridor; a skipped letter keeps its door dark. Free play: run a finger along the doors and they open in turn.
activities.misconception: Knowing the alphabet as one sung blob ("elemenopee") instead of positions between neighbours; in word mode ordering by length, by last letter, or giving up when two words start alike.
activities.pictures: none (lockers and letters are apparatus and content)
activities.settings: Mode: fill the gaps / hop in order / words by 1st letter / words by 2nd letter · Letters: capitals / lowercase · Gaps: 3 / 6
activities.rounds: Letters: 9 rounds; every third of the alphabet gets a gap each round; the locale-specific letters (Å Ä Ö / Æ Ø Å / Ñ) are gaps in ≥ 2 rounds; tray shuffled so each tile visits every tray slot across a pass. Words: 9 sets of 4–6 library picture words (labels from image-vocabulary.js, lower-cased per locale), each 2nd-letter set has exactly one pair sharing a first letter; one right order.
activities.distinct_from: No alphabet-order activity exists (the alphabet maze is a deck screen).
activities.risk: Per-locale collation is the content: sv/fi …XYZÅÄÖ, da/no …XYZÆØÅ, de ä=a ö=o ü=u ß=ss (DIN 5007-1), es ñ after n (ch/ll not separate since 2010), nl ij sorted as i+j. Word mode refuses labels whose first letter is ambiguous in that locale (nl ij-words) — one reviewer per locale.
absorbed: grade 1 "The ABC Rail" (abc-rail): Put words in alphabetical order by the first letter, and by the second letter when the first letters are the same. — A RAIL WITH LETTER STOPS: the locale alphabet runs along a rail (26, or 29 with å ä ö / æ ø å). Word cards hang on hooks; dragging a card to the rail makes its hook slide to the stop of its FIRST letter. When two cards land on the same stop, that stop opens into a small second rail for the second letter and the cards slide again. When all cards hang, they drop into the answer row in rail order and the child confirms. A card hung by the last letter or by length will not slide to that stop.

activities.title: The Sound Slide
activities.teaches: Segment a spoken word into its sounds, one token per sound, count the sounds, and see that two letters can make one sound.
activities.invention: THE TRAY THAT GROWS ITS WALLS. A library picture over ONE long open tray; a pile of round tokens below. The child says the word slowly and slides tokens up into the tray, one per sound; each token drops a thin wall behind it, so the tray becomes boxes as the child goes — the number of boxes is the child's answer, never shown in advance. Check: the boxes flip to show the spelling. Right: a box holding two letters for one sound (en sh/ck/ch, de sch/ch, nl ng/ch, fr ou/ch, sv sj/ng…) shows them under ONE curve, and the boxes light left to right. Miss 1, too many (one token per LETTER for "ship"): the two letters join under one curve and the extra token is pushed back out to the pile, its wall dissolving. Miss 1, too few: a box holding two sounds cracks in two and an empty box opens. Miss 2: the walls are pre-drawn and the child refills them. COUNT setting (K-329): after the check the boxes show dots, never letters. FIRST-SOUND-GIVEN setting (K-330): the first token and its letters are already in place.
activities.misconception: One sound per letter (four sounds for "ship"), and blending two sounds into one.
activities.pictures: animals, farm-animals, kitchen-tools, classroom, fruits, toys — nouns in approved-words-<locale>.json, each with a NEW hand-authored phoneme split (~20 words × 11 locales).
activities.settings: Words: 3 sounds / 3–4 sounds with digraphs · Show: letters after check / count only
activities.rounds: 9 words per pass from the authored per-locale list: 3 three-sound words, 3 four-sound words, 3 words with a two-letter-one-sound grapheme (setting 2 only); never more than half the pass with letters = sounds; one right count.
activities.distinct_from: Coco's Sound Boxes asks where a sound sits; the CVC Builder spells. This is segmentation and counting.
activities.risk: No phoneme data exists in the repo: each locale needs a split table checked by the native reviewer (fi/es/it nearly 1:1; en/fr/da/nl/de digraph-heavy; da uses the K-1 orthographic policy pool). Audio is a bonus only.

activities.title: The Bead Rail
activities.teaches: Count the syllables in a picture word by beating them, and sort pictures by syllable count.
activities.invention: THE BEAD RAIL THAT SPLITS THE WORD. A big library picture on a stand; under it an empty bead rail; beside it a round beat pad. The child says the word and taps the pad once per syllable — each tap drops a bead onto the rail with a small bounce (tapping a bead on the rail removes it). Check: the picture's written word (the gated split from approved-words-<locale>.json) slides down and breaks into its syllables, one syllable landing over each bead. Right: every bead wears a syllable and the beads ripple left to right. Miss 1: a bead with no syllable sits dark and rolls off the end, or a syllable with no bead hangs over an empty dip — the child sees which part was not beaten. Miss 2: the word lies over the rail already split with dots between syllables and the child beats again. SORT MODE (K-234): three or four shelves carrying 1, 2, 3, 4 beads (no numerals); the child drags each picture to a shelf and the shelf lays the split word along its beads — a 3-syllable word on the 2-bead shelf leaves one syllable hanging off the end and slides back.
activities.misconception: Counting letters or sounds instead of syllables; counting the first beat only.
activities.pictures: animals, farm-animals, fruits, vegetables, vehicles, toys, clothing — ONLY nouns present in approved-words-<locale>.json (gated splits); da: the policy_managed:false pool only.
activities.settings: Mode: beat and count / sort to shelves · Syllables: 1–3 / 1–4
activities.rounds: 9 words per pass, ≥ 2 of each count (1–3 or 1–4); every pass includes ≥ 2 length lures (a long 1-syllable word and a short multi-syllable word) so letter-counting fails visibly; shelf order fixed 1-2-3-4 (the count is the content); one right count.
activities.distinct_from: The Syllable Builder blends given syllables into a word; this is the other direction (split and count).
activities.risk: fr: the mute-e ruling is open (§20.9) — the fr pool excludes words ending in a mute e until it is ruled; sv uses the school-split carve-out (§A.13.57). Distinct from the syllable-splitter tool only because the rail checks the child's count — keep the pad visually unlike the tool's drum. Legible without sound: the child says the word, the reveal is written.

activities.title: The Vowel Keystone
activities.teaches: Tell vowels from consonants, and see that every word needs a vowel.
activities.invention: THE ARCH THAT HOLDS ONLY ON A VOWEL. A stream with three stone arches, each spelling a CVC picture word with its middle stone missing (c _ t under a library cat). Letter stones lie on the bank; two carts wait: the KEYSTONE cart (arched top) and the WALL cart (flat top). The child loads each stone into a cart. Check: the carts roll onto the bridge row; every stone in the keystone cart is tried in the middle of the next arch — a vowel locks the arch and it rises (a real or a nonsense word, both stand); a consonant makes that arch sag and the stone drops back to the bank. Then any vowel hiding in the wall cart pops up out of it and glows. Miss 1: only the wrong stones return to the bank. Miss 2: vowels on the bank shimmer when held over an arch gap. Success: all arches stand and the picture animal walks across. FIX-THE-ARCH mode: the child drags the one stone that makes the picture's word.
activities.misconception: Thinking any letter can go anywhere; not knowing which letters are vowels (y as a vowel in sv/da/no/fi; å ä ö æ ø as vowels).
activities.pictures: one library picture per CVC arch word (approved-words-<locale>.json)
activities.settings: Mode: load the carts / fix the arches · Vowels: core (a e i o u + locale core) / full locale set (sv/da/no/fi y; å ä ö æ ø; de ä ö ü; accented forms count as the same vowel)
activities.rounds: 9 rounds of 6–8 stones with 2–4 vowels; stone order shuffled; the carts swap sides every other round (cart SHAPE, not side, is the cue); one right sort.
activities.distinct_from: No vowel-class activity exists; the CVC Builder spells words but never names vowels as a group.
activities.risk: Per-locale vowel set authored by the reviewer; en y excluded from the core setting. Arch words from approved-words-<locale>.json CVC entries only (fi/it/es CVC words are rare — CVCV allowed with the middle vowel missing).

activities.title: The Article Caps
activities.teaches: Choose the right article for a noun (en: a or an by the first sound; gendered locales: the article that matches the noun's gender).
activities.invention: THE CAP THAT FITS ITS NOUN. Library pictures stand bare-headed; the locale's article caps hang on pegs (en a · an; de der · die · das; fr le · la · l'; es el · la; it il · lo · la · l'; pt o · a; nl de · het; sv en · ett; da en · et; no en · ei · et; indefinite setting: de ein · eine, fr un · une, es un · una, it un · uno · una · un', pt um · uma). Drag a cap onto a picture: it settles and the picture's word is written under it with the cap as its first word ("ett äpple"). Right: the phrase glows and the cap clicks. en: the "an" cap carries a little bridge that only seats on a word whose first SOUND is a vowel (an umbrella seats; a uniform does not), so the rule is the cap's shape. Miss 1: the cap tips off and the WRITTEN phrase with the right article appears faded under the picture for two seconds (sound off still teaches). Miss 2: the right cap's peg glows. Free play: try every cap and read each phrase. GARAGE mode (absorbed G1 article garages, G1-292): word-only cards (no picture) are sorted under the article caps as columns.
activities.misconception: en: choosing by the first LETTER instead of the first sound; gendered: matching by meaning (a "female" thing) instead of the word's gender.
activities.pictures: Any colour theme; nouns + gender from image-vocabulary.js (per-locale gender authority §A.13.58); en lure pairs available: umbrella / uniform (accessories, clothing), apple, orange, owl, airplane. easter/egg refused (a decorated Easter egg).
activities.settings: Pictures: 4 / 8 per round · Articles: indefinite / definite
activities.rounds: 9 rounds of 4 (or 8) pictures; each article ≤ 40 % of answers per pass; it/fr ≥ 2 elision nouns (l') per pass; it ≥ 1 lo/uno noun (s+consonant, z); es nouns with stressed initial a- (águila) refused; one right article per noun.
activities.distinct_from: No article activity exists; Daisy's Plate Stack is number (plural), not article choice.
activities.risk: fi has no articles → refused in fi (recorded). sv/da/no definite = suffix → indefinite only there. no: bokmål allows en for feminine nouns — feminine nouns refused (or both accepted, reviewer call). nl "een" is gender-blind → nl definite de/het only.
absorbed: grade 1 "The Article Garages" (article-garages): Each noun takes its article: a/an (en), der/die/das (de), en/ett (sv), un/une (fr) ... — GARAGES WITH DOORS: two or three garages carry the article words on their doors (the content). Noun cars (a picture plus its word) drive in when dragged to a door; on parking, the plate prints the whole phrase ("ett äpple") and the car is used in a little sentence above the garage. A car in the wrong garage stalls in the doorway and the door shows the sound / ending clue (en: the word begins with a vowel sound; de/sv: no visible clue - the garage plays the phrase with the right article and the child tries again).

activities.title: The Word Ribbon
activities.teaches: Trace and then write a whole word left to right, and a short sentence with a finger-space between words.
activities.invention: THE SPACE STONE. Writing lines across the stage hold a word (or a sentence of sight words) in dotted letters. The child traces each letter in order along its guide; only the next letter's start dot is lit, so a word is a left-to-right run, not a set. In sentence rounds, after each word the child must drag a small grey "space stone" (a finger-space) to the line before the next word's dots appear; dropped too close, it nudges the next word along until there is a gap. Copy setting: the model word is above and the line below is empty — the child traces on a faint guide that fades letter by letter (the guide steps away, the child keeps writing).
activities.misconception: Writing letters in the wrong order, running words together, and starting a word anywhere on the line.
activities.pictures: one library picture per word for picture words (first words); none for sight-word sentences
activities.settings: Content: picture words / long words / capitals / sight-word sentences · Guide: dotted / fading
activities.rounds: 9 words per content set from the per-locale sight-word and picture-word lists (the worksheet banks), sentences 3–5 words; trace completion only by path so one right result.
activities.distinct_from: Penny / Snippy trace single letters; the Fading Line traces numerals. Word order and the space between words are new.
activities.risk: Per-locale fonts and letterforms (de Grundschrift, sv/no school letters) — must use each locale's school print, as the letter traces do; tracing accuracy at 360 px.

activities.title: The Body Map
activities.teaches: Name and find the parts of the body and face, count them, and know which come in twos.
activities.invention: THE LABEL THAT PINS ITSELF. The library doll (toys/doll, front-facing full body) stands centre stage at ≥ 60 % stage height, with small pin dots at hand-set points (head, eyes, nose, mouth, arms, hands, fingers, legs, feet — plus elbow, knee, shoulder as word-only labels in setting 2). Labels wait in a rail: library part pictures (body-parts: eye, ear, nose, mouth, hand, foot, finger, leg, arm, head) for pre-readers, or words. The child drags a label; near its own point it pins itself with a little thread and the dot fills. Miss 1: it swings back and the dot it was dropped on flashes its own label for a moment. Miss 2: its own dot pulses. Success: every thread drawn, the doll gives a small hop. TWOS mode (K-363, K-360): tap every part we have two of — tapping one hand lights its partner on the other side; a one-of part (nose, mouth) answers with a single ring; then the count chips (1 / 2 / 10 for fingers) are dropped on the part. HIDDEN mode (K-362): a paper sticky note covers one part; the child picks the part picture it hides and the note peels off.
activities.misconception: Mixing up elbow/knee, wrist/ankle, and not realising that most parts come in left–right pairs.
activities.pictures: toys/doll (the figure); body-parts (arm, ear, eye, face, finger, foot, hand, head, leg, mouth, nail, nose, tooth) as labels; elbow, knee, shoulder, wrist exist in the cache but not in lcs-pictures — word labels only (from the K-354 bank) until labelled.
activities.settings: Labels: pictures / words · Mode: label / which come in twos / what is missing
activities.rounds: 9 rounds per mode; parts balanced over head / trunk / limbs; tray order shuffled; one right pin per label.
activities.distinct_from: Sense Face is about what organs do; this is naming and pairing body parts.
activities.risk: The doll's ears are under her hair — ear is pinned on the side of the head and checked by the reviewer, or refused. Pin coordinates are hand-set once for the one picture.
absorbed: grade 1 "The Body Tag Figure" (body-tag-figure): Name the parts of the body. — A FIGURE WITH TAG STRINGS: library body-part pictures assemble into a figure; numbered strings run from parts to empty tags. The child drags word tags (the content words, from image-vocabulary) to the strings; a correct tag tightens its string and the part glows; a wrong one hangs loose and its string points to where that word belongs. Builder setting: the child assembles the figure from the parts first.

activities.title: The Wash Basin
activities.teaches: Wash hands in the right order (wet, soap, scrub, rinse, dry), and know which tool is for which care job.
activities.invention: THE GERMS THAT ONLY THE RIGHT ORDER LIFTS. Two library hands (body-parts/hand, one mirrored) rest over a library sink with a library faucet, dusted with glittery germ dots (apparatus geometry). The step tools stand on a shelf: faucet (wet), soap, a scrub control (the hands rub), faucet again (rinse), towel. The child drags tools onto the hands. Each step does its real job only in its place: soap on dry hands will not lather; rinsing before the scrub washes a few germs away but most cling; the towel before rinsing leaves soap smears. Miss 1: the step happens, the germs stay, and the empty step slot before it pulses. Miss 2: the step strip shows the next tool's outline. Success: the last germ fades in a sparkle and the hands shine. CARE-TOOLS mode (buildable now, K-380): a library body part lights (tooth, nose, hand, head); the child picks the library tool (toothbrush, tissue, sponge, comb); a right tool performs a small motion over the part. HABIT-SHIELD mode (G2-379): habit pictures (toothbrush, bed, apple, ball, sunscreen) dragged onto what they protect. GERM-TRAIL mode (G1-404, G1-403): two action pictures per moment; the glitter spreads or vanishes on the next frame.
activities.misconception: Skipping the scrub, or thinking a quick rinse cleans.
activities.pictures: body-parts (hand, tooth, nose, head), around-the-house (faucet, sink, toothbrush, toothpaste, comb, brush, bed), hospital (tissue), kitchen-tools (sponge), fruits (apple), toys (ball), beach (sunscreen). MISSING: soap, towel, elbow (label).
activities.settings: Mode: wash the hands / which tool · Steps: 4 / 5
activities.rounds: hand-washing: the step order is fixed, so rounds vary which step is pre-placed and the shelf order (each tool in each shelf slot across a pass); tools mode: 9 rounds, body parts balanced; one right sequence / tool.
activities.distinct_from: No health activity exists.
activities.risk: Blocked on art: soap (labelled), towel; elbow needs an lcs-pictures label (art exists). The care-tools mode alone would cover only K-380. G1-405 (habit week chart) is self-report and stays a worksheet.
absorbed: grade 1 "The Germ Trail" (germ-trail): Healthy habits stop germs and keep teeth clean: wash hands, cough into your elbow, brush before bed. — GLITTER GERMS: a short scene strip (lunch table, playground, bathroom) shows germs as glitter dots on a library friend's hands. The child chooses an action card for each moment (wash hands / wipe on shirt; cough into elbow / into hand); the glitter then spreads or vanishes along the next frames of the strip. Brushing setting: before / during / after cards are ordered on a toothbrush timeline.

grade 2 "The Body Shield — Why We Do Healthy Habits" (body-shield): Explain why we do healthy habits by matching each habit to what it protects (hands → germs, teeth → cavities, sleep → energy, food → growing, exercise → heart, sun cream → skin). — A child figure built from library body-part pictures stands in the middle; habit cards (library pictures: toothbrush, soap, bed, apple, ball, sunglasses) are SHIELDS. The child drags a shield onto the body part it protects; the right part glows and a short "because" line appears under it. Reason mode: the reason cards arrive and the child links each to its habit.
activities.blocked: The core skill (hand-washing order K-382, germ-stopping habits G1-404) needs SOAP and a TOWEL, which the library lacks (shampoo is a labelled pump bottle, not soap); "cough into your elbow" needs an elbow label (the art is in the cache, not in lcs-pictures). Design rewritten so it builds the day the art lands.

activities.title: The Everyday Plate
activities.teaches: Tell everyday foods from sometimes foods and build a balanced plate.
activities.invention: THE PLATE THAT FILLS BY HALVES. A big divided plate (apparatus): half for vegetables and fruit, a quarter for grains, a quarter for protein (plus a side cup for dairy where the locale model has one), and a small side saucer with a star for sometimes-foods that holds ONE thing. Library foods tumble onto a tray. The child drags a food to a section; a right drop settles and that section's fill line rises. Miss 1: the food slides back to the tray and the section it belongs to breathes once. Miss 2: the food's section shows a faint outline of that same food. A second sweet on the saucer slides off. Success: when every section reaches its line the plate turns a slow quarter turn and steam curls rise — balance is the goal and a treat on the saucer is allowed. EVERYDAY/SOMETIMES mode (K-203): two places only, the plate and the saucer.
activities.misconception: Some foods are "bad"; any plate with one vegetable is healthy.
activities.pictures: vegetables, fruits, at-the-supermarket (bread, rice, pasta, cheese, milk, fish, ham, sausage, candy, soda, popcorn), breakfast (cereal, oatmeal, porridge), desserts-and-sweets (cake, cookie, lollipop, donut). Refused as ambiguous: pizza, pancake, juice, butter, pretzels, jam.
activities.settings: Mode: everyday or sometimes / build the plate · Foods: 6 / 10
activities.rounds: 9 rounds of 6 (or 10) foods; every section is an answer in every round; sweets ≤ 2 per round; one right section per food from a per-locale reviewed table.
activities.distinct_from: Grow-Where is botany; this is nutrition.
activities.risk: Per-locale model: en MyPlate (dairy cup), sv Tallriksmodellen, fi lautasmalli, no/da/de/nl/fr/es/it/pt national guides; G1-207 says FOUR groups — align with each locale's worksheet bank. Wording "everyday / sometimes", never good / bad.
absorbed: grade 1 "The Food Group Plate" (food-group-plate): Foods belong to food groups (fruit, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy) and a healthy plate has them all. — A DIVIDED PLATE: the plate has sections sized like the plate model (vegetables biggest), each with a food-group icon. Foods tumble onto a tray; the child drags each to its section and it settles; a wrong section rejects it with a gentle slide and the section's icon pulses. A "build a balanced lunch" setting asks for one of each group: the plate glows when every section has food.

activities.title: The Pencil Path
activities.teaches: Control the stroke: trace straight lines, slants, zigzags, waves, loops, spirals and shapes from the start dot in the right direction.
activities.invention: THE CART THAT ONLY ROLLS ON THE ROAD. Each stroke is a road shaped as the stroke (a zigzag mountain road, a wavy sea lane, a loop-the-loop track, a spiral snail shell road) with a library vehicle or animal at the orange start dot. The child's finger drives it: the vehicle follows the finger only while the finger stays on the road; leaving the road stalls it at the edge, waiting, and the road behind it stays painted, so a lift-off resumes from where it stopped (no restart). Direction matters: dragging backward does nothing. Reaching the end delivers the passenger to a library picture (picture-to-picture path). Road width is the precision setting.
activities.misconception: Starting at the wrong end / wrong direction, and lifting and jumping instead of a continuous stroke.
activities.pictures: vehicles (car, train, boat, plane, tractor), animals (snail, bee, frog) as the mover; goal pictures from any colour theme
activities.settings: Stroke family: lines & slants / zigzags & waves / loops & spirals / shapes / picture-to-picture · Road: wide / narrow
activities.rounds: 9 roads per family, each a different stroke; start side varies (left, top) so direction is read, not habit; completion only by the full path so one right result.
activities.distinct_from: The Fading Line (#4) and the letter traces trace FORMED symbols; this is the stroke control before symbols, and the road (not a fading guide) is the invention.
activities.risk: Precise tracking at 360 px with a fat finger — road width must be measured, and the "trace-path" maze screen code is a precedent but is a deck screen, not an activity core (own core needed).

activities.title: The Zebra Crossing
activities.teaches: Read the traffic and pedestrian lights and cross the road safely: stop at the kerb, look both ways, wait for the green figure, cross.
activities.invention: THE KERB THAT HOLDS YOU UNTIL IT IS SAFE. A street (apparatus): kerb, zebra stripes, a three-lamp traffic light, and library cars (vehicles car, bus, taxi, van) rolling in two lanes. A library animal walker (farm-animals/pets, one per round) waits at the kerb line. The child presses round step buttons beside the street: Stop · Look left · Look right · Wait for green · Cross. Look turns the walker to face that way (mirror flip) and the lane it faces shows whether a car is coming. Crossing works only after the full sequence with the walkers' green. Miss 1: the walker steps out, a car rolls slowly into the lane it did not check, and the walker steps calmly back onto the kerb (never a collision); the missed step button glows. Miss 2: the buttons light in order. Success: the walker crosses on the stripes while the cars wait. READ-THE-LIGHT mode (K-369, K-373): one lamp is lit; the child drags Stop / Get ready / Go onto the light. ORDER mode (K-374): four step cards into four boxes. SIGNS mode (G1-384, G2-360/361): blocked on pictogram art — shape/colour classes (triangle, red ring, blue disc, square, stop octagon) are drawable once the symbols exist.
activities.misconception: Crossing on green without looking; thinking the car light is the walker's light.
activities.pictures: vehicles (car, bus, bicycle), animals (one walker per round); street, crossing and lights drawn as apparatus
activities.settings: Mode: read the light / cross the road / steps in order · Lights: car light / walker light (walker light only once the figures exist)
activities.rounds: 9 rounds; the green arrives after a different number of passing cars each round (no timing tell, no timer); in order mode the step cards are shuffled so each card visits every position across a pass; one right action per state.
activities.distinct_from: No safety activity exists.
activities.risk: Sub-part BLOCKED: road-sign pictograms (pedestrian crossing, children, cyclist, no-entry…) and pedestrian-signal figures (red standing / green walking). Look left first in all 11 locales (right-hand traffic). Step wording per locale by the native panel.
absorbed: grade 1 "The Street Corner" (street-corner): Traffic signs and lights tell us what to do: stop, cross here, give way, no bikes. — A LITTLE STREET: a corner with a crossing, cars and a library friend wanting to cross. Sign posts are empty; the child places the sign that fits the situation from a sign tray (signs drawn as standard geometric sign shapes). When the sign is placed, the scene plays it: the car stops at the stop sign, the friend crosses at the zebra. A wrong sign makes the scene pause with the car and the friend facing each other.

grade 2 "The Sign Sieve — Kinds of Road Signs" (sign-sieve): Know that the shape and colour of a road sign tells its kind (warning triangle, must-not red circle, must-do blue circle, information square) and pick the sign a situation needs. — A SIEVE with three holes shaped like a triangle, a circle and a square. Signs drop from the top; the child drags each to the hole it fits — only the shape decides, so the hole is the rule. Situation mode: a street scene (library vehicles, crossing guard, children) with an empty sign post; the child plants one of three signs and the scene plays what happens (cars stop at the stop sign, slow down at the school sign).

activities.title: The Tile Twin
activities.teaches: Copy a picture square by square onto an empty grid, first by looking, then by using letter–number labels.
activities.invention: THE COPY THAT SLIDES OVER THE MODEL. A model mosaic (6×6, later 8×8) and an empty grid of the same size (side by side ≥ 560 px; stacked model-above-copy on phones). The child picks a colour pot and taps squares on the empty grid to tile them (tap again to clear). Check: the copy slides over the model like a transparency sheet. Right: the two merge and the hidden library picture the mosaic depicts fades in under it. Miss 1: every square that disagrees flickers in BOTH grids at once, so the error is located exactly; the copy slides back. Miss 2: the row with the first mismatch is outlined across both grids. LABELLED setting (K-299/K-300): rows carry numbers, columns letters (A–H); tapping a model square lights its letter-number pair, and the same pair glows on the copy — the coordinate is the bridge. G1-416 (draw with the grid) is the 8×8 set with no labels.
activities.misconception: Losing the row when counting across, and mirror-copying (counting columns from the wrong side).
activities.pictures: none (tiles in the shell palette); optionally a library picture as the "finished" reward revealed under the completed mosaic
activities.settings: Grid: 6×6 no labels / 6×6 labels / 8×8 labels · Colours: 1 / 2
activities.rounds: 9 model pictures per grid size, each asymmetric left-right (a mirror copy is always wrong) and with 8–16 tiles; one right copy (a construction, no answer position).
activities.distinct_from: No grid or coordinate activity exists below the tools.
activities.risk: Tap targets: 8×8 at 320 px stacked = 34 px cells (cell floor met, ≥ 34); 2-colour pots ≥ 44 px. Labels A–H safe in all 11 alphabets.
absorbed: grade 1 "The Grid Copy Loom" (grid-copy-loom): Copy a picture square by square onto an empty grid by keeping track of rows and columns. — TWO LOOMS: a coloured mosaic on the left loom; an empty loom on the right. The child taps a cell on the empty loom and picks a colour bead; a finger-shadow follows the same row and column on the model so the child can check. When a row is finished, a slider bar runs across both looms and marks any cell that does not match. A "no guide" setting hides the shadow.

activities.title: The Sorting Cabinet
activities.teaches: Use rows, and then rows AND columns, to find the missing picture in a grid.
activities.invention: THE DRAWER THAT WILL NOT SHUT. A 3×3 cabinet of drawers; each row holds one kind (apples, ducks, cars) and one drawer stands open and empty. The child drags a piece from the tray into the open drawer; it slides shut only if the piece fits its row. Miss 1: the drawer jams half-open and the row's other drawers glow. Miss 2: the jammed piece and the row's pictures pulse side by side. Success: the drawer shuts with a click and all nine knobs light. ROWS-AND-COLUMNS setting (G3-351): each column also holds one SIZE (big, middle, small — the same library picture at three scales), so a piece must satisfy both; a piece that fits the row but not the column jams with the COLUMN glowing, one that fits the column but not the row jams with the ROW glowing.
activities.misconception: Matching to the nearest neighbour or the column alone; ignoring one of the two constraints.
activities.pictures: fruits, animals, vehicles, toys, farm-animals — identical instances per row; sizes are scale transforms (100 / 72 / 50 %) of one picture, never different art.
activities.settings: Rule: rows only / rows and columns · Tray: 3 pieces / 4 pieces
activities.rounds: 9 rounds per setting; the empty drawer visits all nine positions across a pass; tray of 3 (or 4) pieces shuffled, the right piece in any tray slot ≤ 40 %; the two-rule tray always holds a right-row-wrong-size piece and a right-size-wrong-row piece; one right answer.
activities.distinct_from: Not Mim's Baskets (category sort into bins) and not the Bunting Line (sequence): this is two-dimensional constraint reasoning.
activities.risk: The smallest scale must stay ≥ 64 px at 360 (cabinet cell ≥ 96 px). Colour as the column attribute is refused (no same-noun colour variants in the library).

activities.title: The Bunting Line
activities.teaches: Find the repeating unit of a pattern (AB, ABC, AABB, ABB, by picture, size, position or shape), extend it, fill a missing piece, and extend a growing pattern.
activities.invention: THE UNIT THAT FOLDS UNDER. Bunting flags carrying library pictures hang on a line across the stage, with empty pegs at the end (or one empty peg in the middle). The child drags flags from a basket onto the pegs. Each time a full unit is completed, that stretch of bunting FOLDS down under the previous unit, so the units stack in a column like rows of a table: a correct pattern makes perfectly aligned columns, a wrong flag sits visibly out of line under a different picture. The child is not told the unit — they see it. Position setting hangs flags high/low; size setting hangs big/small; growing setting hangs groups that grow by one flag each unit (the folded stack becomes a staircase).
activities.misconception: Copying the last picture instead of the unit, and not seeing where the unit restarts (treating AAB as AB).
activities.pictures: fruits, animals, vehicles, toys (identical instances per kind); shapes theme (circle, square, triangle, star, heart, hexagon) for the shape setting (K-077); size = scale transform, position = high/low peg.
activities.settings: Pattern: AB / ABC / AABB / ABB / growing · Attribute: picture / size / position / shape · Task: extend / one gap / two gaps
activities.rounds: 9 rounds per setting; 2–3 visible units, the stopping point mid-unit in ≥ half the rounds; missing-piece rounds put the gap at each unit position equally; TWO-GAP rounds (G1-155, absorbed Pattern Quilt) in the missing setting; basket shuffled with each candidate in every slot across a pass; one right answer.
activities.distinct_from: No activity teaches patterns. Not the Animal Train or Counting Necklace (count instruments); the folding unit stack is a new invention.
activities.risk: Low. Must keep pictures ≥ 64 px on a phone with 9–12 flags: fold early (two-row line) on narrow screens.
absorbed: grade 1 "The Pattern Quilt" (pattern-quilt): A repeating pattern has a core unit that repeats; find the missing pieces by finding the unit. — A QUILT WITH LOOSE PATCHES: a strip quilt of library pictures (AB, AAB, ABC, AABB) has two holes. Loose patches lie in a basket. The child can drag a "stitch frame" over any stretch: if the stretch is exactly one core unit, the frame locks and copies of the unit shimmer along the quilt, showing where each picture repeats; then the child drops patches into the holes. A wrong patch puckers the quilt at that seam and the stitch frame over its unit flashes the mismatch.

activities.title: The Shadow Lamp
activities.teaches: Match a picture to its outline (shadow), and recognise a whole picture from a small part of it.
activities.invention: THE BEAM THAT DRAWS THE OUTLINE. A wall carries 3–4 dark silhouettes; a lamp stands at the side. The child drags a library picture into the lamp's beam; the picture's real shadow is cast and slides onto the wall over the silhouette it is dropped near. If it is the same shape the shadow sinks exactly into it (edges vanish); if not, the mismatched edges stay bright where shadow and silhouette disagree — the child SEES what differs (ears, tail, handle). Part-to-whole setting: the lamp is a narrow spotlight that shows only a part of a hidden picture on the wall; the child drags the whole picture into the beam and the lit part must coincide.
activities.misconception: Matching by colour or by one feature (any four-legged animal for any four-legged shadow).
activities.pictures: animals, farm animals, kitchen tools, vehicles, toys (silhouettes generated from the same library picture by alpha mask — no new art)
activities.settings: Mode: whole shadow / part only · Look-alikes: easy (different kinds) / close (same family: cat–dog–fox)
activities.rounds: 9 rounds; silhouette positions shuffled, the right one in each wall slot ≤ 40 %; "close" rounds always include a same-family distractor; one right answer.
activities.distinct_from: No activity matches outline to object; the Peek Window hides and shows a GROUP for counting, not a part of one picture for identification.
activities.risk: Silhouettes from alpha masks must survive pictures whose webp has a white (non-transparent) background — check the library alpha per noun.

activities.title: The Fold Mirror
activities.teaches: Recognise the mirror image of a picture (a reflection is flipped, not turned), and tell whether a picture is the same on both sides of a line.
activities.invention: THE HINGE THAT FOLDS ONTO THE ORIGINAL. A library picture stands left of a vertical hinge (a mirror edge). Three candidates wait: the true reflection, the same picture unflipped, and the picture turned (rotated 180°/90°). The child drags a candidate to the right of the hinge; the right page folds over the hinge onto the left. Right: the reflection lands exactly on the original — outlines merge and a shine runs down the mirror. Miss 1: the copy or the turned picture lands crooked; the non-matching parts stay visible in a second tint (the duck's head on the wrong side). Miss 2: a faint true reflection appears on the right page for the child to pick. SAME-ON-BOTH-SIDES rounds (G2-248): three library pictures each with a dashed line through the middle; the child folds one — a symmetric one closes on itself, others leave an overhang. Free play: drag any picture to the hinge and watch its reflection appear.
activities.misconception: Thinking the same picture (or a turned one) is the mirror image.
activities.pictures: animals with a clear facing direction (duck, dog, horse, fish), vehicles (car, train), shoes, kitchen tools (asymmetric nouns only — a symmetric ball is refused)
activities.settings: Mirror: side (vertical hinge) / water (horizontal hinge) · Distractors: copy + turn / copy only · Task: find the reflection / which is the same on both sides
activities.rounds: 9 rounds per task; candidates shuffled with the answer in each slot ≤ 40 %; reflection rounds use only asymmetric pictures (duck, dog, horse, fish, car, train, shoe, watering-can-like kitchen tools), symmetric rounds use shapes theme (heart, star) and front-facing pictures checked for true symmetry.
activities.distinct_from: No reflection activity exists; Pip's Museum turns shapes (rotation invariance), this flips pictures (reflection).
activities.risk: Low. Pictures that look symmetric but are not exactly (a front-facing cartoon) are refused for the symmetric rounds — measure the alpha mask's left/right difference.
absorbed: grade 3 "The Fold Mirror" (fold-mirror): A line of symmetry folds a shape onto itself exactly; some shapes have several, some none. — THE FOLD MIRROR: a shape cut from paper on the stage. The child drags a fold line through it (it snaps through the centre at 8 angles) and presses Fold: the half flips over the line. If the halves match, the fold glows and the line is kept as a crease; if not, the overhanging part sticks out in a different shade. The child folds until they think all mirror lines are found and taps the count; a miss shows one fold not yet tried that works.

activities.title: The Pairing Pegs
activities.teaches: Look closely to find two pictures that are exactly the same, and the one that is different (in a detail, its size or its shape).
activities.invention: THE PEG THAT ONLY CLOSES ON TWINS. A washing line holds 6–8 cards (library pictures, some subtly altered: mirrored, a detail recoloured, scaled, a shape with a corner cut). The child drags one card onto another; a clothes-peg tries to clip them together. Exact twins clip and leave the line together; non-twins: the peg will not close and the two cards hold side by side with the differing spot pulsing. Odd-one-out setting: every card has a twin except one — when all pairs are pegged, the card left alone on the line IS the different one, so "different" is discovered by pairing, not guessed.
activities.misconception: Accepting "nearly the same" as the same (same kind ≠ same picture), and missing size or orientation differences.
activities.pictures: animals, toys, fruits, vehicles, shapes (drawn); alterations are transforms of the same picture (mirror, scale, hue rotate) — no new art
activities.settings: Task: find the pairs / find the odd one out · Difference: size and shape / small details
activities.rounds: 9 rounds; card positions shuffled; the odd one sits in each line position ≤ 25 % across a pass; every altered card differs in ONE attribute so one right answer.
activities.distinct_from: Ziggy's Odd One Out is category reasoning; Partner Bows pairs for COUNTING. Here identity is the content.
activities.risk: Detail-alterations (hue on one region) need region masks; keep v1 to mirror / scale / whole-hue / shape variants.

activities.title: The Search Lens
activities.teaches: Search a busy field systematically for every copy of a target — a picture, a shape, a letter among look-alikes, or a sight word — without missing any or marking one twice.
activities.invention: THE LENS THAT LEAVES A TRAIL. A dense scene (or a grid of letters / words) fills the stage; the target sits in a small frame. The child drags a magnifying lens over the field; under the lens things enlarge, and everything the lens has passed over is faintly tinted, so the unsearched parts stay visibly bright — a scanning strategy the child can see. Tapping a found item under the lens pins a tag on it and adds a bead to the counter tray. Check: missed copies glow inside the still-bright region first ("you have not looked there yet"); a wrong tag (a d for a b, a cat for a fox) flips the two side by side. Shapes-around-us setting: library objects (clock, plate, book, window) and the child finds every one shaped like the target shape.
activities.misconception: Random searching (missing items in unvisited corners), double-counting, and accepting mirror-twin letters (b/d/p/q) or look-alike words.
activities.pictures: any colour theme for scenes (identical instances of the target), plus school/classroom, kitchen tools, household nouns for the shapes setting; letters and words are type
activities.settings: Target: pictures / shapes in objects / letters / sight words · Field: sparse / busy
activities.rounds: 9 rounds; 3–8 copies of the target, copies spread across all four quadrants every round (no quadrant empty in more than 1 round in 3); count answered by the tray beads, so no option position tell; letter rounds include its mirror-twins ≥ 2 each.
activities.distinct_from: Classify-and-count (Sort and Count) works on a handful of pictures; this is SEARCH through clutter. Not the Peek Window (glance) nor the Counting Table (tagging a small set).
activities.risk: Dense scenes must keep each item ≥ 44 px at 360 px — the lens solves legibility but the tap target under the lens must be measured; the per-locale sight-word lists already exist.

activities.title: The Plant Builder
activities.teaches: A plant has parts (roots, stem, leaves, flower, fruit, seed) that each do a job; the foods we eat are different plant parts (fruits hold seeds); a flower has petals, sepals, stamens and a pistil.
activities.invention: A POT AND A WATER DROP. The child builds a plant from library parts: roots only click below the soil line, the stem on the roots, leaves on the stem, the flower at the top (a part held anywhere else drifts back). A water drop placed on the soil then travels visibly up through the roots and stem to the leaves; a missing part stops the drop there and that gap glows. WHICH-PART-WE-EAT mode (K-202 merged grow-where, G2-363): a library food (carrot, celery, lettuce, broccoli, apple, tomato, corn) is hung on the part we eat; the plant fills that part with the food's colour; fruits show their seeds. JOBS mode (G2-364): job cards climb to their part. FLOWER mode (G3-392, merged flower-press): the flower opens apart into petal, sepal, stamen, pistil; name tags go onto them, one tag (bark, thorn) is not a flower part.
activities.misconception: Thinks the plant drinks through its leaves or that roots are just "the bottom".
activities.pictures: MISSING: a plant-parts set (root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed as separable layers of one plant) and a flower-parts set (petal, sepal, stamen, pistil). Foods exist: vegetables (carrot, celery, lettuce, broccoli, cauliflower, corn, tomato), fruits (apple, pear).
activities.settings: Task: build and water / name the parts · Parts: 4 / 5 (+ seed).
activities.rounds: 8+ plants from different library flowers; the part asked to name varies; tags shuffled.
activities.distinct_from: Not a duplicate of the Cycle Wheel (growth over time); this is structure and function.
activities.risk: Blocked on two library assets. The tomato/cucumber/pepper honesty line ("a fruit of the plant, cooked as a vegetable") is needed in the eat mode.
absorbed: grade 2 "The Root-to-Fruit Ladder — Parts of a Plant" (root-to-fruit): Name the parts of a plant (root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed), what each does, and which part of a plant a food is. — A tall ladder beside a plant column, one rung per part from root (bottom, underground) to seed/fruit (top). Food cards (library vegetables and fruits: carrot, celery, lettuce, broccoli, apple, peas, corn) are hung on the rung of the part we eat; the plant column fills that part in (the root zone shows a carrot shape). Function mode: function cards (takes up water, makes food from light, holds the plant up, makes seeds) climb to their rung, and a little water drop travels up from root to leaf to show the path.

grade K "The Grow-Where Garden" (grow-where): Tell fruits from vegetables by which part of the plant we eat: fruits hold the seeds, vegetables are roots, leaves and stems. — THE KNIFE AND THE PLANT. A cutting board and a plant diagram (a plant with roots, stem, leaves, flower and a fruit, drawn as apparatus). The child drags a food onto the board; a cut opens it: seeds inside → it is a fruit; no seeds → the child drags it onto the plant part it is (carrot to the root, lettuce to the leaf, celery to the stem). Then it goes into the fruit bowl or the vegetable crate. Culinary rounds (tomato, cucumber) show seeds and are honest: "a fruit of the plant, cooked as a vegetable".

grade 3 "The Flower Press" (flower-press): Name the parts of a flower (petal, stem, leaf, root, and grade-3 sepal/stamen/pistil) and what each does. — THE FLOWER PRESS: a flower in a pot; the child pulls it from the soil and presses it flat between two glass plates, where its parts separate slightly. A job card appears ('drinks water from the soil', 'makes food from sunlight', 'attracts bees', 'holds the flower up'); the child drags it to the part that does that job, and the part lights and acts (roots draw a blue line of water up the stem; a bee lands on the petals). Label mode: name tags go onto numbered parts, with one tag that is not a flower part to cross out.
activities.blocked: Separable plant parts (root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, seed) and a flower-parts set (petal, sepal, stamen, pistil) do not exist in the library, and drawing them is hand-drawn objects (rule 5). It now also holds grow-where (fruit/vegetable by plant part, K-202) and flower-press (G3-392), all on one apparatus once the art exists.

activities.title: The Sense Face
activities.teaches: Match each experience to the sense and body part we use for it (see, hear, smell, taste, touch).
activities.invention: THE SOCKET THAT LIGHTS ITS SENSE. Five large library body-part pictures sit in a row as sockets: eye, ear, nose, mouth, hand (body-parts). A library thing slides in on a cable from the left (bell, drum, rainbow, rose, onion, lemon, honey, sponge, icicle…). The child drags its plug into a socket. Right: the socket responds with an apparatus effect (rings of waves round the ear, a swirl into the nose, a sparkle round the eye, a little shake of the hand, the mouth pulses) and the thing docks beside it. Miss 1: the socket stays still and the plug drops back. Miss 2: the right socket's ring of effect shows faintly. Two-sense rounds (setting 2) show two empty plug-holes on the thing (lemon: taste + smell). ODD-ONE-OUT mode (G1-359): three things docked on one sense plus one that does not belong; the child unplugs it. FIND-ALL mode: one socket lights and the child plugs in every thing for it.
activities.misconception: One sense per thing; thinking we taste with the nose only or hear with the eyes on picture books.
activities.pictures: body-parts (eye, ear, nose, mouth, hand); things: christmas (bell), music (drum, trumpet, whistle from accessories), weather (rainbow), flowers (rose, lavender), vegetables (onion), at-the-supermarket (garlic, lemon, popcorn), breakfast (honey), kitchen-tools (sponge), winter (icicle), farm-animals (rooster).
activities.settings: Senses per thing: one / one or two · Mode: drag to the sense / find all things for one sense
activities.rounds: 9 things per pass, each sense the answer ≥ once and ≤ 3 times; two-sense things only in setting 2 and the plug-holes say how many; socket order fixed (the organ is the content); one right set per thing from a reviewed table.
activities.distinct_from: Not the body map (names of body parts): this is what each organ does.
activities.risk: Each thing must have ONE obvious sense in setting 1 (refuse cake, cat, apple — several senses). Taste is shown by the mouth picture (lips); tongue is in the cache, not labelled.
absorbed: grade 1 "The Sense Switchboard" (sense-switchboard): We learn about the world with five senses, each through one body part: eyes see, ears hear, nose smells, tongue tastes, skin touches. — A FACE WITH FIVE SOCKETS: a large library face/body part set (eye, ear, nose, tongue, hand) as plug sockets. A picture of a thing to sense (bell, rainbow, flower, lemon, cactus) slides in on a cable; the child plugs it into a socket. The right socket makes the sense "light up" (the eye opens, the ear wiggles) and a short effect plays (sound waves, a smell swirl drawn as tool-grade lines). A wrong socket shows nothing happening. Odd-one-out setting: three things for the same sense plus one other.

activities.title: Mother and Baby
activities.teaches: Match baby animals to their parents and notice how young animals are like and unlike the grown-ups.
activities.invention: THE MAGNIFIER OF LIKENESS. Four grown-up library animals stand in a meadow; a baby waits at the gate. The child drags the baby to a parent; it trots there. A round magnifier then slides between the two and lights the features they share at hand-set points (beak and webbed feet; hooves and mane; woolly coat; spots). Right: several features light in pairs, the baby nuzzles in. Miss 1: one or no feature lights, the baby looks round and walks back to the gate. Miss 2: the true parent lifts its head. CHANGE round (caterpillar → butterfly): few features light even though it is right, and the magnifier shows the two side by side with "changes a lot" shown by an arrow between them. REVERSE mode: a parent stands alone and three babies wait — the child brings its own baby.
activities.misconception: Babies always look like small copies of their parents.
activities.pictures: farm-animals (hen/chick, cow/calf, horse/foal, sheep/lamb, duck/duckling), forest-creatures (caterpillar), insects-and-bugs (butterfly); distractors from the same family (goose for duckling, goat for lamb, donkey for foal, rooster/turkey for chick, ox for calf).
activities.settings: Mode: find the parent / is it alike? · Change rounds: off / on
activities.rounds: 12 rounds per pass (6 baby→parent + 6 parent→baby), parent positions shuffled with the right one in each slot ≤ 30 %; every round has a same-family distractor; one right parent.
activities.distinct_from: Home Finder is about where animals live; this is about offspring.
activities.risk: Only six pairs; more pairs (kitten, puppy, piglet, tadpole) would widen it. Feature coordinates are hand-set per picture and checked by the reviewer.

activities.title: The Where-From Thread
activities.teaches: Tell things found in nature from things made by people, and trace a made thing back to its natural material.
activities.invention: THE THREAD BACK TO THE SOURCE. The stage has two sides: NATURE (a strip of library sources: tree, sheep, beach rock, sea water, cow) and MADE (a workbench of apparatus geometry). Each thing in the tray trails a loose thread. The child drags a thing to a side. Then its thread pulls tight: a natural thing's thread ends right where it lies (a pinecone, a seashell, a leaf, a rock — it IS nature); a made thing's thread runs across the workbench and back to the natural source it was made from (wooden chair → tree, wool scarf → sheep, glass jar → sand/rock, milk carton? refused). Right: the thread draws in one smooth line. Miss 1: a made thing put on the nature side shows its thread running out across the workbench to its source; a natural thing on the made side shows its thread ending at itself. Miss 2: the side glows. Success: all threads drawn, the strip of sources gives a small bounce.
activities.misconception: Thinking made things have nothing to do with nature, and that anything wooden is natural.
activities.pictures: Natural: miscellaneous (leaf, acorn, pinecone), beach (seashell, rock, water), camping (log), flowers (rose), easter (feather). Made: furniture (chair, table), kitchen-tools (jar, glass, spoon), accessories (scarf), toys (ball, car, robot), at-the-supermarket (can, bag). Sources: tree theme (apple tree), farm-animals (sheep, cow), beach (rock).
activities.settings: Mode: sort / pull the thread · Things: everyday / tricky (paper, wooden spoon, wool)
activities.rounds: 9 things per pass, natural and made balanced (4–5 each), ≥ 2 wooden lures (log natural / chair made) per pass in the tricky setting; one right side from a reviewed table (refuse contested items: paper, cotton, honey).
activities.distinct_from: No materials activity exists.
activities.risk: Plastic has no picturable natural source for K — plastic items are made things whose thread ends at the workbench (no source shown), stated honestly. Code: K-214 natural vs made is closest to NGSS K-2-ETS1/2-PS1-1 (materials); keep 2-PS1-1.

activities.title: The Water Tub
activities.teaches: Predict and test whether things float or sink; see that size or weight alone does not decide, that shape can make clay float, and draw a conclusion from a record of tests.
activities.invention: THE TUB THAT TELLS THE TRUTH. A clear tub of water (apparatus) with a surface line and a sand floor. The child predicts by dragging a library object to the surface band or to the floor; on release it falls in, splashes and settles where it really goes — bobbing at the surface or resting on the floor, sliding away from the predicted place if the prediction was wrong. The prediction stays as a faint ghost beside the result, so the child compares. BALANCE setting (G1-408): two objects first sit on an apparatus balance that tips to the heavier; then both go in — the heavy log floats, the light key sinks. CLAY setting (G2-382): a grey clay lump (geometry) with a shape slider ball → flat → bowl → boat; only the hollow boat floats, though the clay is the same. RECORD setting (G3-400, merged test-tank): a question card ("Do heavy things always sink?"), six objects predicted and tested; each fills a row of a record card (prediction · result · match mark); then the child picks the conclusion the record supports from three — a conclusion the data contradicts is shown crossed against the row that disproves it.
activities.misconception: Big things sink, small things float; heavy = sinks without exception.
activities.pictures: Float: camping (log), fruits (apple, lemon), toys (ball, boat, balloon), kitchen-tools (sponge), miscellaneous (leaf, pinecone), at-the-supermarket (water bottle, empty with cap). Sink: around-the-house (key, hammer, spoon if metal), tools (nail, bolt, hammer), beach (rock), accessories (ring). Refused: acorn (varies), grape, plastic spoon, coin (no picture).
activities.settings: Mode: predict and test / balance first / shape the clay / record and conclude · Objects: everyday / tricky (big floater vs small sinker)
activities.rounds: 9 objects per pass, floaters and sinkers balanced, ≥ 3 tricky pairs; record rounds: 7 object sets of 6, each chosen so the naive rule (heavy sinks / big sinks) fails at least once; conclusion options shuffled; one right answer from a reviewed float/sink table.
activities.distinct_from: No sink/float activity exists.
