activities.risk: Every object's behaviour must be checked against its PICTURE (the spoon must look metal; the bottle must look empty and capped) — the G1-204 plastic-spoon defect is the precedent.
absorbed: grade 1 "The Float Tank" (float-tank): Predict, then test, whether an object floats or sinks; heavy does not mean it sinks. — A WATER TANK WITH A PREDICTION LINE: the child drags an object to the shelf above the tank and first sets the prediction marker (top half = float, bottom = sink), then lets go. The object falls in and settles: floats at the surface or rests on the bottom. A tally board records predicted vs real. Balance setting: two objects on a scale first show which is heavier; then both go in the tank, and the heavier one floats (log vs coin) to break the "heavy sinks" idea.

grade 2 "The Water Tank — Sink or Float?" (water-tank): Predict and test whether objects sink or float, and see that changing a shape (a clay ball into a boat) can make it float. — A glass water tank with a prediction shelf (sink side / float side). The child sorts objects onto the shelf, then drops each in: it sinks to the floor or bobs at the surface (true to the material). Clay mode: a clay lump with a shape slider — ball → flat → bowl → boat; the child shapes it and drops it; only the hollow boat floats, though the clay is the same.

grade 3 "The Test Tank" (test-tank): Run a fair test: predict, test, record, and draw a conclusion about why things sink or float. — THE TEST TANK: a glass tank of water and a shelf of library objects. A question card is chosen ('do heavy things always sink?'). The child drags each object onto a prediction board (sink / float column), then drops it in the tank: it sinks or floats, and a record card fills in the 'what happened' column beside the prediction with a match/mismatch mark. After 6 objects the child picks the conclusion that the record supports from three; a conclusion the data contradicts is shown crossed against the row that disproves it (a big log floats).

activities.title: The Helper Dispatch
activities.teaches: Know community helpers, the jobs they do and the tools they use.
activities.invention: THE CALL THAT NEEDS THE RIGHT HELPER. A town street (apparatus) with five doorways; at one door a request lights up as a library picture (a car to mend, a cat to treat, a cake order, a book to return, a vegetable patch to dig). Helpers (library occupations) wait at the station, each with their tool beside them. The child drags a helper to the lit door; the helper walks there. Right: the helper's tool acts on the request (the mechanic's car drives off, the vet's stethoscope pulses over the cat and the cat sits up, the baker's cake appears in the window). Miss 1: the helper arrives, the tool does nothing, the helper walks back. Miss 2: the right helper's tool glows at the station. TOOLS mode (K-213): the helper stands at the door; the child gives one of three tools.
activities.misconception: Thinking any helper can fix any problem; gendered assumptions about jobs (the library pictures show varied helpers).
activities.pictures: occupations (firefighter, doctor, veterinarian, chef, baker, farmer, teacher, mechanic, librarian, gardener, barber, pilot, nurse); requests and tools: vehicles (car, airplane), animals/pets (cat, dog), bakery (cake), classroom (book), vegetables (carrot), around-the-house (hose, rake, shovel), hospital (stethoscope, bandage, thermometer), kitchen-tools (whisk, pan), tools (hammer, ladder). MISSING: postal worker, police officer.
activities.settings: Mode: send the helper / give the tool · Helpers: 4 / 6
activities.rounds: 9 requests per pass, each helper the answer ≤ 2 times, station order shuffled; one right helper per request (the firefighter appears only in tools mode, with the hose).
activities.distinct_from: No community activity exists.
activities.risk: Occupation pictures show one gender each — the reviewer checks the set is varied overall. Postal worker/police absent from both modes until art exists.

activities.title: The Family Tree
activities.teaches: Name family members (mother, father, sister, brother, grandmother, grandfather …) from their place on a family tree.
activities.invention: THE TREE THAT HOLDS EVERY FRAME. A tree with three branches of frames: grandparents at the top, parents in the middle, the children (one marked "me" with a star) at the bottom; joining lines show who is whose. The child drags family-word cards onto frames; a card snaps only onto the frame its word names (relative to "me"); a wrong card slides back and the line from "me" to the right frame lights, so the relationship is read along the tree. Me-moves setting: the star moves to another child, and the same frames change names (my brother's father is my father) — kinship is a relation, not a label on a person.
activities.misconception: Family words as fixed labels on people rather than relations to "me"; mixing up grandparent sides.
activities.pictures: MISSING: seven family figures as library pictures (grandmother, grandfather, mother, father, older girl, older boy, baby — toys/baby could serve as the baby). Frames, branches and the "me" star are apparatus.
activities.settings: Words: core (mother, father, sister, brother) / plus grandparents · Me: fixed / moves
activities.rounds: 9 trees per pass, the structure fixed (one family shape, as K-370 rules), the words' frames shuffled; one right frame per word.
activities.distinct_from: No family activity exists.
activities.risk: Blocked on family-figure art. Nordic lineage words (farmor/mormor, farfar/morfar) need a fixed grandparent side per frame — the tree must mark the mother's and father's side by branch colour. The clue mode (G1-386: names placed from clues) could be built with abstract name tokens, but without figures it teaches name logic, not family words.
absorbed: grade 1 "The Family Tree" (family-tree-rows): Families have generations: grandparents, parents, children; family words name each place. — A TREE WITH THREE BRANCH LEVELS: grandparents on the top branch, parents in the middle, children at the bottom. Family-word cards (grandma, dad, baby, aunt) are dropped on a branch; a card on the wrong level slides along the branch to the trunk. The clue setting reads clues ("Mia is Tom's sister") and the child places the name cards; the branch lines connecting people light when a relation is right.

grade 2 "The Family Tree Path — Who Is Who?" (family-tree-path): Use family words (mother, father, sister, brother, grandmother, grandfather, aunt, uncle, cousin) for relationships. — A three-generation family tree of library people on branches. A riddle ("my mother's sister") is a PATH: the child starts at the "me" child and walks up and across the branches step by step, each step tapping a branch (up to parent, across to sibling, down to child). The person where the path ends lights, and the child picks the family word for them from the bank. Reverse: a person lights; the child builds the path.
activities.blocked: Family words need people who look like a grandmother, grandfather, mother, father, sister, brother and baby; the library has only toys/baby, toys/girl, toys/doll and uniformed occupations, and drawing silhouettes with hair/age cues is hand-drawn characters (rule 5). The design is sound and builds as soon as family figures exist.

activities.title: The Season Wheel
activities.teaches: Name the four seasons in order as a cycle, and tell which season a picture or a piece of clothing belongs to.
activities.invention: THE WHEEL THAT ONLY TURNS FORWARD. A big wheel in four quarters around a hub; the hub shows the season sign of the quarter under the pointer, built from library pictures (spring: tulip + bud; summer: sun + swimsuit; autumn: autumn leaf + pumpkin; winter: snowflake + snowman). Things wait in a basket (clothing, weather, food, activities). The child turns the wheel to a quarter and drags each thing into it. Right: it settles on the rim of its quarter. Miss 1: it slides along the rim back to the basket and the right quarter's sign flashes once. Miss 2: the right quarter tilts toward the child. ORDER mode (K-339): one sign is on the wheel; the child drags the other three signs into the blank quarters; the pointer can only turn forward, and a wrong order makes the hub jump backwards (autumn after winter) and stop. ODD-ONE-OUT mode (K-340): one thing in a quarter does not belong; the child flicks it out.
activities.misconception: Thinking the seasons are a list that ends, and placing summer next to winter; clothes for the wrong weather.
activities.pictures: Signs: flowers (tulip), spring (bud), beach (sun), clothing (swimsuit), miscellaneous (leaf — autumn), vegetables (pumpkin), weather (snowflake), christmas/winter (snowman). Things: clothing (coat, scarf, mitten, snowsuit, raincoat, swimsuit, t-shirt), winter (sled, skiing), summer (pool, popsicle, sandcastle), thanksgivinng (acorn); refused as all-year: umbrella, kite, pinecone.
activities.settings: Mode: sort into seasons / put the seasons in order / odd one out (one thing in a quarter does not belong) · Hemisphere: north (all 11 locales are north; pt-BR note below)
activities.rounds: 9 rounds; each season the answer equally often; ambiguous things refused by the reviewer (umbrella, pinecone, rainbow); order rounds start at a different season each; one right season.
activities.distinct_from: No seasons activity exists; the Weather Window is the day's weather, this is the year.
activities.risk: pt = Brazilian Portuguese: seasons are inverted and weak — follow the worksheet program's pt decision (south ordering with December = summer, or a refusal recorded). Christmas pictures are refused as winter signs (summer in Brazil, and religious).

activities.title: The Weather Window
activities.teaches: Read and name weather symbols, match the sky to its symbol, tell cold / warm / hot on a thermometer, and tell day from night.
activities.invention: THE WINDOW AND ITS THERMOMETER. A big window frame (apparatus) whose pane shows the sky as a colour and one library weather picture outside (sunny, cloudy, rainy, stormy, snowflake, rainbow); a weather card hangs on the frame and a band thermometer (cold blue · warm yellow · hot red, no numerals) on its side. WEATHER mode (K-356, G1-362): the child drags the matching symbol card onto the frame's card holder; a wrong symbol sits on the holder while the sky stays different, so the two are compared, then drops off (miss 1); miss 2: the sky's picture pulses. TEMPERATURE mode (K-211, K-365): the child drags the thermometer liquid up or down and the scene outside changes its clothing pictures (coat → t-shirt → swimsuit); or a scene is shown and the child sets the liquid to its band. DAY/NIGHT mode (K-208): the pane is split day | night under a sun–moon dial; things (owl, rooster, breakfast foods, moon, bed, sunglasses) are dragged into a half. WEEK mode (K-364, G1-363 + absorbed wardrobe): seven small windows, each with a symbol; questions ("which day can we fly a kite?") answered by tapping a window; WARDROBE: a library animal is dressed for the asked day (raincoat, boots, scarf, mitten, sunglasses) and walks through that window — rain lands on it without the raincoat.
activities.misconception: Thinking sunny always means hot (sunny winter day), reading the thermometer by colour alone.
activities.pictures: weather (sunny, cloudy, rainy, stormy, snowflake, rainbow, raincoat, scarf, sunglasses, umbrella, thermometer), clothing (coat, t-shirt, swimsuit, mitten), space (moon), animals (owl), farm-animals (rooster), breakfast foods, furniture (bed). MISSING: wind (refused), pyjamas.
activities.settings: Mode: weather symbols / thermometer / day and night · Week chart: off / on (a 7-day strip to fill)
activities.rounds: 9 rounds per mode, each symbol or band used ≥ once, tray order shuffled with the answer in each slot ≤ 40 %; one right answer.

activities.title: The Home Finder
activities.teaches: Tell pets, farm animals and wild animals apart, and match animals to their homes.

The child drags an animal to a place; on release it walks there. Right: it settles in front of its place and three need badges above it (food · water · shelter, apparatus icons) fill. Miss 1: it stops, one or more badges stay empty, it turns and walks back; Miss 2: its real place gives a small wave. WHO-DOES-NOT-LIVE-HERE mode (G1-406): a place holds four animals, one wrong — tap the one whose badges are empty. WHAT-IT-EATS mode (G1-206, G1-407): drag the animal onto plants / animals / both. ADAPT mode (G2-380): a feature card (a written sentence: thick fur, fins, long neck) is dropped on the animal it describes; one animal is left over.

activities.pictures: Animals: animals, farm-animals, pets, forest-creatures, ocean-life, zoo-animals, birds, winter (penguin, seal, walrus). Places: miscellaneous (house), thanksgivinng (haystack), camping (forest, lake, river, mountain), beach (water, island), winter (icicle as the snowy sign), spring (nest, birdhouse, garden). activities.title: The Recycling Bins with Windows
activities.teaches: Sort finished things into the right recycling bin (paper, plastic, glass, metal, food waste).
activities.invention: THE BIN WITH A WINDOW. Three to five bins (apparatus) in the locale's bin colours with a material icon on the lid and a see-through window low down showing what each already holds (two library things of its material). All slots are the same size, so shape is never a tell. The child drags a finished thing to a bin. Right: it drops through and appears in the window lying with its own material. Miss 1: it taps the lid and stays out; the lid icon of the right bin lights. Miss 2: the window of the right bin glows. Success: all things in, the bins' lids close one after another.

activities.title: The Life Test
activities.teaches: Tell living things from non-living things by what living things do: they grow, they need food and water, they make young.
activities.invention: THE THREE LAMPS. A test bench with three lamps (apparatus icons): GROWS · NEEDS FOOD AND WATER · MAKES YOUNG. The child drags a library thing onto the bench and it is tested: a living thing lights the lamps one by one with evidence — grows: its young picture swaps to its grown picture (chick → hen, bud → flower); food and water: a water drop is drawn in; makes young: a small copy (the young picture) appears beside it. A non-living thing lights nothing, even if it moves (the car drives across the bench and the lamps stay dark; the clock's hands turn and the lamps stay dark). Then the child sorts it into LIVING or NOT LIVING. Miss 1: the basket refuses and the lamps re-run. Miss 2: the lamps stay lit over the right basket. LAMPS-AFTER setting: sort first, then the lamps test it.
activities.misconception: Moving = alive (a car, the wind, a clock), and plants are not alive.
activities.pictures: Living: farm-animals (hen, chick, cow, calf, sheep, lamb, horse, foal), forest-creatures (caterpillar), insects-and-bugs (butterfly), spring (bud), flowers (tulip, sunflower), tree (apple tree), vegetables. Not living: vehicles (car, train), around-the-house (clock), toys (robot, ball, kite), beach (rock), camping (log → refused: once living).
activities.settings: Things: obvious / tricky (cars, clocks, robots, plants, seeds) · Lamps: shown first / test after sorting

activities.title: The Window-Sill Pot
activities.teaches: Know what plants need to grow: water and light (and soil and air).
activities.invention: THE PLANT THAT ANSWERS WHAT YOU GIVE IT. A pot (apparatus) on a window sill holds a library flower at small scale; a watering can (apparatus control), a curtain (open/closed) and a cupboard door wait. The child decides what the plant gets for a week — taps the can to water, opens or closes the curtain, or drags the pot into the cupboard — then pulls the week lever: the plant grows (scales up and stands tall) only with both water and light; with water but no light it grows pale (desaturated) and does not grow; with light but no water it droops (a slow lean). COMPARE mode (K-376): three pots get different treatment shown by icons (drop, sun, both); the child picks the one that will grow best, then the week lever runs all three. Miss 1: the chosen pot droops or pales while another grows; Miss 2: the missing need's icon flashes on the chosen pot.
activities.misconception: Plants need only water (or food); light does not matter.
activities.pictures: flowers (sunflower, tulip, daisy-like zinnia) — one flower per round; pot, can, curtain and cupboard are apparatus.
activities.settings: Mode: grow your pot / which pot grows best · Needs: water and light / plus soil
activities.rounds: 9 rounds; compare-mode pots shuffled with the right one in each slot ≤ 40 %; grow-mode rounds alternate the starting state (in the cupboard / dry / both missing); one right answer.
activities.distinct_from: No plant activity exists.

activities.title: The Rising Camera
activities.teaches: See that an object seen from above looks different from the side, and match side views to top views — the first step to reading a map.
activities.invention: THE SLIDER THAT LIFTS THE EYE. A table carries a few solid objects drawn as apparatus geometry (a cup = cylinder, a book = box, a cone hat, a ball, a table seen as a rectangle). A camera on a vertical slider looks at the table from the side; sliding it up rotates the view in steps until it looks straight down, and the outlines morph (cylinder → circle, box → rectangle, cone → circle with a dot). Task: the stage shows a top view on a map card; the child slides the camera to see the top views and drags each object's side card onto its top-view footprint — or arranges the objects on the table to match a small map.
activities.misconception: Expecting the top view to look like the side view (drawing the cup as a cup from above).

activities.distinct_from: No perspective or map activity exists at any grade.

activities.title: The Camping Backpack
activities.teaches: Tell needs (what we must have to live: water, food, shelter, clothing) from wants (nice to have).
activities.invention: THE FOUR POCKETS. A backpack for a camping trip has four shaped pockets — a water drop, a food bowl, a tent, a shirt — and a small open side net. The child drags library things into it: a need snaps into its pocket and the pocket glows full; a want (a toy car, a game, a lollipop) fits no pocket and goes in the side net. The trip can start only when all four pockets are full; filling the net with wants never starts it. So "need" is defined by the four pockets, not by liking.
activities.misconception: Anything I really like is a need; wants are bad.
activities.pictures: food, fruits, clothing, toys, household (bottle, bread, coat, blanket, tent if present)
activities.settings: Mode: pack the bag / need or want · Items: 6 / 10

activities.distinct_from: No economics activity exists.

activities.title: The Face Dial
activities.teaches: Recognise feelings from faces (happy, sad, angry, scared, surprised, calm), name them, and connect a situation to a feeling.
activities.invention: THE FACE THAT YOU SET. A big round dial (apparatus geometry: a circle, two dot eyes, one curve mouth, two short line brows) with two handles — the mouth handle bends the curve (smile ↔ frown, open), the brow handle tilts the brows (raised, flat, angled down). Setting them morphs the face continuously. A situation card shows a library picture (a lost balloon floating away; a present; a thunderstorm; a birthday cake) or a feeling word. The child sets the dial; each feeling is a REGION of handle space. Check: the dial slides next to the library emotions face of the target feeling. Right: the two overlap and the dial's outline glows. Miss 1: the dial and the library face sit side by side and the part that differs (brows or mouth) pulses. Miss 2: the handle that is wrong shows a faint target. GOOD-OR-HARD mode (K-333): library emotions faces slide to a "feels good" or "feels hard" cloud. TODAY mode: free play, no right answer.
activities.misconception: Reading only the mouth (a smile = happy, everything else = sad) and not the eyebrows; thinking some feelings are "bad" to have.
activities.pictures: emotions (happy, sad, angry, scared, surprised, tired, excited, bored); situations: toys (balloon), christmas (present), weather (stormy), bakery (cake); refused: a dog (it can carry any feeling).
activities.settings: Mode: set the face / match face to word / good or hard / today (explore) · Feelings: 4 / 6
activities.rounds: 9 situations per pass, each feeling ≥ once, chosen by the reviewer to be unambiguous in 11 locales; tolerance regions measured so neighbours (happy/excited, sad/tired) never overlap; one right feeling per situation.
activities.distinct_from: No SEL activity exists. Not a mascot: the face is an abstract dial, like the learning clock's hands.

activities.title: The Three Lanes
activities.teaches: Sort vehicles by where they travel — on land, on water, in the air — and tell which things can fly.
activities.invention: THE ROAD, THE SEA AND THE SKY. The stage is three bands: sky on top, sea in the middle, road at the bottom. The child drags a vehicle into a band and lets go: in the right band it moves off (the boat sails, the car drives, the plane flies); in the wrong band it cannot — a car on the sea bobs and drifts back, a boat on the road scrapes to a stop, a train in the sky drops gently down to its band. Fly mode: the bands are "can fly" (sky) and "cannot fly" (ground) with animals and things (a bee, a penguin, a kite, a balloon).
activities.misconception: Every bird flies (penguin), anything with wings flies, a seaplane / hovercraft (shown only in tricky rounds as "two lanes").
activities.pictures: vehicles theme (car, bus, train, boat, ship, plane, helicopter, bicycle, tractor), animals and insects (bird, penguin, bee, butterfly), toys (kite, balloon)
activities.settings: Mode: land–water–air / can fly or not · Things: everyday / tricky
activities.rounds: 9 things per pass, bands balanced, ≥ 2 tricky things in the tricky setting; one right band (two-lane vehicles accept either).
activities.distinct_from: No transport activity exists.

activities.title: The Fact Family Bar
activities.teaches: Three numbers make four facts: two additions and two subtractions read off one whole and its two parts.
activities.invention: THE BAR THAT ONLY CUTS ONE WAY. On top lies one whole bar (e.g. 9 squares); under it two part bars (4 and 5, two colours) that together exactly cover it. Beside them four empty fact rails, two printed '▢ + ▢ = ▢' and two '▢ − ▢ = ▢'. An addition rail takes two bars laid end to end and then the whole: it snaps only when the two parts end exactly where the whole ends, and 4 + 5 = 9 appears under the bars. A subtraction rail takes the whole first, then a part laid ON it: the uncovered stretch lights and becomes the third bar, 9 − 4 = 5. A part in the whole's place fails physically: the 9 bar laid on the 4 bar overhangs and slides back, so '4 − 9' cannot be made. A rail that would repeat a fact already made shakes and refuses. When all four rails hold four different facts, the bars stack back into the whole and the four sentences glow together. Miss 1 rings the overhang or the repeat; miss 2 numbers every square on the bars.
activities.misconception: Thinks a fact family is "any four sentences with these numbers" and writes 4 - 9 = 5, or does not see that the whole is always the biggest number and is the start of every subtraction.
activities.pictures: none (bars drawn as square-strips in the shell palette); optional identical library counters inside the squares (fruits) for the within-10 setting
activities.settings: Numbers: within 10 / within 20 · Show squares: always / only as a help.
activities.rounds: 9+ rounds from distinct (part, part) pairs with parts never equal in 7 of them (equal parts make only two facts, used once as a talking round); the order in which the four rails must be filled is free, so there is no answer position; the bars start shuffled left/right.
activities.distinct_from: match-pairs.add-it-both-ways shows only commutativity; numberbond.subtraction-unknown-addend shows one subtraction as a missing part. Neither makes all four facts from one whole, and neither makes an impossible subtraction physically refuse.
activities.risk: Equal-parts rounds have only two distinct facts; the round generator must treat them as a special case.

activities.title: The Mirror Tray
activities.teaches: Doubles (n + n) and halves: a double is a group and its mirror image; a half splits a group into two equal parts.
activities.invention: THE HINGED MIRROR. A tray with a hinge line down its middle. Double mode: a numeral card says how many to put on the left; the child taps that many identical library objects onto the left half (one tap, one object) and the hinged mirror swings over and shows the same objects on the right, each reflection joined to its object by a faint thread. The child types the total. Wrong: the reflected side dims away, leaving n on one side so the child sees the double is n and n again; miss 2 numbers the objects 1…2n across both halves. Halve mode: a row of objects lies across the tray and the child drags the hinge along it. Wherever it rests, the left side is reflected over the right as see-through ghosts: off-centre, the ghosts hang past the end of the row or leave real objects uncovered — equal halves are seen as a perfect overlay, never as a running count. When every object has its ghost the child types how many are on each side. An odd row can never overlay: one object always sits on the hinge (the 'can it be shared?' round; the child types how many on each side, and the lonely one stays in view). Right: the mirror flashes and the two halves slide apart into two matching rows.
activities.misconception: Doubles 6 as 6 + 1 or 12 + 12; halves by taking "some" off instead of making two EQUAL parts.
activities.pictures: nouns that read well mirrored: fruits/apple, orange, cherry; bakery/cupcake, doughnut; toys/ball, blocks; flowers/sunflower (identical instances per round, mirrored by CSS)
activities.settings: Mode: double / halve / mixed · Up to: doubles of 1–5 (totals to 10) / 1–10 (totals to 20)
activities.rounds: 8+ per mode from distinct n (never 0); keypad answers, so no answer position; in halve mode the row's length and start vary and its true centre is at the stage centre in ≤ 2 rounds (dragging to mid-screen is no shortcut); odd rows ≤ 1 per pass; mixed alternates double/halve.
activities.distinct_from: fractions.partition-equal-shares halves shapes, not quantities; the Twin Pools (#15) make a second group the same COUNT without the doubling sum; dealing-table (below) is about odd vs even, not the double fact.
activities.risk: Mirrored library pictures must be symmetric enough not to look wrong (pick nouns that read well flipped).

activities.title: The Number Wall
activities.teaches: In a number wall each brick holds the sum of the two bricks under it; a missing lower brick is found by subtracting.
activities.invention: BRICKS THAT POUR UP. A wall of 3 (or 4) rows; each brick is a small open crate. A filled bottom brick shows its numeral and, in the counter setting, that many identical library objects. The child taps two side-by-side bricks; their objects pour up into the empty brick resting on both and settle there — but its numeral stays blank: the child types the total, and only a right number lets the brick take its weight (a wrong one wobbles and the objects stay heaped; miss 2 numbers the objects). A pour is refused unless the two bricks are the pair that brick actually stands on: a diagonal or far pair makes the target brick tilt and shake. Missing-bottom face (and the start-at-the-top face): the top brick shows its total as a crate with that many slots; the child pours the known neighbour up into it and the slots it fills light, so the slots left empty ARE the missing brick — the child types that number. Numbers setting: bricks show numerals only and a pour rises as a filling bar; miss 2 brings the objects back. Right: the brick settles with a solid thunk.
activities.misconception: Adds the wrong pair (diagonal or non-adjacent bricks), or adds instead of subtracting when the top brick is known.
activities.pictures: fruits / vegetables (identical instances) for the counter setting; none for the numbers setting
activities.settings: Wall: 3 rows to 10 / 3-4 rows to 20 · Missing: top bricks / one bottom brick / start at the top.
activities.rounds: 8+ walls from random base triples/quads with every sum within the cap; the missing-brick position rotates across left, middle and right (measured 30-40% each); no wall repeats in a pass.
activities.distinct_from: No existing activity uses the additive pyramid; number bonds use one whole and two parts with no stacking or chaining.
activities.risk: Four-row walls at 20 must fit a phone at 360 px; counters give way to numerals above 10 per brick.

activities.title: The Hundreds Chart Patches
activities.teaches: The hundreds chart is rows of ten: one step right is +1, one step down is +10.
activities.invention: JIGSAW PATCHES. A 1–100 chart (1–50, 1–120 by setting) has holes. A plus- or L-shaped patch of 3–5 cells lies beside it with ONE number printed. The child fills the patch's other cells (tap a cell, then the keypad), then drags the patch onto the chart: it seats only where every cell matches its neighbours; a wrong cell glows and the patch pops back. Wrong-number task: a filled patch has exactly one error and the child taps it. Paint task: two starting cells are painted; the child paints the next ones; a cell off the step will not take paint, and the columns or diagonals appear as the pattern grows. Arrow-path task (absorbed Chart Rover): the chart is under fog except the start square; the child lays 2–4 arrow cards (→ +1, ↓ +10, ← −1, ↑ −10) into a short program, types the predicted landing number, then presses Go: a library toy car drives the path, lifting the fog square by square, so a wrong prediction shows along the trail; 'two paths' rounds meet on one square, 'jumps' rounds show start and end and ask for the shortest program. Miss 1 (patch tasks): the row and column through the anchor light with their +1 / +10 steps; miss 2: the true numbers ghost under the wrong cells. Right: the patch sinks flush into the chart and its numbers join the chart's ink.
activities.misconception: Thinks the number below is +1 (reads the chart as one long line), or that the cell left of 31 is 32.
activities.pictures: toys/car as the rover; otherwise none (chart tool-grade)
activities.settings: Chart: 1–50 / 1–100 / 1–120 · Task: fill the patch / find the wrong number / paint a counting path (2, 5, 10) / arrow path
activities.rounds: 8+ per task: random anchors and shapes (never only on the chart edge); the error in wrong-number rounds sits at each patch position equally often; paint starts distinct; rover programs never leave the chart and their landings are spread across the chart's rows; keypad answers.
activities.distinct_from: Track Repair is a linear number line; Number Lift (#19) is a vertical 1-10 shaft. Nothing uses the two-dimensional +1/+10 grid.
activities.risk: Ten columns at 360 give < 34 px cells: on phones the patch tasks zoom to the three rows round the hole and the rover task to a 5×5 window that scrolls with the car.
absorbed: grade 2 "The Chart Rover — Moving on the Hundreds Chart" (chart-rover): Use the hundreds chart's structure (right = 1 more, down = 10 more) to find where a path of arrows lands, find a square from two paths, and count the jumps between two numbers. — A hundreds chart under FOG: only the start square shows its number. A rover sits on it and the child lays arrow cards (↑ ↓ ← →) into a program slot, then predicts the landing number on a keypad BEFORE pressing Go. The rover drives the path, lifting the fog square by square, so a wrong prediction is visible along the trail. Two-paths mode: two programs from two starts meet on one square. Jumps mode: start and end both show; the child builds the shortest program (tens down, ones right) and the arrow counts are the difference.

activities.title: The Washing Line
activities.teaches: Skip counting by 2s, 5s and 10s is counting equal groups: each peg holds one group and its tag is the running total.
activities.invention: A LINE WITH PEGS. A washing line with pegs; each peg holds one equal group in a little net bag: a pair of socks (2s), 3 or 4 identical fruits (3s, 4s), 5 strawberries in a row (5s), 10 crayons as two rows of five (10s). Under each peg hangs an empty tag. The child hangs the next bag (drag from the basket) and drags the running-total numeral onto its tag from a small tray. A tag only takes the total of everything hung so far: a wrong number makes the line sag at that peg and the groups behind it slide together into one heap with its count in ones, so counting the groups (1, 2, 3) or adding 1 after a ten is seen to be wrong. Ticks setting: the bags vanish and the line becomes a number line with pegs 2, 5 or 10 apart, starting at 0, 25 or 50, with only some tags printed; the child pegs the missing ones. Miss 2 (both settings): the step is drawn as a bracket between two neighbouring pegs. Right: the line pulls tight with a little bounce and the finished tags are read as the count-by chant.
activities.misconception: Counts the groups (1, 2, 3) instead of the objects, or adds 1 instead of the step after a ten (10, 20, 21).
activities.pictures: accessories/sock (2s); fruits/strawberry, cherry, plum (3s, 4s, 5s); classroom/crayon (10s) — identical instances per bag; line, pegs and bags drawn as apparatus
activities.settings: Count by: 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 / 10 · Line: groups on pegs / number line with ticks (starts 0, 25 or 50; 3s and 4s start at 0)
activities.rounds: 7+ lines per step: missing tags at random positions (never only the last), starts vary; the tray offers the right total, total ± 1, total ± step and the count-of-groups distractor, reshuffled every tag so the right numeral has no fixed place.
activities.distinct_from: skipcount.fill hops a frog over numbered pads (5/10/100) with no objects; Posy's Egg Cartons count tens only; the Counting Necklace (#9) counts by ones. This links the count-by to equal groups and to interval ticks.
activities.risk: Need a clear identical "group of 2" and "group of 5" picture from the library (socks/gloves exist in clothing; check).
absorbed: grade 2 "The Stepping Stick — Count by 3s and 4s" (stepping-stick): Skip count by 3s and 4s from 0 (and from another start) and name the missing numbers in the sequence. — A long number track (0–50, ten stones a row, drawn apparatus) and a wooden STEPPING STICK exactly 3 (or 4) stones long. The child drags the stick so it starts where the last one ended; it snaps only end-to-end (no gap, no overlap) and the stone under its far end lights. Some landing stones are blank; on a blank one a keypad asks the number. Miss 1: the stick turns translucent so the child can count its stones; miss 2: dots under each stone the stick covers.

activities.title: The Number Name Builder
activities.teaches: Number words are built from parts (six, -teen, -ty / twen-, ones before or after tens in some languages) and say how many tens and ones.
activities.invention: WORD TILES THAT CARRY QUANTITY. A numeral sits above an empty name rail; beside the rail its value is shown as tens rods and ones cubes. Word-part tiles lie below — the parts a child of that language actually learns (en six, -teen, -ty, twen-, thir-; de sechs, und, zwanzig; fr seize, soixante, dix; fi kaksi, kymmentä, kuusi, toista; da tens words such as 'halvtreds' as ONE tile). As each tile snaps into the rail, its quantity appears under it as rods and cubes (a multiplicative tile such as fr 'quatre-vingts' shows four bundles of twenty). The rail lights only when the rods and cubes under the whole name equal the ones beside the numeral; 'sixty' for 16 shows six rods against one rod and six cubes, and the rail rejects it — the tiles bounce back. Where the language says the ones first (de/nl/da 'sechsundzwanzig'), the quantities still add up, so the spoken order is learnt without being told the digits are swapped. Reading mode: a name is given as tiles and the child builds its rods and cubes (tap to add a rod or a cube), then types the numeral. Miss 1: the quantity under the wrong tile glows; miss 2: the numeral's rods and cubes slide next to the rail's for a direct comparison. Right: the rail and the numeral glow together and the name is read in the bubble.
activities.misconception: Confuses -teen and -ty (sixteen / sixty), or (de/nl/da) writes the tens first because the digits read left to right.
activities.pictures: none (word tiles are the content; rods drawn tool-grade)
activities.settings: Numbers: to 20 / tens to 100 / to 50 · Direction: numeral to word / word to numeral.
activities.rounds: 8+ rounds per pass with at least two teen/ty confusables; tile tray always contains the confusable partner tile; numerals distinct within a pass.
activities.distinct_from: No activity reads or writes number names; place-value activities never attach words.
activities.risk: High native load: one morphology table per locale (fr 70–99, da 50–99 vigesimal names as unanalysed tiles, de/nl/da ones-before-tens, fi agglutinated 'kaksikymmentäkuusi' split kaksi|kymmentä|kuusi, sv/no regular). Each locale's tray must contain its own confusable partner (en sixteen/sixty, de sechzehn/sechzig, fr seize/soixante, fi kuusitoista/kuusikymmentä). Strong native review per locale.

activities.title: The Picture Graph Shelf
activities.teaches: Organise objects in up to three categories into a picture graph (one per cell) and read it: which has most, how many more.
activities.invention: SHELVES WITH SLOTS. A jumble of identical library objects of 2–3 kinds tumbles onto a table. Beside it a shelf with one row per kind (each row labelled by the library picture of its kind), all rows starting at the same line with equal slots, so a row can never be made longer by spacing. The child drags each object into its row; it snaps into the next free slot (the wrong row refuses and the object slides back). When the table is empty a question card asks: which has most / fewest (the child taps the row), or how many more X than Y — the child taps the OVERHANG (the slots of the longer row beyond the end of the shorter one) and types how many. Table setting: each row's count writes itself into a small table beside the shelf as the row fills. Miss 1: a straight edge slides down from the end of the shorter row; miss 2: the overhanging slots get numerals. Right: the question card turns over to the answer sentence.
activities.misconception: Judges "most" by how spread out the pictures look; computes "how many more" by naming the bigger count instead of the difference.
activities.pictures: fruits, vegetables, toys, farm animals, insects and bugs (identical instances per kind)
activities.settings: Categories: 2 / 3 · Question: most and fewest / how many more.
activities.rounds: 8+ rounds; counts per row distinct within a round (no ties unless the question is "same"), the answer row index balanced over a pass; objects fall in shuffled order.
activities.distinct_from: Sort and Count stops at a count; Pip's Stacking Fence builds bars from given numbers. This builds the graph from objects and reads the difference as cells.
activities.risk: Library art must give three same-size kinds per round.

activities.title: The Vowel Scoops
activities.teaches: Every syllable has exactly one vowel sound: split a word so that each part keeps its vowel.
activities.invention: SCOOPS UNDER THE WORD. A picture word lies on a line (letters as tiles) with its library picture above. The child drags little dividers into the gaps between letters; under each part a scoop forms and holds those letters. A scoop holding no vowel sags and drops its letters back onto the line (the divider springs out); a scoop holding a vowel lights the vowel like a heartbeat. Check (when every letter is scooped): right — the gated syllable split matches and each scoop beats once in order, then the picture nods. Miss 1: a scoop with two vowel sounds (ba|nana as two scoops) pulses twice, showing it needs another divider. Miss 2: the vowels on the line glow and the child tries again. COUNT setting: before splitting, the child taps how many scoops the word needs (1–3 scoop tiles), then splits to check.
activities.misconception: Splits a word into chunks of equal length or into letters, ignoring the vowel; counts letters instead of beats.
activities.pictures: animals, fruits, toys, vehicles — nouns in approved-words-<locale>.json (gated splits).
activities.settings: Words: 2 syllables / 2-3 syllables · Task: find the vowels / split and find the vowels.
activities.rounds: 9 words per pass (2- and 3-syllable), split positions never in the middle of the word in more than a third of rounds; core setting excludes silent-e and vowel-team words; team setting (en ea/ou/ai, de ei/au/eu, nl ij/ui/oe, fi long vowels aa/uu) lights the team as one vowel; one right split.
activities.distinct_from: Domino's Two-Part Words and the syllable builder assemble given syllables; neither states or tests the vowel-per-syllable rule.
activities.risk: Per-locale: fi/es/it are clean; en/fr/da need careful pools (no silent final e in the core pool; fr mute-e ruling open); da uses the K-1 orthographic pool.

activities.title: The Instruction Paintbox
activities.teaches: Read a sentence and do exactly what it says: how many, which colour, which picture, in which place, two steps.
activities.invention: A PAINTBOX AND A PICTURE ROW: a sentence ("Colour 3 fish red.") sits above a row of library pictures; colour pots (no words, swatches only) sit below. The child dips the brush and taps pictures; as each part of the sentence is satisfied, its words light in the sentence (the number, the colour, the noun). Painting a 4th fish, or a crab, makes the extra drip off and the matching word in the sentence blinks. Settings add place words (the 2nd bird, between the cat and the dog) and two-step sentences (colour ... and circle ...), and a true/false face where the child stamps the sentence true or false against the row.
activities.misconception: Paints all the fish (ignores the number), ignores the colour word, or does only the first half of a two-step instruction.
activities.pictures: ocean life, fruits, farm animals, toys, insects and bugs (identical instances where counting)
activities.settings: Sentence: one step / two steps / place words · Check: do it / true or false.
activities.rounds: 8+ sentences from templates over the vocab; the target pictures are scattered among distractors of the same kind count + 2; true/false 40-60%.
activities.distinct_from: Granny's Mending Basket checks meaning; Otto's Picture Book picks a picture. Neither makes the child execute a multi-part instruction.
activities.risk: Colour words must be readable to grade-1 readers: TTS bonus only; colour-blind safe palette (the swatch shows a texture/letter-free pattern too).

activities.title: The Word Class Frames
activities.teaches: Sort words into nouns, verbs and adjectives by testing them in a frame: "a ___", "I can ___", "the ___ dog".
activities.invention: TEST FRAMES. A sentence-strip machine holds two or three frames, each a short sentence with a gap and a little library picture beside it: "Look at the ___." (picture: an empty stand), "I can ___." (a library friend from animals), "a ___ ball" (a library ball). The child drops a word card into a frame; the frame READS itself (written; TTS bonus). If the word fits, the frame acts: the noun's library picture appears on the stand, the friend does the action (activities picture), the ball changes size or colour. If it does not fit, the strip crumples and the card drops out. The child may test the card in every frame, then drops it into the bin under the frame that worked. Miss (wrong bin): the card flies back to the frame that works and that frame replays. Success: all cards binned, the three bins glow in turn.
activities.misconception: Calls every word for something you can see a noun ("run" because there is a picture of running), or treats colours and sizes as nouns.
activities.pictures: Nouns: any colour theme; verbs: activities (dancing, running, reading, writing, jumping, baking…); adjectives: scale/colour transforms of toys/ball.
activities.settings: Classes: noun or verb / noun or adjective / all three.
activities.rounds: 10 cards per pass, classes balanced (40–60 % for two, 25–40 % for three); only words that belong to one class in that locale (no brush/run/play); one right bin.
activities.distinct_from: Glim's Describing Words separates adjectives from adverbs (grade 2); no activity makes the child TEST a word in a frame.
activities.risk: de: every noun is capitalised — in de the noun class carries a visible cue the native panel accepts as part of the skill (Nomen groß), and the real challenge is verb vs adjective; fi: frames authored with the right case so the gap takes a base form; native review of every card.
absorbed: grade 2 "The Slot Test — Noun, Verb or Adjective?" (slot-test): Classify words as nouns (naming), verbs (doing) or adjectives (describing). — Three test-frame slots sit above three bins: "I see a ___." · "I can ___." · "It is ___." A word card is dropped into each frame in turn and the frame READS the sentence (text + optional TTS); the frame where it makes sense lights and the card drops into that bin. The child decides which frame to try first and makes the final drop; a word that fits two frames (e.g. "run") is excluded from the pool so there is one answer. Picture help shows a library picture on noun cards.

activities.title: The Unchanging Picture
activities.teaches: Synonyms are different words with the same meaning: swapping one for the other leaves the picture the same.
activities.invention: THE PICTURE THAT DOES NOT CHANGE. A library picture sits under a sentence with a coloured swap slot ("The dog is big."). Word cards lie below. Dropping a card into the slot makes the picture redraw to match the new sentence: "large" leaves it still and the slot locks with a click; "small" shrinks the dog; "brown"/"red" tints it; "happy"/"sad" swaps the emotions face beside it. The task is to find the word that keeps the picture still. Miss 1: the picture changes and stays changed for a moment beside a faint copy of the original, so the change in meaning is seen; then the card returns. Miss 2: the cards that change the picture grey a little. PAIRS mode (G2-373, absorbed Meaning Mirror): left words are dropped on right words; each pair is tested in the same sentence. TWO-WORDS rounds (G1-395): two cards keep the picture still — both must be found.
activities.misconception: Picks a word from the same topic (big -> tall, or big -> dog) instead of one with the same meaning.
activities.pictures: animals, toys, fruits (scale and tint transforms only), emotions (happy, sad, angry, scared, tired) for feeling adjectives.
activities.settings: Words: size and colour / feelings · Choices: 3 / 4 · Task: find the swap / make pairs
activities.rounds: 9 rounds from a native-authored bank of picturable synonym pairs (big/large, small/little/tiny, happy/glad, scared/afraid, angry/cross, tired/sleepy…); distractors always one antonym + one same-topic word that redraws differently; the synonym's tray position balanced; one right word (two in two-word rounds).
activities.distinct_from: Shades of meaning orders by strength; Quill's opposites finds antonyms; this tests meaning-preservation.
activities.risk: Some locales have few picturable pairs — the native panel authors ≥ 9 per locale or the setting is refused there; G2-358 synonym worksheet faces that are verb-based go to doing-stage.
absorbed: grade 2 "The Meaning Mirror — Words That Mean the Same" (meaning-mirror): Recognise synonyms by testing whether a swapped word keeps the meaning of a sentence. — A short sentence with one word in a coloured slot ("The dog is big.") and, beside it, a MEANING MIRROR that shows the sentence as a picture (a big dog at large scale). The child drags a candidate word into the slot: if it means the same ("large"), the mirror picture stays still and the slot locks; if it changes the meaning ("small", "brown"), the picture changes to match the new sentence (the dog shrinks) — the child sees that meaning moved. Pairs mode: drag left words onto right words; each pair is tested in the same sentence.

activities.title: The Same-Way Machine
activities.teaches: Picture analogies: find the relation between a pair and apply it to a new picture.
activities.invention: THE SAME-WAY MACHINE. A machine with two input chutes and one output tray; a gear window in the middle. The first pair goes in by itself (chick → hen): the gear turns and shows the relation as a moving glyph (grows-up: a small dot growing; part-of: a piece fitting into a whole; lives-in: a dot entering a shape; used-with: two shapes clicking together). The third picture drops into the first chute (calf); three library pictures wait for the output (cow, barn-like haystack, milk). The child drags one into the output tray. Right: the gear turns the same way and both pairs light together. Miss 1: the gear grinds, the output pops out, and the first pair re-runs slowly beside it. Miss 2: the first pair's glyph is placed between the third picture and each candidate in turn — the one that fits clicks.
activities.misconception: Picks by theme association (cow goes with farm, so barn) instead of by the same relation.
activities.pictures: farm-animals (chick/hen, calf/cow, lamb/sheep, foal/horse, duckling/duck), body-parts (hand/finger, face/nose), around-the-house (key/lock, door, toothbrush/toothpaste), spring (bird/nest), ocean-life (fish) + beach (water), kitchen-tools (cup/teapot), clothing (glove/hand).
activities.settings: Relations: young-adult and whole-part / plus where-it-lives and what-it-is-used-for.
activities.rounds: 9 rounds with distinct triples, ≥ 2 relations per pass; the three outputs always include one same-theme distractor (calf → haystack); answer position balanced among 3; one right answer checked by the reviewer.
activities.distinct_from: No activity in the catalogue teaches analogical relations; Ziggy's Odd One Out is category exclusion.
activities.risk: Glyph legibility without words must be tested with the reviewer; triples where two outputs fit are refused.

activities.title: The Clue Table
activities.teaches: Logic grids: use yes/no picture clues to cross out impossibilities and find what each child has.
activities.invention: THE CLUE STAMPS. A grid: library animal friends down the side (3 or 4), things across the top (toys, fruits, pets). Clue cards lie beside it, each made of pictures only: friend + thing with a ring (has it) or a cross (does not). The child drags a clue card onto the grid; it stamps its tick or cross into the right cell and fades to a small mark at the side. When a row or column has all but one cell crossed, the last cell glows and the child taps it to tick it; the thing then slides to that friend's plate. Miss 1 (a tick against a clue): the cell shakes and the clue that forbids it flips back over. Miss 2: the forced cell glows brighter. SWEEP setting (G3-378/379): a tick does not cross its row and column automatically — the child taps the crosses; a wrong sweep cell shakes. READ mode (G2-345): a solved grid and picture sentences dropped on tick or cross.
activities.misconception: Reads a cross as "has it", or stops after one clue instead of using elimination.
activities.pictures: Friends: farm-animals/animals (cat, dog, rabbit, duck, pig, sheep). Things: toys (ball, kite, car, doll), fruits (apple, banana, pear), pets.
activities.settings: Grid: 2×2 / 3×3 / 4×4 · Clues: yes/no / with either-or (G2-344) · Sweep: automatic / by hand
activities.rounds: 9 puzzles per grid size with a unique solution found by an exhaustive solver; clue order shuffled; the first forced cell varies across rows and columns; one right grid.
activities.distinct_from: No activity teaches elimination; the Sudoku Garden is placement under constraints, this is deduction from clues.
activities.risk: Child pictures in the library are few (baby, baby_girl, girl, occupations) — may need animal friends instead.
absorbed: grade 2 "The Clue Board — Logic Grid Puzzles" (clue-board): Solve a small logic grid (3 children × 3 pets/foods) from yes, no and either-or clues, and read a solved grid. — A 3×3 grid: children down the side (library children/occupations), things across the top (pets, fruits, toys). Clue cards lie beside it. Dragging a clue card onto the grid stamps it: a "yes" clue places a check AND automatically crosses out the rest of its row and column (the rule of the grid pushes back); a "no" clue places an X. When a row has two X's, the last square glows — the child taps it to check it. Read mode: a solved grid and true/false sentence cards the child drops on ✓ or ✗.

grade 3 "The Clue Stamps" (clue-stamps): Solve a logic grid by turning each clue into crosses and ticks and using 'one per row and column'. — THE CLUE STAMPS: a 3×3 or 4×4 grid of children × pictures; each clue is a card shown with pictures (e.g. 'Mia does NOT have the kite'). The child drags a clue card onto the grid; it stamps the cross or tick it proves into the right cell and fades. When a row gets a tick, the child taps the rest of the row and column to cross them (the 'sweep'); a wrong sweep cell shakes and the clue that forbids it lights. A tick placed against a clue makes that clue card turn back over. The puzzle is solved when each child has one picture.

activities.title: The Sudoku Garden
activities.teaches: In a 4x4 picture sudoku every row, column and box holds each picture once; use what is already planted to decide.
activities.invention: GARDEN BEDS: a 4x4 bed in four 2x2 boxes with some flowers already planted. The child drags seed packets onto empty soil. A seed that repeats a flower already in its row, column or box will not root: a thread lights between the two same flowers and the seedling wilts back into its packet. A "why" tap on an empty cell lights its row, column and box together so the child sees the three missing sets.
activities.misconception: Checks only the row (or only the box), and guesses rather than finding the cell with one possibility.
activities.pictures: flowers (4 distinct), vegetables, fruits
activities.settings: Size: 4x4 with 8 given / 6 given · Pictures: 4 flowers / 4 fruits.
activities.rounds: 8+ puzzles from a generator that guarantees a unique solution; at least one forced single per puzzle; given cells never form a solvable pattern by position alone.
activities.distinct_from: No activity uses Latin-square constraints.
activities.risk: Uniqueness generator must be verified exhaustively (4x4 is small: enumerate).
absorbed: grade 3 "The Latin Garden" (latin-garden): Each row, column and box holds every picture exactly once; deduce empty cells from what is already there. — THE LATIN GARDEN: a 6×6 (4×4 on the easier setting) garden of beds; six flower or vegetable pictures. The child drags a picture into an empty bed; if that picture already grows in the same row, column or box, a vine draws from the new one to its twin and the new one wilts back to the tray — the constraint is visible. Tapping an empty bed shows little ghost pictures of only those still possible there, as a help the child can switch on. The garden blooms when full.

activities.title: The Moon Lamp
activities.teaches: The sun, earth and moon move in patterns; the moon's shape seems to grow and shrink in a regular order.
activities.invention: A LAMP, A GLOBE AND A MOON ON A TRACK. A lamp (apparatus) shines from the left; the library Earth sits in the middle; the library Moon rides a ring track around it. The child drags the Moon round the track; a round window "from Earth" shows the Moon's lit part computed from the angle (a white disc and a shadow, geometry). ORDER task (G1-391): phase cards (geometry) are laid on the track in order from a given start, growing or shrinking; a card out of order does not match the window and slides back. NAME task (G2-367): a phase lights in the window and the child picks its name card. DAY/NIGHT task (G2-368): pins with tiny library houses sit on Earth; the child turns Earth and taps day or night for each pin — the lamp decides. Miss 1: the window shows the true phase for the dropped place beside the card; Miss 2: the right place on the track glows.
activities.misconception: Thinks the moon changes because the earth's shadow covers it, or that the moon makes its own light.
activities.pictures: space (earth, moon), miscellaneous (house) for pins; lamp, track and phases are apparatus.
activities.settings: Task: phases in order / name the phase / day and night · Phases: 4 / 8
activities.rounds: 9 rounds with different starting phases and directions; name rounds cover each phase once per pass; day/night rounds 3–5 pins; one right answer.
activities.distinct_from: No space activity exists.
activities.risk: pt-BR: the lit side is mirrored in the southern hemisphere — a pt setting renders the window mirrored (decided by the pt panel). Phase names ×11 by the native panel.
absorbed: grade 2 "The Orbit Lamp — Day, Night and the Moon" (orbit-lamp): Explain day and night by the Earth turning toward or away from the Sun, and name the Moon's phases from where the Moon is on its orbit. — A sun lamp on the left lights one half of a turning Earth (library earth, lit half bright, far half shaded). Pins with small library houses sit on the Earth; the child turns the Earth with a drag and taps day or night for each pin — the lamp decides. Moon mode: the Moon (library moon) can be dragged around the Earth on its orbit ring; a window shows how the Moon looks from Earth at that place (the lit part computed from the angle); the child names the phase or drags the Moon to make a named phase.

activities.title: The Field Lens
activities.teaches: Animals are grouped by their body covering: mammals have fur or hair, birds feathers, fish and reptiles scales, amphibians smooth wet skin.
activities.invention: THE FIELD LENS. Library animals wait on the left; four drawers on the right show a swatch on the front (fur: soft strokes; feathers: chevrons; scales: overlapping arcs; smooth wet skin: plain glossy) — pattern geometry, not drawings of animals. The child drags the lens over an animal: under it a patch of the picture enlarges so the covering can be seen. Then the animal goes into a drawer. Right: the drawer closes and the swatch flashes. Miss 1: the drawer will not close and the lens re-opens on the same patch next to the drawer's swatch. Miss 2: the right drawer's swatch glows. GROUP-NAME setting (G1-201): the drawers carry the class names (mammal, bird, fish, reptile, amphibian) and surprise animals appear (penguin → bird by its feathers; bat → mammal by its fur; turtle → reptile by its scales); whale and dolphin appear ONLY here, with a second lens clue (the blowhole: "breathes air") and go to mammals.
activities.misconception: Calls a whale a fish, a penguin not a bird (it cannot fly), a turtle an amphibian.
activities.pictures: Mammals: animals, zoo-animals, farm-animals; birds: birds, birds-2; fish: ocean-life (fish, clownfish, tuna, shark, angelfish); reptiles: reptiles-and-amphibians (turtle, iguana, gecko, alligator, cobra, chameleon, tortoise); amphibians: frog, salamander; surprises: penguin, bat, whale, dolphin.
activities.settings: Coverings: 3 (fur, feathers, scales) / 4 (+ wet skin) · Show group names: off / on.
activities.rounds: 10 animals per pass, each drawer 20–35 %; covering rounds exclude whale, dolphin, manatee, narwhal, orca; group rounds include ≥ 2 surprises once the basic pass is done; one right drawer from a reviewed table.
activities.distinct_from: No science activity exists; Mim's Memory Baskets sort by everyday category, not by biological trait.
activities.risk: The cartoon patch must actually show the covering (some library animals are flat colour) — the reviewer opens every lens patch; refused if unreadable.

activities.title: The Cycle Wheel
activities.teaches: Living things grow in a cycle: egg/seed, young, adult, which makes new eggs/seeds again.
activities.invention: THE WHEEL THAT GROWS EACH STAGE FROM THE LAST. A round wheel of 4 slots joined by arrows; the first stage sits in place. The child drags stage cards into the slot the arrow points to next. Right: the stage grows out of the one before in a short morph and the arrow lights. Miss 1: a stage dropped out of turn slides back along the arrow it skipped; Miss 2: the next slot shows a faint outline. Full wheel: the child turns it and the adult leads back to the first stage — the cycle does not end. WHAT-NEXT mode (G1-390): one stage, three candidates from the same cycle. WHOSE-YOUNG mode (G2-366): a young stage drops on the hub and the wheel turns to its adult. TWIN-WHEELS mode (G3-393, merged): butterfly and frog wheels side by side; fact cards dropped on the left wheel, the right wheel or the shared hub; the wheel turns to the window that proves it.
activities.misconception: Thinks the cycle is a line that ends with the adult, or that a caterpillar comes before the egg.
activities.pictures: Exist: farm-animals (chick, hen), forest-creatures/spring (caterpillar), insects (butterfly), frog, spring (bud, flower), insects (ladybug). MISSING: plain egg (bird/butterfly/frog), chrysalis, frogspawn, tadpole, froglet, seed, seedling, ladybug larva/pupa.
activities.settings: Cycle: chicken / butterfly / frog / plant / mixed · Task: fill the wheel / what comes next.
activities.rounds: 8+ rounds across cycles; the slot asked to fill varies; next-stage distractors drawn from the same cycle.
activities.distinct_from: Story sequencing orders events of a story; this is a closed biological cycle.
activities.risk: Blocked on stage art. Stage names ×11 by the native panel when built.
absorbed: grade 2 "The Life-Cycle Wheel — From Egg to Butterfly" (life-cycle-wheel): Order the stages of a life cycle (egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly; egg, tadpole, froglet, frog) and match a young stage to the adult it becomes. — A WHEEL with four slots and a hand that turns. The child places the stage cards in the slots; when the wheel is turned, the hand passes each stage and the next one grows out of it in a short morph; a wrong order breaks the growth (the hand stops at the stage that cannot come next). Whose-baby mode: young stages drop onto the hub; the wheel turns to the adult it becomes.

grade 3 "The Twin Life Wheels" (twin-wheels): Compare the butterfly and frog life cycles: both change form (metamorphosis), with different stages. — THE TWIN WHEELS: two turning wheels side by side, each with four windows. The child turns a wheel to put its stages in order (egg -> caterpillar -> chrysalis -> butterfly; egg -> tadpole -> froglet -> frog); a wrong order jams the wheel. Then fact cards ('lays eggs in water', 'has a stage in a case', 'starts life breathing with gills', 'its young look different from the adult') are dropped onto the left wheel, the right wheel, or the hub between them (both); the wheel the fact belongs to turns to the window that proves it.
activities.blocked: The library has no plain egg (easter/egg is a painted Easter egg), chrysalis, tadpole, froglet, frogspawn, seed or seedling; no cycle can be completed honestly. It now also holds twin-wheels (G3-393), the two-cycle comparison, as a mode.

activities.title: The Material Test Bench
activities.teaches: Objects are made of materials (paper, plastic, glass, metal, wood) that we can tell by their properties, and that are recycled separately.
activities.invention: A BENCH OF TESTS. A library object sits on the bench; four test tools wait (apparatus): a MAGNET, a WATER DROP, a BEND clamp, a LAMP. Each test the child drags onto the object leaves a mark on its card: magnet — sticks (steel) or not; water — soaks in (paper) or beads up; bend — bends (paper, plastic) or stays stiff (glass, metal, wood); lamp — shines through (glass, clear plastic) or not. The marks make a signature: metal = sticks; paper = soaks; plastic = bends, no soak; glass = light through, does not bend; wood = none of these. Then the child drops the object into a material bin. Right: it lands and its marks light as the proof. Miss: the bin rejects it and shows the mark that contradicts it (a clear bottle in "glass" — its BEND mark lights). ODD-ONE-OUT mode (G2-348): three objects of one material and one different; the tests reveal the odd one.
activities.misconception: Thinks all shiny things are metal, or that a plastic bottle is glass because it is clear.
activities.pictures: kitchen-tools (jar, glass, bottle, spoon), at-the-supermarket (can — steel food can, water bottle — plastic), post-office (envelope, letter, package), classroom (notebook, ruler), furniture (chair, stool — wood), tools (nail, hammer, bolt).
activities.settings: Materials: 3 / 5 · Tests: available / off (sort only).
activities.rounds: 10 objects per pass, materials balanced; each object a single clear material whose picture shows it (steel can, wooden chair); one right bin; tests may be switched off (sort only).
activities.distinct_from: The K recycling-which-bin face sorts by bin; this tests properties to decide the material.
activities.risk: Every object's test results come from one reviewed table; aluminium drinks cans refused (the library can is a food tin = steel). G1-365 (draw three things you recycle) stays a worksheet.
absorbed: grade 2 "The Material Test Bench — What Is It Made Of?" (material-bench): Group objects by the material they are made of (metal, glass, plastic, paper, wood) using their properties, for recycling. — A bench with test tools: a MAGNET, a LAMP (does light shine through?), a WATER DROP (soaks in?), a BEND test. The child runs tests on an object; each test shows its true result (the magnet pulls a tin can, light shines through a glass jar, water soaks into paper). Then the object goes into the recycling bin for its material. Odd-one-out mode: three objects of one material and one different — the tests reveal the odd one.

activities.title: The Map Key
activities.teaches: A map uses symbols, and the key tells what each symbol means; you can find and count things using the key.
activities.invention: THE KEY STENCIL. A bird's-eye town of apparatus blocks (streets, a park, a river) dotted with small map symbols (simple geometry: a triangle tree, a square house, a cross, a circle pond) drawn at two sizes and two shades. The key strip shows each symbol beside its library picture (tree, house, car, tent, lake). The child drags a key symbol over the map like a stencil: every matching symbol, whatever its size or shade, lights through it. The child sets the count on the key with + and − beads. Right: the count locks and the lit symbols ripple. Miss 1: one unlit match blinks; Miss 2: the stencil sweeps the map once by itself. WHERE-IS-IT task: "the tree next to the river" — the child taps the one symbol that fits the key and the place.
activities.misconception: Takes a symbol's size or colour for its meaning, or counts the key itself.
activities.pictures: Key pictures: tree (apple tree), miscellaneous (house), vehicles (car, bus), camping (tent, lake), around-the-house (mailbox); map symbols are apparatus geometry.
activities.settings: Symbols: 3 / 5 · Task: find and count / where is it.
activities.rounds: 9 maps, symbols placed on a grid at random with 2–6 of each; every map has the asked symbol at two sizes; counts distinct per symbol; one right count.
activities.distinct_from: Bramble's Parking Tower is position words; no map activity exists.
activities.risk: Map symbols are geometry (tool-grade) but must not become hand-drawn objects.

activities.title: The One-Digit Box — Column Addition and Subtraction
activities.teaches: Add and subtract 2- and 3-digit numbers in written columns, ones first, recording the carried ten above the tens and the borrowed ten in the ones.
activities.invention: THE ONE-DIGIT BOX. The written sum on squared paper with digits aligned in H/T/O columns; under each column an answer box that holds exactly ONE digit. Only the ones box is open first, so the child must work right to left. Addition: if the ones make 13, the child types 13 and the box keeps the 3 while the extra ten pops out as a small '1' tag the child drags up to the carry hat on top of the tens column; the tens box opens only when the hat is filled. Subtraction: when the top ones digit is too small the ones box refuses (no negative fits); the child taps the tens digit above, which ticks down by one while a '1' hops in front of the ones digit (5 becomes 15). Across a zero: tapping a 0 in the tens does nothing; the tap must start at the hundreds digit, which ticks down, the tens 0 becomes 10, then ticks to 9 as the ten moves on. Miss 1: the column lights and its two digits are read in the bubble; miss 2: a ten-frame of that column's ones appears beside it. Counter help (absorbed Carry Chute): every digit is also a stack of counters in its lane; ten counters slide down a chute into the next lane as one, and a borrowed counter breaks into ten on landing. Right: the finished answer is read and the column digits flash once.
activities.misconception: Writing 13 in the ones place (or forgetting the carried ten); starting at the left; subtracting the smaller digit from the bigger regardless of position (52 − 27 = 35).
activities.pictures: none (paper, digits and boxes are the content)
activities.settings: Operation: add / subtract / mixed · Size: 2-digit / 3-digit · Regrouping: none / one place / two places (incl. across a zero) · Help: digits only / counters in the lanes
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 rounds per setting, generated to the setting (no-regroup rounds never need a carry, one-place rounds exactly one); answers never repeated in a pass; mixed mode balances + and −.
activities.distinct_from: Tuck (place-value-regroup) regroups BLOCKS and Exchange Machine (tool #45) co-locates material and digits; this is the written algorithm alone — the step after the blocks, which every column worksheet drills.
activities.risk: Low.
absorbed: grade 3 "The Carry Chute" (carry-chute): Add and subtract within 1000 in columns: carry when a column passes 9 and borrow across a zero, writing the digits. — THE CARRY CHUTE: a column board with ones, tens and hundreds lanes; the problem is written at the top in digits and each digit is also a little stack of counters in its lane. The child works one column at a time from the right: tapping the ones column adds (or takes) its counters; if there are ten or more, ten counters slide into a chute and drop into the tens lane as one counter while a small '1' is written above the tens column — the carry is the counter. For subtraction the child drags one counter down from the next column; it breaks into ten on landing, and when that column is empty (a zero) the drag must start further left and break twice. The child types each answer digit under its column.

activities.title: The Dealing Tray — A Fraction of a Set
activities.teaches: Find one half, one third or one fourth of a set of 4–24 objects by dealing it into equal shares, and say how many one share is.
activities.invention: THE DEALING TRAY. A tray with 2, 3 or 4 equal compartments under a strip of lids, and a pile of identical library objects. Each tap deals the next object into the next compartment in turn (round-robin, like dealing cards), so the shares stay equal by construction — the tray cannot take objects any other way. When the pile is empty the task line asks for one third (or 2/3, 3/4 in the several-shares setting): the child lifts the lids of that many compartments and types how many objects are under the open lids. Miss 1 (typed the number of shares, 3 for one third of 12): the closed compartments shake and the open share's objects number themselves; miss 2: every compartment shows its count. Right: the open share slides out onto a plate beside its fraction card (1/3) while the rest stays in the tray, so the share is seen as a part of the whole set.
activities.misconception: "One third of 12 is 3" (the denominator taken as the answer): the tray makes 3 the NUMBER OF SHARES, and the answer is what is in one share.
activities.pictures: fruits / toys / vegetables (identical instances)
activities.settings: Fraction: halves / thirds / fourths / mixed · Take: one share / several shares (2/3, 3/4 — absorbed Fence Pens)
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 rounds per setting: set sizes that are multiples of the denominator, 4–24, never a set equal to the denominator twice in a row; the compartment to lift is chosen at random (all hold the same, so the reading cannot be guessed by position).
activities.distinct_from: Maple's Bakery shares cookies onto plates (division answer = per plate); the tray names the share as a FRACTION of the whole set and asks for one share only, the bridge to 3.NF.A.1. Not the Treat Box or Fruit Crates.
activities.risk: Low.
absorbed: grade 3 "The Fence Pens" (fence-pens): A fraction of a set: split the group into b equal pens and take a of them. — THE FENCE PENS: a meadow holds N identical animals. The child drags fence posts across the meadow to split it into b pens; the animals walk into the pens one at a time (round-robin), so unequal pens are impossible to leave unnoticed — a pen with one more animal sways. Then the child taps a pens to open their gates, and the animals that come out are counted into a barn readout: that number is a/b of N. Miss 1 shows the count in each pen; miss 2 rings one pen as 1/b.

activities.title: The Tick Comb — Where on the Number Line?
activities.teaches: Locate and read numbers on a number line that does not start at 0 and labels only every 5th or 10th tick.
activities.invention: THE TICK COMB. A number-line window (40–60, 60–100, or a random 20-wide window up to 100) labels only every 5th or 10th tick. A dot sits on an unlabelled tick. The child drags a COMB out of any label: each tooth drops onto the next tick and shows +1, +2, +3 …; the comb pulls right or left, so counting back from the next label works too. The child types the number at the dot. Place mode: a number is given and the child drags the dot onto a tick; the comb then comes out from the nearest label and shows how far off it landed. Miss 1: the nearest label pulses and the comb snaps out from it to the dot; miss 2: every tick between the two neighbouring labels gets a faint numeral. Right: the dot becomes a labelled tick that stays on the line for the rest of that window's rounds.
activities.misconception: Counting from 0 or from the left end of the window, counting the label tick itself as 1, or treating each tick as 10 because the labels go up in tens.
activities.pictures: none
activities.settings: Window: 40–60 / 60–100 / random 20-wide window up to 100 · Labels: every 5 / every 10
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 rounds: dot positions never on a label, spread left/right of the nearest label (≥ 3 rounds where counting back is shorter); windows shuffled.
activities.distinct_from: Track Repair numbers every tie from a start; Hopper adds by hops from 0; the Landing Strip and Open Number Line are tools. The comb counts ticks from a sparse label, which is the 2.MD.B.6 reading skill.
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Wallet Bar — Is There Enough Money?
activities.teaches: Add the prices of 2–3 items, decide if a sum of money is enough, and find how much more is needed or how much is left.
activities.invention: THE WALLET BAR. The money in the purse is a long bar ruled in tens (one square per whole unit of the locale's currency: €, $, kr, R$). The child drags 2–3 items (library pictures with price tags) from the shop shelf. For 'total' and 'enough?' their price blocks wait stacked above the bar while the child answers (types the total, or taps the full-bar icon / the overhang icon); then the blocks lay along the bar end to end from the left to show the truth. For 'how much more' and 'change' the blocks lay along the bar at once and the child types the overhang or the empty end. Blocks inside the bar = enough, and the empty end is the change; blocks sticking out = not enough, and the overhang is how much more. Miss 1: the blocks' ends get running totals (12, 27 …) above the bar; miss 2: the empty end or the overhang is ruled in ones. Right: the items drop into a library basket (at-the-supermarket/basket) and the bar's leftover glows.
activities.misconception: Adding money and price together, or subtracting the wrong way ("how much more" taken as the total); confusing "enough" with "the most expensive item".
activities.pictures: At the Supermarket / fruits / toys / bakery (shelf items)
activities.settings: Question: total of a basket / enough? / how much more / change · Money: to 20 / to 100 (whole units only)
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 rounds per question: baskets of 2–3 items with fresh prices; enough/not-enough balanced; the shelf order is shuffled so the item to pick is never in a fixed place.
activities.distinct_from: coin-stall / money.* count COINS to a target; Money Mat (tool #18) is coin play. The wallet bar is about the arithmetic of prices (sum, compare, difference) shown as lengths — the part those activities skip. Not the Fruit Stand.
activities.risk: Prices must be plausible per currency (kr-locales: the same goods cost ~10× the € price — per-locale price tables; keep 'to 20' for small items such as fruit and pencils); the currency symbol position follows the locale (5 € / € 5 / 5 kr / R$ 5).

activities.title: The Gram Balance — Weigh in Grams
activities.teaches: Find the mass of an object in grams on a pan balance with weights (100 g, 50 g, 20 g, 10 g, 5 g) and read a dial scale with small steps.
activities.invention: THE GRAM BALANCE. A pan balance with one library object on the left pan and a box of drawn weights stamped 100 g, 50 g, 20 g, 10 g, 5 g. The child drags weights onto the right pan; the beam tilts by the real difference and levels only when the weights equal the object's mass, while a small needle at the pivot shows how far off it is. When level, the child types the total of the weights. Dial mode: the same object sits on a drawn kitchen scale whose dial is marked every 10, 20 or 50 g with numerals only every 100; the child drags a reading tag to the needle's mark and types the reading. Miss 1 (balance): the weights on the pan show their running sum above it; (dial) the marks between the two numbered marks light one by one; miss 2: the bubble names the step ('each mark is 20 g'). Big-looking-but-light objects (a balloon, a pillow) are weighed against small heavy ones, so size never decides. Right: the beam settles level with a soft click (balance), or the tag locks onto the needle (dial).
activities.misconception: Bigger looks heavier (a big balloon vs a small apple — masses chosen to contradict size in some rounds), and on the dial counting each small mark as 1.
activities.pictures: single library objects with a hand-checked mass table: fruits/apple, banana, pineapple, watermelon; vegetables/potato, carrot, pumpkin; toys/ball, balloon, car; kitchen-tools/mug, pot, teapot; around-the-house/pillow; tools/hammer — the balance, weights and dial are drawn apparatus (no scale picture exists in the library)
activities.settings: Mode: balance with weights / dial scale · Range: to 500 g / to 1000 g
