activities.rounds: ≥ 8 objects per setting with masses on the 5 g grid, ≥ 2 rounds where the larger-looking object is lighter; dial step size varies (10/20/50 g) between rounds; order-only reshuffle.
activities.distinct_from: Pond-Juice reads capacity; Measurement Bench (tool #17) weighs in CUBES (non-standard). Grams with standard weights and a scale with small steps are not covered.
activities.risk: Medium: per-locale unit words (g) are fine; object masses must be plausible — a native/pedagogy check of the mass table.

activities.title: The Double Stamp — Pictographs Where Each Picture Counts 2
activities.teaches: Read and make a pictograph whose key says each picture stands for 2 (half a picture for 1).
activities.invention: THE DOUBLE STAMP. A graph board with 3–4 rows, each labelled by a library picture, and a key card: one picture = 2. Make mode: a small table gives each row's count; the child presses a rubber stamp along a row, and each press prints one picture worth 2. An odd count can only be reached with the HALF-STAMP, which prints half a picture worth 1; a whole picture where a half is needed overshoots and the row's last print flashes. Read mode: a finished graph; the child taps a row and types its real count. Bars setting (absorbed Value Bricks): the board becomes a bar graph whose bricks are stamped with the scale (2, 5 or 10) and the axis counts by the scale — 35 needs seven 5-bricks; a half-brick exists only where the scale needs it. Miss 1: the prints in the row count up by the key under each print (2, 4, 6 …); miss 2: each print splits into its units. Right: the row's total appears at its end and the key card glows.
activities.misconception: Counting the pictures as ones (a row of 4 pictures read as 4, not 8), and not knowing what a half picture means.
activities.pictures: fruits / animals / toys / sports (row labels + stamp face)
activities.settings: Mode: make the graph / read the graph · Graph: pictograph (picture = 2, or = 5) / bar graph of value bricks (brick = 2, 5 or 10)
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 rounds: fresh counts 2–16 per row with ≥ 1 odd count per round in make mode; the row asked is chosen at random; no two rows equal.
activities.distinct_from: Pip's Stacking Fence (graph-it) builds bars at one unit per block; the stamp is a SCALED unit, which no activity teaches.
activities.risk: Low.
absorbed: grade 3 "The Value Bricks" (value-bricks): Read and build scaled bar graphs and pictographs where one brick or picture stands for 2, 5 or 10. — THE VALUE BRICKS: a data table on the left; on the right a graph whose bricks each carry a stamped scale value (5). The child drags bricks onto each column until it reaches the table value — 35 needs 7 bricks, and the axis numbers count by 5 beside them. A half-brick (worth 2 or 5 of 10) is available only on the scale settings that need it. In read mode the bars are built and the child types each value; a pictograph setting swaps bricks for library pictures with a key 'one picture = 5'. Miss: the bricks in the column count up by the scale aloud and on screen.

activities.title: The Week-Drop Calendar — Read a Month
activities.teaches: Find the weekday of a date, the date one week later, and the number of days between two dates on a month calendar.
activities.invention: THE WEEK-DROP CALENDAR. A month calendar (7 columns, weekday initials on top, a fresh month layout each round) and a sticker the child drags. One square right = 1 day later; one row DOWN = 7 days later; the sticker leaves a footprint on every day it passes. Weekday question: the child slides the sticker straight up its column to the weekday header. One week later / earlier: the child drops it one row down or up — the next square (12 → 13) is a lure the footprints expose as 1 day, not 7. Days between: the child walks the sticker from one date to the other and types the number of days; only after the answer do the footprints number themselves (the start day carries no footprint, so counting the start day shows as one too many). Miss 1: the footprints on the path pulse; miss 2: they number themselves. Right: the event sticker (a library picture: bakery/cake, vegetables/pumpkin, christmas/present) lands on its date and the date ring closes.
activities.misconception: Thinking one week later is the next number (12 → 13), or counting the start day when counting days between.
activities.pictures: none (drawn calendar); seasonal library pictures (birthday cake, pumpkin…) as event stickers
activities.settings: Question: weekday / one week later / days between / mixed · Month: starts Monday (eu) / Sunday (us) by locale
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 rounds per question with a fresh month layout (start weekday and length 28–31 vary) and fresh dates; weekday answers spread over all 7 columns.
activities.distinct_from: No calendar activity exists; Calendar Wall (tool #7) is the class's daily routine tool. Here the 7-day row structure is the mechanic.
activities.risk: Low. First weekday and weekday letters per locale.

activities.title: The Shadow Table — Tangram Shadows
activities.teaches: Compose a shape from tangram pieces to fill a shadow exactly, and tell a turned or flipped arrangement from the matching one.
activities.invention: A dark SHADOW on a light table and the seven tangram pieces in a tray. The child drags pieces into the shadow, tapping a piece to turn it 45° and a flip handle to flip it; a piece only settles when it lies fully inside the shadow without overlapping another — a piece that sticks out casts its own little shadow outside the dark area. Match mode (worksheet face): three finished solutions sit beside the shadow; the child drags each over the shadow — only the exact one lies flat inside; turned and flipped ones stick out.
activities.misconception: Accepting a flipped or turned arrangement as "the same" and thinking a shape only fits one way round.
activities.pictures: none (tangram pieces are apparatus geometry)
activities.settings: Mode: build the shadow / pick the matching solution · Help: piece outlines shown / no outlines
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 shadows (animals, house, boat, rocket… made of 5–7 pieces) per mode; in match mode the right solution's position is balanced across the three slots.
activities.distinct_from: Shapeforge (Mim's Glow Workshop) fuses triangles/rhombi without orientation demands; no activity uses tangrams or tests flips.
activities.risk: Low. Tangram outlines must not read as hand-drawn pictures — they are silhouettes made of the pieces.

activities.title: The Ink-Pad Solids — Faces, Edges and Corners
activities.teaches: Count the faces, edges and vertices of 3D solids, and match a solid to an everyday object of the same shape.
activities.invention: THE INK PAD. A drawn 3D solid (cube, rectangular prism, triangular prism, square pyramid, cylinder, cone, sphere) sits beside an ink pad and a sheet of paper. Faces: the child taps a face; the solid rolls onto it, presses on the pad and prints that face's outline on the paper, and the face keeps an ink dot so it cannot be counted twice — rolling brings the hidden back and bottom faces into view; the prints on the paper ARE the count, and the child types it. A curved surface rolls but prints nothing flat (a cylinder prints two circles, a sphere nothing). Edges: a turn handle rotates the solid; the child runs a finger along each edge (a trace path; hidden edges show dashed until turned into view) and a traced edge turns ink-blue. Corners: each tap on a vertex leaves a dot. Real-objects setting: a library object is pressed on the pad and its prints are compared with the prints of three solids; the child drags it to the solid that prints the same. Miss 1: the un-inked faces/edges/corners wobble; miss 2: the solid turns once round slowly showing every part. Right: the paper slides out with the full set of prints.
activities.misconception: Counting only the faces/edges you can see (a cube "has 3 faces"): the ink and the turning reveal the hidden ones; a curved surface prints nothing flat (cylinder = 2 faces).
activities.pictures: real-object setting only: toys/ball, dice, blocks; christmas/present, candle; post-office/package; classroom/book; at-the-supermarket/can; music/drum; space/earth; fruits/orange. No real cone or pyramid object exists, so cone and pyramid appear only as drawn solids, never in the real-object match. Solids, pad and paper drawn as apparatus.
activities.settings: Count: faces / edges / corners · Objects: solids only / real objects match
activities.rounds: ≥ 7 solids per count setting (curved solids only in faces/corners), order reshuffled; real-object mode ≥ 8 objects among cube / prism / cylinder / sphere candidates, the right solid's slot balanced across the three.
activities.distinct_from: choice-board.flat-solid only sorts 2D vs 3D; Blueprint (tool #44) builds cube structures, not the parts of a solid. No activity counts solid parts.
activities.risk: Medium: a believable rotating solid in SVG geometry (isometric projection, 2–3 px outlines) is apparatus, not illustration — fine under rule 5, but needs care so hidden edges read as hidden.

activities.title: The Proof Highlighter — Answer from the Story
activities.teaches: Read a short story (3 short paragraphs) and answer who, what, where, when and why questions with a detail found in the text.
activities.invention: The story sits on a page; a question card shows its question word (Who? Where? When? Why?). The answer cards beneath are BLANK until the child drags a yellow highlighter across the sentence that holds the answer; only then the answer cards fill in with words from that sentence and its neighbours, and the child taps one. Highlighting a sentence that does not hold the answer fills the cards with words that do not answer the question word (no person for Who?) — miss 1 rings the paragraph, miss 2 the sentence.
activities.misconception: Answering from memory or the picture instead of the text, and answering a Why? with a What? detail: the highlighter makes the child go back to the text, and the question word decides which kind of answer fits.
activities.pictures: library pictures as one story illustration per story (animals, farm animals, food…); no hand-drawn art
activities.settings: Questions: who/what/where / plus when/why · Story length: 2 paragraphs / 3 paragraphs
activities.rounds: ≥ 7 stories × 3 questions per setting, native-written per locale; answer position among 3 cards balanced; the answer sentence is in a different paragraph across questions.
activities.distinct_from: Marlo's Magnifier finds proof for a character TRAIT; Fable's Picture Stories are 3-picture K stories. This anchors every RL.2.1 answer in a highlighted sentence.
activities.risk: Medium: 7+ native stories × 11 locales is content cost (one native reviewer per locale batch).

activities.title: The Clue Curtain — Who Am I?
activities.teaches: Use informational clues one at a time to narrow down and identify a mystery animal.
activities.invention: Nine library animals stand on a stage. A curtain hides the mystery animal. Clue cards turn over ONE at a time; after each clue the child taps every animal the clue rules out, and those animals step behind a screen. Only after the field is narrowed can the child pull the curtain cord on the last one. Ruling out an animal the clue does not rule out makes it shake its head (it fits the clue); keeping one that does not fit lets the next clue fail visibly.
activities.misconception: Guessing from the first clue, or ignoring a clue (keeping a fish after "it has fur").
activities.pictures: animals / zoo animals / farm animals / ocean life / birds / reptiles and Amphibians
activities.settings: Clues: 3 / 5 · Field: 6 / 9 animals
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 mysteries per setting with clue sets that leave exactly one animal and each clue removing ≥ 1; field positions shuffled.
activities.distinct_from: The Clue Board is a grid deduction about people and things; the curtain is elimination using animal knowledge. No activity does either.
activities.risk: Low–medium: clue sentences native per locale.

activities.title: The Full-Stop Gate — Where Does the Sentence End?
activities.teaches: Split run-together words into sentences, end each with . or ?, and start each new sentence with a capital.
activities.invention: A word train runs along a track: "the dog ran home it was hungry". The child drops a GATE (a full stop or a question mark) between two words; the train splits into two sentences at the gate, and the first car of the new train automatically flips its first letter to a capital. A gate in the wrong place makes two broken sentences that the child can read and see are wrong ("the dog ran. home it…"); a ? gate on a telling sentence or . on an asking one is the second check: the question sentence starts with a question word or flipped verb, and the child chooses the gate shape.
activities.misconception: Putting a full stop at the end of the line instead of where the thought ends; using . for questions; leaving the second sentence lowercase.
activities.pictures: none (word cars are text content); one library picture per item as a meaning cue
activities.settings: Task: add the end mark / choose . or ? / split two sentences · Capitals: flip automatically / child flips them
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 items per task, native-written per locale; the split point falls at different word positions (never always the middle); . and ? balanced in choose mode.
activities.distinct_from: Wally's Capital Crane capitalises NAMES; Dr. Plume's Sentence Clinic repairs grammar; Wiggles' Sentence Builder orders words. Sentence boundaries are not taught.
activities.risk: es: a question takes ¿ … ? — the ? gate in es places a ¿ at the start of its sentence too (the child chooses the shape, the pair is automatic). fr: U+202F before ? and !. de: nouns are capitalised anyway — the flipped first letter is shown by its colour change, and de rounds avoid a noun at the split point. Native-written items ×11.

activities.title: The Rule Stencil — Spelling by the Rule
activities.teaches: Choose the spelling a rule gives by its position in the word (e.g. en: -ck after a short vowel, -k after a long vowel or consonant; -tch/-ch; -dge/-ge; ai inside / ay at the end; -s / -es / -ies) and sort words by rule.
activities.invention: Each word is a row of letter boxes with the rule spot empty; the rule card shows a stencil — a short strip with a POSITION mark (after a short vowel / at the end / inside). The child slides the stencil along the word; it only seats at its position, and the rule letters it carries can only drop into the box where the stencil seats. Picking ay for a middle-of-word gap makes the stencil refuse to seat; ai at the end likewise. Sort mode: picture words drop into two rule bins whose stencils test them.
activities.misconception: Spelling by sound only (both ai and ay say /ai/): the stencil shows the rule is about WHERE the sound is.
activities.pictures: library nouns per rule (duck, cake, watch, bridge, rain, tray…) chosen per locale
activities.settings: Rule pair: per locale list (2–4 pairs) · Task: fill the gap / sort by rule / plurals
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 words per rule pair, half for each spelling; the gap position varies; pictures opened and checked.
activities.distinct_from: Word Doctor's Clinic spells by ear and the Doubling Pond does irregular plurals; neither teaches a positional rule.
activities.risk: Per-locale rule pairs (native-authored, ≥ 8 words each): en -ck/-k, -tch/-ch, -dge/-ge, ai/ay; de -ck/-k and -tz/-z after a short vowel, ie; nl -d/-t at the end (verlengen), ei/ij refused; sv -ck/-k, -mm/-m; da/no double consonant after a short vowel; es c/qu before e/i, z/c before e/i, g/gu; it c/ch, g/gh before e/i; pt c/qu, ç before a/o/u; fr c/ç, g/ge before a/o/u. fi refused (recorded). Pictures opened and checked per locale.

activities.title: The True Caption — Write About the Picture
activities.teaches: Compose complete, true sentences about a picture with a starter and a word bank.
activities.invention: THE CAPTION THAT CHECKS ITSELF AGAINST THE PICTURE. A scene grid (apparatus: a floor and a wall) holds 3–4 library objects in placed relations (a cat on a bed, a ball under a chair). Below, a caption strip and word tiles: starters, nouns from the word bank (with their article from LCSGrammar), position tiles (on, under, next to, in front of) and an end mark. The child builds a sentence; the tiles snap into the only grammatical order frames the engine allows (prepSentence prefix · expected · suffix), so word order and articles are always right — the child's job is the MEANING. Tap Read: each named object lights when it is named and the relation is tested against the scene. True: the caption fills one of three lines on the caption card. False: the named object wobbles at its real place and the false tile lifts. A sentence without a position tile or an end mark does not light. Three different true sentences fill the card; a repeat is refused.
activities.misconception: Writing a list of words instead of a sentence, or writing something not in the picture.
activities.pictures: around the house / furniture / pets / toys placed by the apparatus in a scene grid
activities.settings: Starters: given / free choice · Sentences: 2 / 3 per picture
activities.rounds: 9 scenes built from library objects in randomized relations, each with ≥ 4 different true sentences; the word bank shuffled; no single answer to copy.
activities.distinct_from: Wiggles' Sentence Builder unscrambles a GIVEN sentence; Bramble's Parking Tower places vehicles by position words. This composes original sentences and checks them for truth.
activities.risk: fi postpositions and de dative (handled by LCSGrammar, with its refusals); G2-300 free writing is not reproduced — the activity composes from tiles.

activities.title: The Film Strip — Retell with First, Next, Then
activities.teaches: Retell a four-picture story in order and pick the time-order starter each frame needs.
activities.invention: A FILM STRIP with four empty frames and a reel of four story frames (library pictures composed into simple scenes) out of order. The child drags each picture into a frame, then each frame needs a starter tile (First / Next / Then / At the end) and a short caption tile chosen from two. Pressing Play runs the strip like a little film: the pictures animate in order, so a wrong order shows the story going backwards (the cake eaten before it is baked).
activities.misconception: Ordering by picture position on the reel, and using "Then" for the first event or "First" twice.
activities.pictures: Stories composed only from library pictures in sequences whose order a K-2 child can see: e.g. snow day: weather (snowflake) → winter (snowman) → weather (sunny) → weather (puddle); camping: camping (tent) → camping (campfire) → space (moon) → beach (sun). Stories needing a made state (a baked cake) are refused. The story-line tool's card sets may be reused if (and only if) they are library pictures.
activities.settings: Frames: 3 / 4 · Starters: shown in order / child chooses
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 stories per setting, the reel order shuffled (never already in order); caption choices swap position.
activities.distinct_from: Wake Up, Pip! retells key details to a friend; Dot's Story Spine names start/trouble/fix. The film strip adds temporal sequence words, the W.2.3 skill.
activities.risk: Story supply is the risk: ≥ 8 four-frame stories with an unambiguous order from library pictures; the reviewer refuses any story whose order is not visible. Starter words (First / Next / Then / At the end) ×11 by the native panel.

activities.title: The Fact Cabinet — Animal Fact Files
activities.teaches: Organise true facts about an animal under headings (eats, lives, moves, body covering, babies), and compare two animals' facts as same or different.
activities.invention: A filing cabinet with five drawers, each with an icon heading (food, home, movement, skin/fur/feathers, babies). Fact cards about the round's animal come off a pile; the child files each in its drawer. A card that is TRUE for another animal but not this one does not fit any drawer and slides to a "not this animal" tray — the child must judge truth too. Two-animal mode: two cabinets side by side and a shared middle drawer; facts true for both go in the middle.
activities.misconception: Filing by the word on the card ("lives" in every card) instead of the meaning, and accepting any animal fact as true for this animal.
activities.pictures: animals / zoo animals / ocean life / birds / insects (one large picture per cabinet); heading icons drawn as apparatus
activities.settings: Mode: one animal / compare two · Cards: 5 / 8 with false cards
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 animals per mode with native-checked fact sets; the card order is shuffled and false cards appear at random positions.
activities.distinct_from: Atlas's Fact Files reads one fact for one question; Linc's Fact Chain links two facts; Willow compares stories. Sorting facts into headings and comparing animal facts is not taught.
activities.risk: Headings are written words (eats · lives · moves · body covering · babies) — reading them is part of the G2 task — plus a library picture where one fits (plate, house, feather). Animal facts must be scientifically right in every locale (one science + native reviewer).

activities.title: The Cursive Ribbon — Joined Handwriting
activities.teaches: Form cursive lowercase letters, capitals, the joins between letters and whole words; read words written in cursive.
activities.invention: A RIBBON of ink follows the finger along a ghost path of the letter in the locale's school script. The ribbon never lifts between joined letters: a join stroke connects the end of one letter to the start of the next, and the ribbon only advances when the finger stays inside the path (it frays and stops if the child cuts a corner). Dots on i/j and crosses on t are added last, after the word — they appear as separate small targets that light only when the joined word is complete. Read mode: a cursive word on the ribbon and three library pictures; the child taps the picture.
activities.misconception: Lifting the pen between letters, forming letters separately and joining afterwards, dotting/crossing mid-word.
activities.pictures: library nouns for words and the read mode (animals, fruits, toys)
activities.settings: Level: letters / joins / words / capitals with names · Mode: write (trace) / read cursive
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 items per level from the locale script; read mode answer position balanced across 3 pictures.
activities.distinct_from: Penny's Alphabet Trace and Snippy's Letter Trace are print letters. The ribbon is about joining, which print tracing never asks.
activities.risk: HIGH: per-locale school cursive fonts (Playwrite vendored for 9 locales; sv/fi have no joined school script — refusal as in the worksheets); tracing must follow the font's centre-line path (the letter-tracing centerline precedent). No free handwriting recognition.
absorbed: grade 3 "The Joined Line" (joined-trace): Trace joined (cursive) letters and a short sentence, keeping the pen on the line through each join. — THE JOINED LINE: a sentence in a vendored school cursive font on writing lines; a pen tip waits at the first entry stroke. The child drags along the grey guide; ink follows only while the finger stays within the guide's corridor, and each join between letters is a marked bridge — lifting the finger before a bridge leaves a gap that blinks. When the sentence is done, the inked sentence slides up and a second copy line shows the same sentence as dots only (fading guide) for a second trace.

activities.title: The Crossing Lights — Grid Coordinates
activities.teaches: Find a square from its letter-number code (B2) and name the code of a square, on 5×5 to 10×10 grids.
activities.invention: A grid with letters along the top and numbers down the side. Each letter and number is a LIGHT SWITCH: tapping B lights the whole column B, tapping 2 lights row 2, and the one square where the two beams cross glows. The child paints the crossing square with its group colour; a hidden picture appears square by square. Code mode: a square is already painted; the child switches on the column and the row that cross on it and the code is written from the two switches.
activities.misconception: Reading the code as row-then-column (2B for B2) or counting the label row as square 1.
activities.pictures: none (grid apparatus); the revealed picture is pixel art made of grid squares
activities.settings: Grid: 5×5 / 6×6 / 10×10 · Mode: find the square / write the code
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 rounds = 8 pixel pictures per grid size, each with 6–12 coded squares in random order; codes never repeat; code-mode squares spread across all rows and columns.
activities.distinct_from: Parking Tower teaches position words; no activity uses coordinates.
activities.risk: Low. Letter labels per locale alphabet (A–J is safe in all 11).

activities.title: The Fold Press
activities.teaches: Decide whether a line is a line of symmetry, complete a half-painted grid picture so both halves match (vertical and horizontal lines), and count how many mirror lines a shape has.
activities.invention: THE WET-PAINT PRESS. A square-grid sheet with a crease line; one half is painted in WET paint squares. COMPLETE mode (G2-253, G2-264–268): the child paints squares on the blank half, then pulls the press lever — the sheet folds along the crease and presses the wet half onto the other side like a butterfly blot. Right: every painted square lands on a painted square and the halves lock with a shine. Miss 1: a wrong square shows as a smudge, a missing one as a pale gap, and the sheet unfolds with those squares marked. Miss 2: the mirrored partner of the first wrong square glows. IS-IT-A-MIRROR-LINE mode (G2-247): shapes (shapes theme) and grid pictures carry a dashed line; the child predicts tick or cross, then presses — overhangs show in a second shade if it is not a mirror line. HOW-MANY-LINES mode (G3-342): the child drags a fold line through a shape (it snaps through the centre at 8 angles) and presses; a true mirror line is kept as a crease; when the child taps the count, a not-yet-found line that works is shown on a miss.
activities.misconception: Copying the half picture without flipping it (translating instead of reflecting), counting squares from the wrong edge, and thinking every shape has exactly one (or a diagonal) mirror line (a rectangle has two, not four).
activities.pictures: shapes theme (heart, star, square, rectangle, triangle, hexagon, circle) for line and count modes; grid pictures are painted squares (apparatus); no other art.
activities.settings: Mode: complete the picture / is it a mirror line / how many lines · Line: vertical / horizontal · Grid: 6×6 / 8×8
activities.rounds: 9 half-pictures per grid size (asymmetric halves, 6–14 painted squares, never symmetric about the crease already); line rounds: tick and cross 40–60 %; count rounds cover 0, 1, 2, 4 and many (circle) lines; one right answer.
activities.distinct_from: Split out of fold-mirror (K reflection of pictures). The folding-sheet TOOL lets a teacher fold freely with no task; here a given half must be completed or a given line judged, each with one right answer.
activities.risk: Low. Grid cells ≥ 34 px at 320 (8×8 stacked); the 8-angle snap for the count mode must hit true mirror lines exactly for regular shapes.

activities.title: The Compass Walker — North, East, South, West
activities.teaches: Know the four compass directions on a compass rose and use them to find things on a map.
activities.invention: A town map made of library pictures placed on a grid, with a compass rose whose orange tip points north. A walker stands on a start picture. The child taps a direction on the rose (N/E/S/W letters are the content) and the walker's gaze beam shines that way across the map; the child taps the picture that lies in that direction. Rose mode: the rose is missing letters; the child drags E, S, W onto the arms, and the walker turns to face each one in turn.
activities.misconception: East and west swapped; north always meaning "up the page" even when the map's rose is turned (some rounds rotate the rose 90°).
activities.pictures: Map landmarks: miscellaneous (house), tree (apple tree), vehicles (car, bus), camping (tent, lake, mountain), the compass rose is apparatus (camping/compass refused — its letters are English).
activities.settings: Mode: label the rose / directions on the map · Rose: always up / turned
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 rounds: start points and landmarks shuffled; directions balanced; three candidate pictures, one in the direction asked.
activities.distinct_from: Parking Tower uses above/below/next to; no activity uses compass directions.
activities.risk: Rose letters per locale: en N E S W; de N O S W; fr/es/it N E S O; pt N L S O; nl N O Z W; sv N Ö S V; da/no N Ø S V; fi P I E L. Turned-rose rounds (north not up) only in setting 2.

activities.title: The World Jigsaw — The Continents
activities.teaches: Name and place the seven continents on a world map.
activities.invention: A world map outline (oceans blue) with seven empty continent sockets. Continent pieces in a tray snap only into their own socket (shape-locked). After placing, name tags (native names) drop onto the continents; Name mode: all pieces placed, a numbered continent glows and the child picks its name from a bank.
activities.misconception: Confusing North/South America and Asia/Europe; thinking Australia is a country only.
activities.pictures: space (earth) as cue; library animals (kangaroo, penguin, lion…) as optional continent hints
activities.settings: Mode: place the pieces / name the continents · Hints: animal on each piece / none
activities.rounds: ≥ 7 rounds (each continent asked once per pass), order shuffled.
activities.distinct_from: No geography activity exists.
activities.risk: Blocked on art: a world outline with seven continent pieces and five ocean basins. Locale content: es/pt/it/fr schools often use one "América" (6 continents) and the Olympic 5 — the native panel decides the set per locale. Only 7 + 5 items: rounds must vary which pieces are pre-placed.
absorbed: grade 3 "The World Jigsaw" (world-jigsaw): Locate the seven continents and five oceans on a world map. — THE WORLD JIGSAW: an empty world with ocean blue and continent-shaped holes. The child drags each continent piece into its hole; pieces only seat in their own outline, and a piece held over the wrong hole shows its outline does not fit. Then ocean labels are dropped onto the water: the label floats until it is in the right ocean basin, where it docks. Find mode: a name is given and the child taps the place.
activities.blocked: Continent outline art and ocean basins are not in the library (apparatus from public-domain map data needs an operator ruling), and the continent count differs by locale (es/pt/it/fr schools often teach 5–6 continents with one America).

activities.title: The Measuring Rod
activities.teaches: Multiplication as a equal jumps of b from 0, and division as how many rods of b fit back from N to 0.
activities.invention: THE MEASURING ROD: a wooden rod exactly b units long lies beside a 0-100 number line; the child drags it from 0 and it clicks end to end, each landing lighting its multiple. Lay-out mode: the task asks for 6 rods of 4 — the child lays rods and the landing is read as 6×4. Measure-back mode: the rod starts at N and is laid back toward 0; the count of rods is the quotient (and a gap shorter than the rod is left over if the setting allows). A rod cannot be laid with a gap or overlap — it snaps only to the previous rod's end, so 'jumps of different sizes' is physically impossible. Miss 1: the rods already laid show their count above them; miss 2: the multiples of b under the line get tick dots.
activities.misconception: Counting tick marks instead of jumps (landing on 6×4 by counting 24 single steps), and treating division hops as unequal; the rigid rod makes every jump identical and the count of rods visible.
activities.pictures: none (rod and number line drawn tool-grade); a library animal (frog/kangaroo) may ride the rod end as a marker
activities.settings: Mode: lay out (×) / measure back (÷) · Rod sizes: 2, 5, 10 / any 2-10
activities.rounds: Generated (a,b) pairs with a,b in 2-10, ≥ 9 rounds per mode, no product repeated; the answer is a typed number or a landing tap whose position on the line is spread across the full 0-100 range (measured: landing position decile balanced).
activities.distinct_from: Hopper's Number Line hops variable add/sub amounts and Lily Hops fixes the step at 5/10/100; the rod makes the step a rigid physical length of any size and runs both directions of one structure. Not the Fading Line (K) or Creek Map.
activities.risk: Low; the number line must show 0-100 legibly at 360 px (zoom to the used range).

activities.title: The Story Tray
activities.teaches: Decide from a word problem which number is the number of groups and which the size of each group, then solve by multiplying or dividing.
activities.invention: THE STORY TRAY: the story is the task line (read aloud where TTS works); its two numbers sit as tags in the sentence. Below is a tray with two slots: 'how many groups' (drawn as a row of empty plates) and 'how many in each' (drawn as a scoop showing its count). The child drags each number tag into the slot it describes; the tray then ACTS the story — plates appear and are filled scoop by scoop (multiplying), or a pile is dealt out (sharing) or scooped into groups (grouping). A tag in the wrong slot makes a scene that does not match the story (4 plates when the story said boxes of 4), and the child sees the mismatch before typing the answer.
activities.misconception: Always multiplying the two numbers seen; confusing 'how many groups' with 'how many in each'; treating sharing and grouping as different operations.
activities.pictures: food (cookies, apples, muffins), school (pencils, crayons), toys; plates/boxes drawn tool-grade
activities.settings: Stories: multiply only / divide only (share and group) / mixed · Numbers: tables to 5 / to 10
activities.rounds: Generated story templates × numbers per locale, ≥ 9 rounds, unknown type (product, group count, group size) balanced; typed answer.
activities.distinct_from: Maple's Bakery models division with bare instructions; Vet's Diagnosis Window models K-1 add/subtract stories. The tray adds the decision step from story to model.
activities.risk: Medium: native story templates in 11 locales (reviewer load); reading at grade 3 is fine.

activities.title: The Even Beam
activities.teaches: The equal sign means both sides are the same amount; find the missing number when both sides hold an expression.
activities.invention: THE EVEN BEAM: a balance beam whose two pans hold number blocks whose height is their value (8+4 on the left, a block 5 and an empty socket on the right). The child drags a block from the tray into the socket; the beam tilts by the difference and only levels when the sides are equal. A wrong block (12, the answer 'that comes next') tips the beam far to the right. Miss 2 shows both sides' totals as stacked bars.
activities.misconception: Reading '=' as 'the answer comes next' (8+4 = _ + 5 → 12), or adding all the numbers shown.
activities.pictures: none (beam and blocks drawn tool-grade)
activities.settings: Sides: × and ÷ on both sides (default; 3.OA.A.4) / + and − on both sides · Numbers: tables to 5 / to 10 (sums within 100)
activities.rounds: ≥ 9 per setting: the unknown on either side and in either slot; ≥ 3 rounds where the 'answer comes next' value (12 for 8 + 4 = ▢ + 5, or 24 for 4 × 6 = ▢ × 3) is a tray distractor; tray order shuffled every round; exactly one block levels the beam.
activities.distinct_from: Numbers Court judges given equations (grade 1, within 20); the beam builds a balance with expressions on both sides. Not the Friendship Bridge (balances groups of objects).
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Turntable
activities.teaches: a×b and b×a have the same product: turning an array changes the grouping, not the total.
activities.invention: THE TURNTABLE. An array of identical library pictures (e.g. 3 rows of 5) sits on a round turntable; coloured rails ring each row. The child types the sentence for the array as it stands into three boxes (3 × 5 = 15). Before turning, the child taps a prediction on the table: 'same total' (two equal stacks icon) or 'different' (unequal stacks icon). Then the child drags the turntable's handle a quarter turn: every picture travels with the table but stays upright, the rails now ring the new rows (5 rows of 3), and a count badge fixed to the table never changes during the turn. The child types the second sentence. Wrong 'different' prediction: the badge glows as it rides through the turn unchanged; a wrong product: the rails light one at a time adding a row (5, 10, 15); miss 2 numbers the pictures. Right: both sentences stand side by side with an equals bar between them.
activities.misconception: Believing 3×5 and 5×3 are different amounts (or must be counted again).
activities.pictures: one noun per round from fruits, flowers, toys, insects
activities.settings: Arrays: up to 5×5 / up to 10×10 · Ask: total both times / predict before the turn
activities.rounds: Pairs (a,b) a≠b in 2-10, ≥ 8 rounds; which orientation appears first alternates; answers typed.
activities.distinct_from: Echo Grove teaches that 3 groups of 4 is a different picture from 4 groups of 3; the turntable teaches the product is the same. No existing activity rotates an array.
activities.risk: Low; the turn animation must keep pictures upright (rotate positions, not images).

activities.title: The Array Frame
activities.teaches: Find the unknown factor of a known total and read one array as four related facts.
activities.invention: THE ARRAY FRAME: a box of N counters (library pictures, identical) waits above an empty frame whose number of rows is fixed and shown. The child drags the frame's right edge outward one column at a time; counters pour in row by row. When the frame is too wide the last column hangs half-empty, too narrow and counters stay in the box — the only stopping place where both are clear is the missing factor. Then a cover card slides over one side's label at a time: the four number sentences (r×c, c×r, N÷r, N÷c) are completed by tapping the uncovered numbers, so each fact is read off the same frame.
activities.misconception: Treating division and multiplication as unrelated facts; adding the two given numbers to find the missing factor (24 and 6 -> 30).
activities.pictures: one library picture per round as the box label (fruits, vegetables, toys, insects-and-bugs); the counters inside the frame are identical library pictures only when the total ≤ 30 (cells ≥ 64 px at 360), otherwise drawn apparatus dots in the shell palette
activities.settings: Missing: the columns / either side · Facts: missing factor only / all four facts
activities.rounds: Totals from tables 2-10 with both factors ≥ 2, ≥ 8 rounds, no total repeated; which side is fixed alternates with no streak > 2; numeric answers so position is not a tell.
activities.distinct_from: Build an Array (2.OA.C.4) builds from two given numbers; the frame starts from the TOTAL and one side. Echo Grove only matches a written product.
activities.risk: Medium: a 10×10 frame of pictures must keep pictures ≥ 64 px at 360 — use small counters with a picture legend above; check rule 4 floor.

activities.title: The Table Ladder
activities.teaches: Know a multiplication table: each rung is one group more than the one below, and unknown facts come from known ones.
activities.invention: THE TABLE LADDER. A ladder of ten rungs for the table of n; rung k holds k × n as a bar of k equal groups of n. The anchor rungs (×1, ×2, ×5, ×10) are filled and lit. The task asks for one rung (7 × 6). The child may climb from any lit rung: dragging the '+6' group bar up (or the '−6' bar down) one rung fills that rung's bar and shows its bracket (+6), so 7 × 6 is built from 5 × 6 = 30 in two climbs. At any moment the child types the answer on the keypad. Wrong: the rung does not fill; the bracket from the nearest lit rung to the asked one appears (+6 +6), so the next try is derived, not guessed; miss 2: the asked rung's bar counts its groups by n. Right: the rung fills, lights and stays lit for the rest of the pass, so the ladder fills up over the session. Fluency setting: anchors start dim and climbing is off until a miss.
activities.misconception: Thinking each fact must be memorised alone (or counted from 1); off-by-one-group errors (7×6 = 36).
activities.pictures: none (ladder drawn tool-grade)
activities.settings: Table: 2, 3, 4, 5, 10 / 6, 7, 8, 9 / mixed · Anchors: shown and climbable / dim (fluency)
activities.rounds: All ten rungs of the chosen table(s), asked in reshuffled order, ≥ 10 rounds per pass; answers typed.
activities.distinct_from: Echo Grove interprets products; skip-rod shows multiplication on a line. The ladder is the fluency instrument and its feedback is the neighbouring fact, not a red X.
activities.risk: Low; needs a big readable keypad (shared shell keypad is fine).

activities.title: The Estimate Flags
activities.teaches: Estimate a sum by rounding each addend, then judge whether an exact answer is reasonable.
activities.invention: THE ESTIMATE FLAGS: two cargo numbers (e.g. 48 and 273) each sit on their own number line; the child drags a flag from each to its nearest ten/hundred (the snap is the rounding). The two flags then slide onto one long line and stack end to end, planting an estimate flag (50 + 270 = 320). Then a 'friend's answer' card drops onto the line at its own value — the child taps 'close' or 'far off' by seeing how near it lands to the estimate flag. Miss on a rounding: the halfway mark lights on that line.
activities.misconception: Rounding then forgetting to add, rounding only one addend, and accepting an exact answer that is far from any sensible estimate.
activities.pictures: none (number lines and flags drawn tool-grade)
activities.settings: Round to: nearest ten / nearest hundred · Ask: estimate only / estimate then judge an answer
activities.rounds: Generated addend pairs within 1000, ≥ 9 rounds, the friend's answer is reasonable in ~50% of rounds and the unreasonable ones err by place value (a dropped carry) not random; positions of close/far choices fixed but balanced 4/5.
activities.distinct_from: Halfway Harbors rounds a single number; the flags combine rounding with an estimated sum and a reasonableness check.
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Number Machine
activities.teaches: Find a function rule from input/output pairs and apply it forwards and backwards.
activities.invention: THE NUMBER MACHINE: a machine with a funnel, a rule slot and an output chute; two known pairs come out first as balls. The child slots a rule tile (+3, -4, ×2, ×5...) and drops the test balls back in: the machine runs the child's rule and a ball whose output does not match the known one rolls into a reject bin. With the right rule, the remaining inputs drop through and the child types each output; a final ball comes out of the chute with its input missing, and the child must run the machine backwards (the 'reverse' lever).
activities.misconception: Picking a rule that fits only the first pair; not inverting the rule for an unknown input.
activities.pictures: none (machine drawn tool-grade)
activities.settings: Rules: + and - / also × · Ask: outputs only / outputs and one missing input
activities.rounds: Generated rule per round, ≥ 9 rounds, the two known pairs always ruled so that at least one wrong tile fits the first pair but not the second; tile order shuffled; typed answers.
activities.distinct_from: No machine or rule-finding activity exists; spring-frog has one constant step between neighbours, the machine maps unordered inputs to outputs.
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Spare Sock
activities.teaches: Odd + odd = even, even + odd = odd: decide a sum's parity from the addends without adding.
activities.invention: THE SPARE SOCK: each number is a washing line of socks pegged in pairs; an odd number has one lonely sock left at the end. Two lines are pushed together into one basket: the child predicts 'all paired' or 'one lonely' by tapping, then the lonely socks find each other (two lonely socks pair) and the basket shows the truth. Then bigger numbers appear only as numerals with the ones digit underlined and the socks are hidden — the child decides, and a tap on 'show me' brings the socks back.
activities.misconception: Thinking the sum of two odd numbers is odd; needing to add to know.
activities.pictures: accessories/sock (identical instances per round); washing lines and basket drawn as apparatus
activities.settings: Numbers: up to 20 (socks visible) / up to 1000 (numerals only) · Addends: two / three
activities.rounds: Generated pairs/triples, ≥ 9 rounds, odd and even answers balanced 45-55%, each of the four parity combinations ≥ 2 rounds.
activities.distinct_from: Even or Odd? classifies a single number; the socks show WHY parities combine. Not Partner Bows (K pairs).
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Spring Grasshopper
activities.teaches: Find the constant step of a growing or shrinking number pattern and continue it.
activities.invention: THE STEP SPRING. A row of stepping stones with some numbers shown and some blank; a library grasshopper sits on the first. The child sets the grasshopper's spring with a step dial (+ or −, and the size, including 25, 50, 100) and presses Hop: it hops stone to stone by that step, and at the first stone whose shown number disagrees it misses the stone, tumbles into the grass beside it and hops back to the start — so the wrong step is located, not just rejected. When the spring is right it lands on every shown number; the child then types the blank stones it passed. Miss 2: the difference between two neighbouring shown numbers is drawn as a bracket. Right: the grasshopper makes a last long leap off the end of the row.
activities.misconception: Using the difference of the first two numbers when they are not neighbours, adding when the pattern shrinks, and assuming every pattern grows by 1, 2, 5 or 10.
activities.pictures: forest-creatures/grasshopper as the hopper; stones and the step dial drawn as apparatus
activities.settings: Direction: growing / shrinking / both · Steps: 2-10 / 25, 50, 100
activities.rounds: Generated start and step, ≥ 9 rounds, blanks at varied positions (never only the last), at least 2 rounds where shown numbers are not adjacent; typed answers.
activities.distinct_from: Lily Hops skip-counts with the step given; the spring makes the child discover the step and the splash locates the wrong one. Distinct from skip-rod (multiplication from 0).
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Lantern Square
activities.teaches: Use addition and missing-addend reasoning so every row and column has the same sum.
activities.invention: THE LANTERN SQUARE: a 3×3 grid; at the end of every row and column hangs a lantern holding a bar whose length is that line's current sum, next to a fixed glass marking the magic number. The child drags number tiles from a tray into the empty cells; each lantern's bar grows with the line's sum and lights only when it fills its glass exactly — too high and the bar overflows red. The square is done when all six lanterns are lit.
activities.misconception: Filling one line correctly and breaking a crossing line; guessing instead of computing the missing addend.
activities.pictures: none (grid and lanterns drawn tool-grade)
activities.settings: Magic number: 15 / 30+ (larger numbers) · Empty cells: 2-3 / 4-5
activities.rounds: Rotations/reflections of magic squares scaled and shifted, ≥ 8 rounds, tray holds the exact tiles plus 1 distractor; empty cells spread over rows and columns.
activities.distinct_from: No multi-sum puzzle activity; distinct from even-beam (one equation) and latin-garden (no arithmetic).
activities.risk: One right answer: the generator must prove the filled square is the ONLY arrangement of the tray tiles that lights all six lanterns (brute-force the ≤ 6! placements per round) and drop rounds with two; the distractor tile must fit no cell.

activities.title: The Leftover Dealer
activities.teaches: Divide with a remainder and know the remainder must be smaller than the divisor.
activities.invention: THE LEFTOVER DEALER: a pile of N pictures and d boxes. The child deals with a swipe: each swipe sends one picture to every box (a full round). When the pile has fewer pictures than boxes, the next swipe cannot complete a round — the pictures slide into a leftover cup instead. The child types the quotient (per box) and the remainder (cup). In 'find the error' mode a friend's answer is shown with a cup holding d or more pictures: the cup tips and its pictures deal one more round, showing why the remainder was too big. Exact-or-not mode: the child predicts whether the cup will stay empty before dealing.
activities.misconception: A remainder equal to or bigger than the divisor; writing the remainder as part of the quotient; thinking every division comes out exact.
activities.pictures: fruits, toys, school supplies (identical per round)
activities.settings: Mode: share it out / exact or not / find the error · Divisors: 2-5 / 2-9
activities.rounds: Generated N, d with N ≤ 9d, remainder 0 in ~25% of rounds and 1..d-1 otherwise, ≥ 9 rounds; typed answers.
activities.distinct_from: Maple's Bakery uses exact divisions only; skip-rod measure-back shows a leftover gap but does not teach the remainder rule.
activities.risk: Low; 4.NBT.B.6 is above grade 3 — keep the grade-3 label as the worksheets do.

activities.title: The Piece Stamp
activities.teaches: Given one unit-fraction piece, build the whole: 1/b repeated b times.
activities.invention: THE PIECE STAMP. A single coloured bar labelled 1/3 is a rubber stamp; an empty track runs off to the right with no end mark. The child stamps it end to end along the track; each print adds one piece and a counter under the track reads 1/3, 2/3, 3/3 … The child presses Done when the track holds what they think is the whole. Then the whole bar (labelled 1) slides in under the track: if the prints match it exactly it clicks and glows; too few leave a gap, too many hang over its end. Non-unit setting: the given piece is 2/3 (or 3/4); the child first splits it with a cut tool into its equal unit pieces (the cut only divides into as many equal parts as the numerator), then stamps one unit piece. Miss 1: the gap or the overhang flashes and the counter stays; miss 2: each print is labelled 1/3 and the target 3/3 appears beside the counter. Right: the prints and the whole merge into one bar labelled 1.
activities.misconception: Choosing the longest bar as 'the whole' regardless of piece size, or thinking the whole is always b pieces of any size.
activities.pictures: none (bars drawn tool-grade)
activities.settings: Pieces: 1/2 to 1/4 / 1/2 to 1/8 · Ask: build the whole / build a non-unit amount (a/b from 1/b)
activities.rounds: Generated b 2–8, ≥ 8 rounds, no b twice running; the piece's screen length varies from round to round (a 1/2 piece can be shorter than another round's 1/4), so 'the longest bar' is never a cue; the child builds, so there is no answer position.
activities.distinct_from: Fox Forge builds a/b inside a given whole; the stamp works backwards from the piece to the whole. Distinct from folding-strip and cutting-board.
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Folding Strip
activities.teaches: A fraction a/b is a point on the number line: fold 0-1 into b equal spaces and count a spaces from 0.
activities.invention: THE FOLDING STRIP: a paper strip from 0 to 1 lies on the line. The child taps the fold button b times-worth (or drags a fold-count dial) and the strip folds and unfolds, leaving b-1 creases that become tick marks — equal by construction. Then the child drags a bead from 0 along the creases to a/b; the bead counts SPACES as it passes (a small arc appears over each space crossed). Miss 1 (bead on a tick counted by marks, e.g. 1/4 placed at the second mark) lights the spaces already crossed; miss 2 numbers the spaces.
activities.misconception: Counting tick marks (including 0) instead of the spaces between them, and making unequal parts.
activities.pictures: none (strip, creases and bead drawn tool-grade)
activities.settings: Denominators: 2, 3, 4 / 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 · Line: 0 to 1 / 0 to 2
activities.rounds: Generated a/b with b from the setting and a ≥ 1, ≥ 9 rounds, no fraction repeated, includes a = b (1 whole) at least once and a/b > 1 on the 0-2 setting; answer is a position, balanced across the line by thirds.
activities.distinct_from: No number-line fraction activity exists; Fox Forge and fraction-equiv are area models. Not Halfway Harbors (whole-number rounding).
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Cutting Board
activities.teaches: Compare two fractions of the same whole by size of the pieces (same numerator) or count of pieces (same denominator).
activities.invention: THE CUTTING BOARD. Two identical bars (one whole, visibly the same length) lie on one board. The task gives two fractions. For each bar the child slides a knife-count slider to the denominator — the bar is cut into that many equal pieces, and the pieces visibly shrink as the number grows — and taps the numerator's worth of pieces to lift them. With both amounts lifted, the child taps the bigger fraction's numeral (a prediction). Then the lifted pieces slide down onto a comparison rail, both rows starting at one line, so the longer row is the bigger amount. Right: the longer row glows and the bubble reads '3/4 is more than 2/4'. Wrong: the rail shows the other one longer; the child taps again, and miss 2 labels each piece with its unit fraction. Different-wholes setting: one bar is shorter; the rail now shows 1/2 of the small bar coming out shorter than 1/4 of the big one, and the round asks the child whether that was a fair comparison (same-whole / not-the-same-whole icons).
activities.misconception: Bigger denominator means bigger fraction (1/8 > 1/4); comparing fractions of different wholes.
activities.pictures: none — drawn fraction bars (apparatus blocks); no library food, whose uneven shape would contradict 'equal pieces'
activities.settings: Compare: same denominator / same numerator / mixed · Wholes: always the same / sometimes different
activities.rounds: Generated pairs with b in 2-8, never equal, ≥ 9 rounds; the bigger fraction is on the left in 40-60% of rounds; same-numerator rounds ≥ 3 so the 'bigger number wins' strategy fails.
activities.distinct_from: fraction-equiv finds equal amounts only; Twin Pools / Friendship Bridge compare whole-number groups. The beam is a new comparator, not the Friendship Bridge (which balances counts).
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Time Ribbon
activities.teaches: Find the elapsed time between a start and an end time by counting on hours then minutes.
activities.invention: THE TIME RIBBON: a clock with the start time; a coloured ribbon is tied to the minute hand. The child drags the minute hand round to the end time (shown on a second, small clock); the ribbon unrolls along the rim, and each full turn coils into a one-hour loop beside the clock while leftover minutes stay as a short strip marked in 5s. The child types hours and minutes from the loops and the strip. Miss: the loops and strip get numbers.
activities.misconception: Subtracting the clock numbers (3:45 to 5:15 = 2:30) and counting the hours crossed instead of full hours elapsed.
activities.pictures: none (clock drawn tool-grade; reuse no shared core)
activities.settings: Steps: whole hours / hours and 5 minutes / to the minute · Cross noon: never / sometimes
activities.rounds: Generated start/end pairs, ≥ 9 rounds, durations under 1 h, exactly n h, and n h m min all present; typed answers.
activities.distinct_from: clock-elapsed asks for the END time from a duration; the ribbon asks for the DURATION. Not the Learning Clock tool (free play).
activities.risk: Own core (0 lines to the clock cores). Start/end times appear as digital readouts in each locale's convention (24-hour in de/fr/es/pt/it/nl/sv/da/no/fi; 12-hour in en), so 'cross noon' rounds read 11:30 → 13:15 outside en; the analog face is unchanged.

activities.title: The Half-Mark Ruler
activities.teaches: Measure objects to the nearest half unit and record them on a line plot marked in halves.
activities.invention: THE HALF-MARK RULER: a library object (pencil, leaf, worm-like crayon) lies on a ruler marked in whole and half inches/cm; the child slides the object's end against 0 and reads its length by dragging a marker to the nearest half mark. The measurement then flies down as an X onto a line plot whose axis is the same ruler, stacking above the matching half mark. After 6-8 objects the child answers one plot question (how many are 4 1/2 long? the longest minus the shortest?).
activities.misconception: Treating half marks as whole units, starting the measure at 1 instead of 0, and placing X's between marks.
activities.pictures: classroom/pencil, crayon, marker; spring/leaf; vegetables/carrot, celery; insects-and-bugs/worm; accessories/ribbon; around-the-house/key — each drawn at a set length measured from its ink box
activities.settings: Units: whole and half / quarter marks too · Questions: count only / differences
activities.rounds: Generated lengths with ≥ 40% halves, 7+ objects per round set, ≥ 7 rounds; which plot column is tallest is balanced.
activities.distinct_from: Shelly's Tide-Line (2.MD.D.9) uses whole units only; the half mark and measuring are the new content.
activities.risk: Units per locale: inches with half (and quarter) marks in en; centimetres with half-centimetre marks elsewhere (a cm ruler's mid-marks are real). Object lengths come from the ink box at a fixed px-per-unit, verified by a gate.

activities.title: The Tile Roller
activities.teaches: The area of a rectangle is the number of rows times the tiles in each row.
activities.invention: THE TILE ROLLER: a paint-roller whose drum is exactly one row of unit tiles wide (its width is set to the rectangle's side, shown by tile marks on the drum). The child drags it down the empty rectangle; each pass lays one full row of tiles and clicks a row counter beside it. After 1-2 rows the child is asked how many tiles the whole floor needs and types it; the roller then finishes the rows to check. A miss shows the rows already rolled as a running total of equal parts (6, 12, 18...).
activities.misconception: Counting every tile one by one, or adding the two side lengths (perimeter) instead of multiplying.
activities.pictures: none (tiles and roller drawn tool-grade); optional library floor-themed picture as decoration only
activities.settings: Rectangle sizes: up to 5×5 / up to 10×10 · Stop after: 1 row / 2 rows (how much the child must predict)
activities.rounds: Generated w×h with w,h 2-10, ≥ 9 rounds, no repeated product, never a square in two consecutive rounds; answer typed (keypad).
activities.distinct_from: Patchwork Meadow and Mosaic Menders count tiles one at a time; the roller makes the ROW the unit, which is the multiplicative step. Distinct from array-frame (unknown factor) and quarter-turn.
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Fence Loop
activities.teaches: Rectangles can have the same perimeter and different areas (and the same area with different perimeters).
activities.invention: THE FENCE LOOP: a closed fence loop of a fixed number of rails (say 16) on a peg board. The child drags a corner peg; the loop stays the same length — rails slide around the corner — so stretching one side shrinks the other. Grass tiles fill the inside live and the area readout changes while the rail counter never does. Tasks: make a pen with area 15 using these 16 rails; then 'same grass, new fence': a fixed patch of 12 tiles, rearrange into another rectangle and count the new fence.
activities.misconception: Believing the same fence always encloses the same space (and that bigger perimeter means bigger area).
activities.pictures: farm animals (one animal grazing in the pen as delight)
activities.settings: Fix: the fence / the grass · Board: up to 20 rails / up to 30
activities.rounds: Generated targets with exactly one rectangle solution where possible (or any solution accepted, checked by the model), ≥ 8 rounds, alternating fix-fence/fix-grass on the mixed setting.
activities.distinct_from: Mending Fences measures one given fence; the loop holds perimeter constant while area moves, the exact 3.MD.D.8 contrast.
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Cube Stacker
activities.teaches: Count the unit cubes in a solid, including the ones you cannot see.
activities.invention: THE CUBE STACKER: an isometric tower of unit cubes. The child predicts the total, then lifts the top layer off with a drag (it floats up and lays out flat as a grid of squares, so every cube in that layer is visible), then the next layer, until the tower is all laid out; the layers stack back when released. In build mode the child drops cubes onto a footprint grid to make a tower matching a picture from a corner view, and must fill the hidden back cubes for it to match.
activities.misconception: Counting only the visible faces/cubes and missing hidden ones.
activities.pictures: none (cubes drawn tool-grade)
activities.settings: Solids: boxes (layer × rows × columns) / stepped towers · Mode: count / build
activities.rounds: Generated solids of 4-36 cubes with ≥ 1 hidden cube, ≥ 9 rounds; typed answers.
activities.distinct_from: No volume activity exists; Block Towers (#20) stacks one column per number. The layer lift is new.
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Shape Sieve
activities.teaches: Quadrilaterals share attributes in nested categories: every square is a rectangle and a rhombus.
activities.invention: THE SHAPE SIEVE. A chute drops a shape onto a first sieve that tests 'four straight sides' (each side taps once as it is counted); shapes that fail stay on the top tray. Below, the chute forks into two side-by-side tests: a set-square swings into every corner (four square corners) and a ruler measures every side (four equal sides). Passing the corner test drops it into the RECTANGLE tray, passing the side test into the RHOMBUS tray; a shape that passes both drops through both into the SQUARE tray, which sits under both forks, so the child sees a square land as a rectangle and a rhombus at once. Before the drop the child taps the tray where they predict it will land; then the tests animate. Trays are marked by icons (right-angle mark, equal-side ticks, both); names appear in the bubble. Sort mode: the shape stays on the table and the child drags it onto every name tag that fits (quadrilateral, rectangle, rhombus, square); a fitting tag left empty pulses when Done is tapped. Miss 1: the failing test replays (the gap under the set-square, the ruler's two different lengths); miss 2: the shape's sides and corners get marks. Right: the shape settles in its tray and the bubble lists every name it carries.
activities.misconception: A square is not a rectangle; a tilted square is not a square; a shape belongs to only one category.
activities.pictures: none (shapes and sieves drawn tool-grade)
activities.settings: Shapes: rectangles, squares, rhombuses / also trapezoids and kites · Mode: predict the tray / tap every name
activities.rounds: Generated shapes at varied sizes and rotations, ≥ 9 rounds; the deepest tray balanced across top / rectangle / rhombus / square; squares appear turned (diamond-like) in ≥ 2 rounds and non-square rhombuses in ≥ 2.
activities.distinct_from: Sort by Sides counts sides only; Pip's Museum names shapes in any orientation at K. The sieve teaches the inclusion hierarchy.
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Corner Card
activities.teaches: A right angle is a square corner; other angles are smaller or bigger than it.
activities.invention: THE CORNER CARD: a stiff paper card with one square corner. The child drags it onto any corner of a shape or a picture; it snaps vertex to vertex and rotates to align one side. If the angle is right, the card fits flush and glows; if smaller, the shape's side hides under the card; if bigger, a wedge of light shows between card and side. The child taps every right angle (the 'hunt'), then sorts angles into smaller / right / bigger trays.
activities.misconception: Judging angles by the length of their arms or by orientation (a right angle not drawn upright 'isn't one').
activities.pictures: none (shapes drawn tool-grade); optional library objects with clear corners (book, window, envelope) on a later setting
activities.settings: Angles: right vs not / smaller-right-bigger sort · Orientation: upright / any turn
activities.rounds: Generated shapes with 0-4 right angles, ≥ 9 rounds, right-angle count per shape balanced, arms of varied length so length is not a tell.
activities.distinct_from: No angle activity exists; not the shape sieve (which uses square corners only as one test).
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Word Press
activities.teaches: Build words from a root with suffixes (bake -> baker, baking, baked) and use the form a sentence needs.
activities.invention: THE WORD PRESS: a root word block (bake) sits in a little printing press; suffix stamps (-er, -ing, -ed, -s, and native equivalents) hang above. The child pulls a stamp down; the press prints the new word, applying the spelling change visibly (the e drops, the n doubles in runner) and shows what the word now names: a person picture from the occupations theme for -er, the action for -ing. Person mode: the child prints the person word for a picture. Sentence mode: a sentence with a gap shaped like its job (a person slot, an action slot) waits below; the child prints the form and drags it in — a wrong form does not seat.
activities.misconception: Adding the suffix without the spelling change (bakeer, runer); choosing the root form regardless of sentence role.
activities.pictures: occupations theme (baker, painter, teacher, farmer, singer, swimmer), food for 'bake'
activities.settings: Mode: person words / root family in sentences · Spelling changes: none / with e-drop and doubling
activities.rounds: Native root banks per locale (agent-noun suffixes differ: -er, -eur/-euse, -ero/-era, -dor...), ≥ 8 rounds, which suffix is right balanced.
activities.distinct_from: Sage's Root Garden recognises root families and Marigold's machine applies prefixes/suffixes for meaning; the press builds the form and seats it by sentence role. The two settings are separate round sets (two skills).
activities.risk: Medium: agent-noun morphology differs sharply across the 11 locales (gender in fr/es/it/pt/de); native panel must rebuild each bank.

activities.title: The Doing Stage
activities.teaches: Group verbs into word fields by meaning (ways to move, ways to look) and tell close words apart by what they show.
activities.invention: THE DOING STAGE. A library animal stands on a little stage with a path to the left, a window to the right and a speech spot at the front. Each word card (stroll, dash, tiptoe; glance, stare, peek; whisper, shout, ask) is dragged onto the animal: a go-word makes it travel the path in that manner (dash = fast, tiptoe = small slow steps), a look-word turns it to the window for a short or long look, a say-word puts up a speech bubble (whisper = small dotted bubble, shout = big jagged bubble, ask = bubble with a question tail). SORT mode: the child drops each card on the path, the window or the speech spot. Right: it acts there and the card settles in that field. Miss 1: the animal acts the word in the wrong place, then the card floats back. NUANCE mode (and G2-374): two close words act side by side and the child picks the one that fits a sentence.
activities.misconception: Grouping words by spelling or sound instead of meaning; treating all words in a field as the same (glance = stare).
activities.pictures: one library animal or person per round (forest creatures, animals); stage, path and window drawn tool-grade
activities.settings: Fields: go + look / go + look + say · Mode: sort into fields / pick the closer word
activities.rounds: Native word banks per locale (≥ 12 verbs per field), 9 rounds, field answers balanced; nuance pairs never repeated; one right field or word.
activities.distinct_from: Roary's Roar Meter and Pesto's Soup Stall rank strength within one field; this sorts across fields by meaning and acts each word out.
activities.risk: Medium: the manner animation is the meaning — needs per-verb motion specs; native word fields ×11 (reviewer).

activities.title: The Crossroads Sort
activities.teaches: Classify objects by two attributes at once in a two-circle (Venn) diagram, including the overlap and the outside.
activities.invention: THE CROSSROADS HOOPS. Two overlapping hoops on the floor, each with a gate post carrying its rule as a library picture + glyph (left: "is an animal" = a library animal silhouette; right: "is big" = a big/small pair glyph). Pictures wait in a basket. The child drags a picture into a region (left only, right only, both, outside). Both gates test it: each gate nods or shakes. Right: it rests. Miss 1: it slides to the region where both gates agree, passing through the overlap boundary so the child sees which gate changed its mind; Miss 2: the gate that disagrees glows. Success: all pictures placed, both hoops light.
activities.misconception: Seeing only one attribute (putting a big animal in 'animals' but not in the overlap); thinking the overlap means 'neither'.
activities.pictures: animals, fruits, vehicles, toys at two sizes (scale transform, as in comparing-length)
activities.settings: Rules: kind + size / kind + kind (animals + can fly)
activities.rounds: 9 rounds of 6–8 pictures, every region non-empty, overlap and outside ≥ 1 each round; big/small are scale transforms of one picture; one right region per picture.
activities.distinct_from: All existing sorts (Mim's Baskets, Sort Bins, sort-count) are single-attribute; Ziggy's Odd One Out excludes one item.
activities.risk: Distinct from the sorting-hoops TOOL (hidden rule, teacher-led) because the rules here are given and each placement is checked.

activities.title: The Warm Tube
activities.teaches: Read a thermometer whose scale counts by 2, 5 or 10, including below zero.
activities.invention: THE WARM TUBE: a big thermometer stands beside a scene. The child drags a sun (warm) or an ice cube (cold) toward the bulb; the liquid rises or falls. In read mode the liquid stops at a temperature and the child types it; in set mode the child warms or cools until the liquid top reaches a stated temperature. Only some marks are numbered; the unnumbered marks between count by the scale, and a magnifier the child can drag over the top of the liquid enlarges the nearest marks.
activities.misconception: Counting each unnumbered mark as 1 when the scale counts by 2, and misreading below zero (-5 read as 5).
activities.pictures: weather theme (sun, snowflake, cloud), clothing (coat, swimsuit) for a 'what to wear' delight
activities.settings: Scale: by 2 / by 5 / by 10 · Range: 0 and above / below zero too
activities.rounds: Generated temperatures off the numbered marks in ≥ 60% of rounds, ≥ 9 rounds; read and set alternate on mixed.
activities.distinct_from: Pippa's Pond-Juice Lab reads volume in mL on a scale by 50/100; the warm tube reads small-step scales and negatives. Not the Jar Label (K).
activities.risk: Low.

activities.title: The Orbit Rail
activities.teaches: Order the planets from the Sun and tell the small rocky planets from the giant planets.
activities.invention: THE ORBIT RAIL: the Sun at the left edge and eight orbit rails of increasing radius. The child drags each planet onto a rail; a planet set on a rail already taken bumps the other off, and a planet on its own rail starts orbiting (inner ones faster, so the motion itself encodes order). Sort mode: the planets are shown at true relative size; the child drops each into the rocky or giant tray, and a distractor (Moon, Sun, Pluto as dwarf) goes to 'not a planet'.
activities.misconception: Thinking the planets are evenly spaced or random; calling the Moon or the Sun a planet; Pluto still a planet.
activities.pictures: space (earth, saturn, moon, sun, planet) exist; MISSING/WRONG: accurate Mercury (grey, cratered), Uranus (pale cyan), Neptune (deep blue), plus lcs-pictures labels for mercury, venus, mars, jupiter, uranus, neptune, sun ×11.
activities.settings: Mode: order from the Sun / rocky or giant · Planets: first four / all eight
activities.rounds: ≥ 8 rounds: order rounds give 4-8 planets in shuffled trays and sometimes pre-place one; sort rounds draw 5-6 bodies incl. one non-planet.
activities.distinct_from: No space activity exists.
activities.risk: Blocked on corrected planet art + labels. Pluto appears only as "not a planet" (dwarf planet) and needs a picture too.
activities.blocked: The planet pictures are in the image cache but not in lcs-pictures (no vocabulary labels), and three are scientifically wrong: Mercury is drawn banded like a gas giant, Uranus orange-banded, Neptune dark-banded. A planets activity cannot ship wrong planets.

activities.title: The Water Drop's Journey
activities.teaches: The water cycle: evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection, in order and why each happens.
activities.invention: THE DROP'S JOURNEY: a scene with sea, sun, sky and a hill running down to a river (scene geometry drawn tool-grade, sun/cloud/rain from the library weather theme). A water drop sits in the sea. The child must give the drop what it needs to move: drag the sun's warmth onto the sea and the drop rises as vapour (evaporation); drag it into cold high air and it joins a cloud (condensation); add drops until the cloud is heavy and it rains (precipitation); the drop runs down the hill back to the sea (collection). Each stage's word lands on the scene where it happened. Dragging the wrong cause (cold onto the sea) does nothing but frost the sea's edge. Label mode: words from a bank go onto numbered places.
activities.misconception: Thinking clouds are made of smoke or cotton, that rain comes from nowhere, and getting the stages out of order.
activities.pictures: weather (raindrop as the drop, cloud, rainy, sunny, snowflake); scene (sea band, hill wedge, river line, cold high-air band) is apparatus geometry; ocean-life optional decoration refused (clutter).
activities.settings: Mode: make the drop travel / label the diagram · Words: 4 stages / 4 stages + runoff/ground water
activities.rounds: ≥ 7 rounds: label rounds shuffle which places are blank; journey rounds start the drop at a different stage (sea, cloud, hill) so the child must know what comes next.
activities.distinct_from: No science activity exists; distinct from twin-wheels (life cycles).
activities.risk: Medium: the scene is geometry, but must not read as hand-drawn art (rule 5); the stage words are content and need native terms ×11.
